Model 1:
# Subway Crew Scheduling — MILP Formulations

Below I give a complete, self-contained treatment. Section 1 fixes the data, parameters and the feasible-arc generation rule shared by every variant. Sections 2–5 develop the four requested variants. Section 6 compares them. Section 7 gives the recommended formulation in full, ready to be coded. Section 8 gives the chain-extraction algorithm.

---

## 1. Common data, parameters and feasible arcs

### 1.1 Sets

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $T=\{1,\dots,200\}$ | Driving tasks |
| $S=\{A,M,Z\}$ | Handover stations |
| $\mathcal{A}\subseteq T\times T$ | Feasible precedence arcs (defined in §1.4) |

### 1.2 Task data (given)

For every task $i\in T$:

| Symbol | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{trn}(i)$ | train number | 331 |
| $\mathrm{tid}(i)$ | physical train ID | M16 |
| $p_s(i)\in S$ | pickup station | M |
| $d_s(i)\in S$ | drop-off station | Z |
| $p_t(i)$ | pickup time (min from 10:00) | 3.18 |
| $d_t(i)$ | drop-off time | 57.72 |
| $\delta(i)=d_t(i)-p_t(i)$ | task duration (min) | 54.53 |
| $m(i)$ | mileage (km) | 26.4 |

Mileage table: $m(A\!\to\!M)=m(M\!\to\!A)=17.1$; $m(M\!\to\!Z)=m(Z\!\to\!M)=26.4$. The line is bidirectional, so $m(i)\in\{17.1,26.4\}$.

### 1.3 Numerical parameters

| Symbol | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $\tau_{\min}$ | 30 min | minimum changeover gap |
| $R_{\min}$ | 30 min | break threshold (gap $\ge R_{\min}$ resets continuous-driving counter) |
| $T_c$ | 120 min | max continuous driving |
| $D_{\max}$ | 150 km | max duty mileage |
| $L_{\max}$ | 480 min | max duty span |
| $M_1$ | $T_c$ | big-M for continuous-driving |
| $M_2$ | $D_{\max}$ | big-M for mileage |
| $M_3$ | $L_{\max}$ | big-M for span |

### 1.4 Feasible-arc generation rule

An arc $(i,j)$ is feasible (write $j\in P(i)$ and $i\in S(j)$) iff

$$
d_s(i)=p_s(j)\in S,\qquad p_t(j)\ge d_t(i),
$$

and one of

$$
\bigl[\mathrm{tid}(i)=\mathrm{tid}(j)\ \wedge\ p_t(j)=d_t(i)\bigr]\ \ \vee\ \ \bigl[p_t(j)-d_t(i)\ge\tau_{\min}\bigr].
$$

Define the break indicator

$$
\beta_{ij}=\begin{cases}0 & \text{if }\mathrm{tid}(i)=\mathrm{tid}(j)\text{ and }p_t(j)=d_t(i)\\[2pt] 1 & \text{if }p_t(j)-d_t(i)\ge R_{\min}\\[2pt] \text{undefined} & \text{otherwise (infeasible)}\end{cases}
$$

For every feasible arc $\beta_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$. (Same-train continuation has $\beta=0$; any changeover has $\beta=1$.)

### 1.5 Why subtour elimination is unnecessary

All feasible arcs satisfy $p_t(j)\ge d_t(i)$. Hence the digraph $(T,\mathcal{A})$ is a DAG ordered by pickup time. Any chain (path in this DAG) is automatically acyclic and time-ordered. The standard MTZ / DFJ subtour elimination is therefore not required.

---

## 2. Variant 1 — Arc-based flow with big-M cumulatives

### 2.1 Decision variables

| Variable | Domain | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$ | $(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}$ | 1 if task $j$ immediately follows $i$ in the same duty |
| $s_i\in\{0,1\}$ | $i\in T$ | 1 if task $i$ is a chain start |
| $e_i\in\{0,1\}$ | $i\in T$ | 1 if task $i$ is a chain end |
| $u_i\ge 0$ | $i\in T$ | continuous-driving minutes accumulated since the last real break, ending with task $i$ |
| $v_i\ge 0$ | $i\in T$ | cumulative mileage in the duty ending with task $i$ |
| $w_i\ge 0$ | $i\in T$ | duty start time (pickup time of first task) of the chain containing $i$ |

### 2.2 Objective

$$
\min\ \sum_{i\in T}s_i \qquad\Bigl(=\sum_{i\in T}e_i\Bigr) \tag{V1-OBJ}
$$

### 2.3 Constraints

**Coverage and chaining (flow conservation).**

$$
\sum_{j\in S(i)} x_{ij} + e_i = 1 \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-C1}
$$

$$
\sum_{j\in P(i)} x_{ji} + s_i = 1 \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-C2}
$$

$$
s_i + e_i \le 2 \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-C3}
$$

(C3 allows a single-task duty to be both start and end.)

**Continuous-driving time with break reset.** For each task $i$ and each feasible predecessor $j\in P(i)$:

$$
u_i \ge u_j + \delta(i) - M_1(1-x_{ji}) - M_1(1-\beta_{ji}) \tag{V1-U1}
$$

$$
u_i \ge \delta(i) - M_1(1-x_{ji}) - M_1\,\beta_{ji} \tag{V1-U2}
$$

$$
u_i \le u_j + \delta(i) + M_1(1-x_{ji}) + M_1(1-\beta_{ji}) \tag{V1-U3}
$$

$$
u_i \le \delta(i) + M_1(1-x_{ji}) + M_1\,\beta_{ji} \tag{V1-U4}
$$

$$
u_i \ge \delta(i) - M_1(1-s_i) \tag{V1-U5}
$$

$$
u_i \le \delta(i) + M_1(1-s_i) \tag{V1-U6}
$$

$$
u_i \le T_c \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-U7}
$$

Logic: (U1,U3) activate when $x_{ji}=1,\beta_{ji}=0$ (no break) and force $u_i=u_j+\delta(i)$. (U2,U4) activate when $x_{ji}=1,\beta_{ji}=1$ (break) and force $u_i=\delta(i)$. (U5,U6) activate when $s_i=1$ and force $u_i=\delta(i)$.

**Cumulative mileage.** For each $j\in P(i)$:

$$
v_i \ge v_j + m(i) - M_2(1-x_{ji}) \tag{V1-V1}
$$

$$
v_i \le v_j + m(i) + M_2(1-x_{ji}) \tag{V1-V2}
$$

$$
v_i \ge m(i) - M_2(1-s_i) \tag{V1-V3}
$$

$$
v_i \le m(i) + M_2(1-s_i) \tag{V1-V4}
$$

$$
v_i \le D_{\max} \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-V5}
$$

**Duty span.** Let $\sigma_i = p_t(i)$ (start of task $i$) and $\eta_i = d_t(i)$ (end of task $i$). For each $j\in P(i)$:

$$
w_i \ge w_j - M_3(1-x_{ji}) \tag{V1-W1}
$$

$$
w_i \le w_j + M_3(1-x_{ji}) \tag{V1-W2}
$$

$$
w_i \ge p_t(i) - M_3(1-s_i) \tag{V1-W3}
$$

$$
w_i \le p_t(i) + M_3(1-s_i) \tag{V1-W4}
$$

$$
d_t(i) - w_i \le L_{\max} \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-W5}
$$

### 2.4 Discussion

* **Strengths.** Single MILP, no column generation, DAG makes it cycle-free, big-M values are tight ($T_c,D_{\max},L_{\max}$).
* **Weaknesses.** Each arc generates 4 big-M inequalities for $u$, 2 for $v$, 2 for $w$. With $|\mathcal{A}|\sim 10^4$ this is $\sim 8\times 10^4$ rows; LP relaxation is moderately weak because of the big-M links, but integrality is excellent in practice because the DAG forces a topological ordering.
* **Size.** $\sim 200$ binaries for $s,e$, $\sim 10^4$ binaries for $x$, $\sim 600$ continuous cumulatives. Solves in seconds with CPLEX/Gurobi.

---

## 3. Variant 2 — Set-partitioning with column generation

### 3.1 Master problem (MP)

Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the (exponentially large) set of feasible chains. A *feasible chain* is a path $p=(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_k)$ in the DAG such that

* every consecutive pair is in $\mathcal{A}$,
* $\sum_{r=1}^k \delta(i_r)\le T_c$ between any two consecutive real breaks (i.e. cumulative driving between $\beta=1$ arcs $\le T_c$),
* $\sum_{r=1}^k m(i_r)\le D_{\max}$,
* $d_t(i_k)-p_t(i_1)\le L_{\max}$.

Variables $y_p\in\{0,1\}$ for $p\in\mathcal{P}$.

$$
\min \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}} y_p \tag{V2-OBJ}
$$

$$
\sum_{p\ni i} y_p = 1 \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V2-COV}
$$

### 3.2 Pricing subproblem (PSP)

For dual prices $\pi_i$ (one per task), find a feasible chain $p$ with negative reduced cost $1-\sum_{i\in p}\pi_i$. This is a *shortest path with resource constraints* on the DAG with resources

* cumulative duration $\Delta$ (reset to $\delta(i)$ on every break arc, $\le T_c$),
* cumulative mileage $M$ (no reset, $\le D_{\max}$),
* duty span $L$ (no reset, $\le L_{\max}$).

Solve by dynamic programming or label-setting with dominance. Each generated column is appended to $\mathcal{P}$ until no negative-reduced-cost column exists; then solve the integer MP (or branch-and-price).

### 3.3 Equivalent compact arc formulation

By Dantzig–Wolfe decomposition, the LP relaxation of (V2) equals the LP relaxation of (V1). The integer versions are equivalent because the DAG forbids cycles, so the convexity constraints are not needed.

### 3.4 Discussion

* **Strengths.** Tightest LP relaxation (often integral for this problem class); scales to millions of tasks.
* **Weaknesses.** Requires implementing a pricing solver, branching strategy, and column management. Overkill for 200 tasks.

---

## 4. Variant 3 — Driver-indexed / time-indexed formulation

Let $K$ be an upper bound on the number of drivers (e.g. $K=200$). Discretise time in 1-minute slots $t\in\{0,1,\dots,T_{\max}\}$ with $T_{\max}=360$.

### 4.1 Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $a_{ki}\in\{0,1\}$ | driver $k$ performs task $i$ |
| $z_{kt}\in\{0,1\}$ | driver $k$ is on duty at minute $t$ |
| $g_{kt}\in\{0,1\}$ | driver $k$ is driving at minute $t$ |
| $b_k\in\{0,1\}$ | driver $k$ is used |

### 4.2 Constraints

**Coverage:**

$$
\sum_{k=1}^K a_{ki}=1 \quad \forall i \tag{V3-COV}
$$

**Driving implies on-duty:**

$$
g_{kt}\le z_{kt} \quad \forall k,t \tag{V3-DOD}
$$

**Task coverage in time:**

$$
\sum_{t=p_t(i)}^{d_t(i)-1} g_{kt} \ge \delta(i)\,a_{ki} \quad \forall k,i \tag{V3-TIME}
$$

(Forces driver $k$ to be driving during the whole task if assigned.)

**Continuous driving ≤ $T_c$:** for every $t$ and every window of length $T_c$,

$$
\sum_{s=t}^{t+T_c-1} g_{ks} \le T_c + M_1(1-b_k) \quad \forall k,t \tag{V3-CD}
$$

(Trivially satisfied if driver $k$ unused.)

**Break reset:** if gap between consecutive tasks of driver $k$ is $\ge R_{\min}$, the counter resets. This is enforced implicitly by (V3-CD) only if we ensure that "non-driving on-duty" minutes are excluded. Replace $g_{ks}$ by a *driving-since-last-break* counter $c_{kt}$ with $c_{kt+1}=(c_{kt}+1)\cdot g_{kt}$ and $c_{kt+1}\le g_{kt}\cdot T_c$ etc.

**Mileage:** $\sum_i m(i)\,a_{ki}\le D_{\max}$ for all $k$.

**Span:** for each driver $k$, $\max_i\{d_t(i):a_{ki}=1\}-\min_i\{p_t(i):a_{ki}=1\}\le L_{\max}$.

**Driver-count linkage:**

$$
\sum_{k=1}^K b_k \le \sum_{k=1}^K a_{ki}\ \text{(any }i\text{)};\quad b_k\ge a_{ki}\ \forall k,i \tag{V3-LINK}
$$

### 4.3 Objective

$$
\min \sum_{k=1}^K b_k \tag{V3-OBJ}
$$

### 4.4 Discussion

* **Strengths.** Very flexible; can encode complex labour rules (overtime, breaks, days off) by adding columns of $z_{kt},g_{kt}$.
* **Weaknesses.** Huge: $K\cdot T_{\max}\approx 200\cdot 360=72{,}000$ binaries for $z$ alone, plus $K\cdot |T|=40{,}000$ for $a$. Symmetry between drivers requires ordering constraints or driver-indexed branching. LP relaxation is weak due to time-indexing.
* **Verdict.** Not recommended for this problem size.

---

## 5. Variant 4 — Time-expanded network + flow-based

Build a time-expanded DAG whose nodes are the 200 tasks plus a source $\alpha$ and sink $\omega$.

### 5.1 Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $f_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$ | one driver flows from task $i$ to task $j$ |
| $f_{\alpha i}\in\{0,1\}$ | task $i$ is a chain start |
| $f_{i\omega}\in\{0,1\}$ | task $i$ is a chain end |

### 5.2 Constraints

**Flow conservation at every task node:**

$$
f_{\alpha i} + \sum_{j\in P(i)} f_{ji} = \sum_{j\in S(i)} f_{ij} + f_{i\omega} = 1 \quad \forall i \tag{V4-FC}
$$

**Resource cumulatives** carried on each arc, identical in form to (V1-U/V/W) but with $f$ replacing $x$ and $f_{\alpha i}$ replacing $s_i$.

**Objective:**

$$
\min \sum_{i\in T} f_{\alpha i} \tag{V4-OBJ}
$$

### 5.3 Discussion

* Mathematically equivalent to Variant 1 (the $f$ variables are just a re-labelling of $x,s,e$).
* Useful pedagogically: it makes the "one unit of flow = one driver" interpretation explicit.
* Same size and LP strength as V1.

---

## 6. Comparison

| Criterion | V1 Arc-bigM | V2 Set-partition | V3 Driver-indexed | V4 Flow |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Variables | $\sim 10^4$ bin + 600 cont | columns (unbounded) | $\sim 10^5$ bin | $\sim 10^4$ bin |
| Constraints | $\sim 8\cdot 10^4$ | $|\mathcal{P}|$ columns + 200 cover | $\sim 10^6$ | $\sim 8\cdot 10^4$ |
| LP relaxation | moderate (big-M) | tightest | weak | moderate |
| Integrality | excellent (DAG) | excellent | needs symmetry breaking | excellent |
| Implementation effort | low | high (pricing) | medium | low |
| Scales to 200 tasks | **yes, seconds** | yes, but overkill | heavy | yes |

## 7. Recommendation: Variant 1

For 200 tasks the arc-based big-M formulation is the right tool: a single MILP, tight big-M values, DAG structure, and standard solvers handle it in seconds. The set-partitioning variant would dominate only at thousands of tasks. I now give the **complete final model** with all numeric parameters.

### 7.1 Sets and parameters

$$
\begin{aligned}
T&=\{1,\dots,200\},\quad S=\{A,M,Z\},\quad \mathcal{A}\subseteq T\times T \text{ (from §1.4)}\\[2pt]
\tau_{\min}&=30,\ R_{\min}=30,\ T_c=120,\ D_{\max}=150,\ L_{\max}=480\\[2pt]
M_1&=120,\ M_2=150,\ M_3=480\\[2pt]
\delta(i)&=d_t(i)-p_t(i),\quad m(i)\in\{17.1,26.4\}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 7.2 Variables

$$
\begin{aligned}
&x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\ \ (i,j)\in\mathcal{A}\\
&s_i,\,e_i\in\{0,1\}\ \ i\in T\\
&u_i\ge 0,\ v_i\ge 0,\ w_i\ge 0\ \ i\in T
\end{aligned}
$$

### 7.3 Objective

$$
\boxed{\min\ \sum_{i\in T} s_i}
$$

### 7.4 Constraints

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\textbf{(1) Coverage — exactly one predecessor or a start:}\\
&\sum_{j\in P(i)} x_{ji} + s_i = 1 &&\forall i\in T\\[4pt]
&\textbf{(2) Coverage — exactly one successor or an end:}\\
&\sum_{j\in S(i)} x_{ij} + e_i = 1 &&\forall i\in T\\[4pt]
&\textbf{(3) Single-task duties allowed:}\\
&s_i + e_i \le 2 &&\forall i\in T\\[4pt]
&\textbf{(4) Continuous driving (reset on break):}\\
&u_i \ge u_j + \delta(i) - 120(1-x_{ji}) - 120(1-\beta_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&u_i \ge \delta(i) - 120(1-x_{ji}) - 120\,\beta_{ji} &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&u_i \le u_j + \delta(i) + 120(1-x_{ji}) + 120(1-\beta_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&u_i \le \delta(i) + 120(1-x_{ji}) + 120\,\beta_{ji} &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&u_i \ge \delta(i) - 120(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&u_i \le \delta(i) + 120(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&u_i \le 120 &&\forall i\\[4pt]
&\textbf{(5) Cumulative mileage:}\\
&v_i \ge v_j + m(i) - 150(1-x_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&v_i \le v_j + m(i) + 150(1-x_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&v_i \ge m(i) - 150(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&v_i \le m(i) + 150(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&v_i \le 150 &&\forall i\\[4pt]
&\textbf{(6) Duty span:}\\
&w_i \ge w_j - 480(1-x_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&w_i \le w_j + 480(1-x_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&w_i \ge p_t(i) - 480(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&w_i \le p_t(i) + 480(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&d_t(i) - w_i \le 480 &&\forall i
\end{aligned}
$$

### 7.5 Optional fairness tie-breaker

Add a second objective (lexicographic) or a max-min workload term:

$$
\max\ \min_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\Bigl(\sum_{i\in c}\delta(i)\Bigr)
$$

or equivalently, with $W$ a scalar and $\theta$ an auxiliary variable,

$$
\max\ \theta\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \theta \le \sum_{i\in T}\delta(i)\,a_{ci}\ \forall c
$$

where $a_{ci}$ is the indicator of task $i$ belonging to chain $c$. In practice, since the chains are not pre-computed, encode this with chain-start variables: $\theta\le \sum_{i\in T}\delta(i)\,s_i\cdot K - \sum_i \delta(i)\,s_i$ … a simpler proxy is to add a small penalty $\varepsilon\sum_i v_i$ to the objective so the solver spreads mileage across drivers.

|---|---|---|
| $\tau_{\min}$ | 30 min | given |
| $R_{\min}$ | 30 min | given |
| $T_c$ | 120 min | given |
| $D_{\max}$ | 150 km | given |
| $L_{\max}$ | 480 min | given |
| $M_1$ | 120 | $=T_c$ |
| $M_2$ | 150 | $=D_{\max}$ |
| $M_3$ | 480 | $=L_{\max}$ |
| $m(A\!\leftrightarrow\!M)$ | 17.1 km | given |
| $m(M\!\leftrightarrow\!Z)$ | 26.4 km | given |

## 8. Chain-extraction algorithm

After the MILP is solved (binary variables fixed):

```
Input:  x*, s*, e*, u*, v*, w*
Output: list of chains C = {c_1,...,c_K}; K = number of drivers

1.  K := sum(s*)                              # number of drivers
2.  Build adjacency list Adj(i) := {j : x*_{ij} = 1}
3.  Starts := {i : s*_i = 1}
4.  For each i in Starts:
        chain := []
        cur := i
        while cur is not None:
            chain.append(cur)
            nxt := the unique j in Adj(cur)   # at most one by (V1-C1)
            cur := nxt
        C.append(chain)
5.  Sanity checks:
        - every task appears in exactly one chain
        - |C| = K
        - for each chain c: sum(m(i)) ≤ 150, d_t(last)-p_t(first) ≤ 480,
          and for every pair of consecutive tasks the break rule holds
6.  Print connection table: rows = (chain_id, task_index, position,
        task_id, train, pu_station, pu_time, do_station, do_time,
        gap_to_next_min, same_train_as_next, break_after)
```

The connection table row for task $i$ contains:

| Column | Value |
|---|---|
| chain | $\#c$ such that $i\in c$ |
| pos | position within chain (1-based) |
| task | $i$ |
| train | $\mathrm{trn}(i)$ |
| tid | $\mathrm{tid}(i)$ |
| pu_st, pu_t | $p_s(i), p_t(i)$ |
| do_st, do_t | $d_s(i), d_t(i)$ |
| next_task | $j$ with $x^*_{ij}=1$, or `END` |
| gap_min | $p_t(j)-d_t(i)$ |
| same_train | $\mathrm{tid}(i)=\mathrm{tid}(j)$ |
| break | $\beta_{ij}$ |
| cum_u | $u^*_i$ |
| cum_v | $v^*_i$ |
| cum_w | $w^*_i$ |

This table is the deliverable: it gives the optimal task chains (one row per task, grouped by chain), the number of drivers $K=\sum s_i^*$, and a complete audit trail showing where every break, every same-train continuation, and every resource cumulative stands.

---

### Final notes

* The DAG property (all arcs go forward in pickup time) is what makes subtour elimination unnecessary and what guarantees that the chain-extraction algorithm terminates and is unique.
* Big-M values are tight because they equal the natural upper bounds of the cumulatives; this keeps the LP relaxation close to integer.
* For 200 tasks and $|\mathcal A|\approx 10^4$, modern MILP solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi, HiGHS) return the proven optimum in well under a minute on a laptop.
* If the instance grows (e.g. a full day with 1500 tasks), switch to Variant 2 with column generation; the pricing subproblem is a label-setting shortest path with three resources (continuous driving, mileage, span) and runs in milliseconds.

# Subway Crew (Driver) Scheduling — MILP Formulations

Below I give a complete treatment. Section 1 fixes the common data model; Sections 2–5 give the four variants you asked for; Section 6 compares them; Section 7 is the recommended formulation with every equation, every parameter value, the arc-generation rule, and the chain-extraction algorithm.

---

## 1. Common data model (used by every variant)

### 1.1 Sets
- **I** = {1, …, 200} — driving tasks.
- **S** = {A, M, Z} — attendance / handover stations.
- **A ⊆ I × I** — feasible predecessor→successor arcs (rule in §7.2).

### 1.2 Task parameters (read directly from the task table)
For every i ∈ I:
- `t_pu(i)` — pickup clock time (minutes from 10:03, i.e. integer minutes).
- `t_do(i)` — drop-off clock time.
- `s_pu(i), s_do(i) ∈ S` — pickup / drop-off station.
- `trainID(i)` — physical train (e.g. M16, N23, L06, …).
- `dur(i) = t_do(i) − t_pu(i)` — driving time of the task (35–55 min).
- `dist(i)` — mileage of the task = mileage(s_pu(i), s_do(i)) ∈ {17.1, 26.4}.

### 1.3 Mileage table (km, symmetric)
| from \ to | A | M | Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 0 | 17.1 | — |
| **M** | 17.1 | 0 | 26.4 |
| **Z** | — | 26.4 | 0 |

### 1.4 Global parameters (numeric)
| Symbol | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| τ_min | 30 min | minimum changeover / walking time |
| R_min | 30 min | gap that counts as a real break |
| T_c | 120 min | max continuous driving before a break |
| D_max | 150 km | max duty mileage |
| L_max | 480 min | max duty span |
| M₁ | T_c = 120 | big-M for continuous-driving |
| M₂ | D_max = 150 | big-M for mileage |
| M₃ | L_max = 480 | big-M for duty span |

### 1.5 Derived arc parameters (constants, not variables)
For every (i, j) ∈ A:
- `gap(i,j) = t_pu(j) − t_do(i)`.
- `reset(i,j) = 1` if `gap(i,j) ≥ R_min`, else `0`.
- `same(i,j) = 1` if `trainID(i) = trainID(j)` and `t_pu(j) = t_do(i)`, else `0`.

### 1.6 DAG justification (no subtour elimination needed)
Every feasible arc (i, j) satisfies `t_pu(j) ≥ t_do(i)` (strict for normal changeovers, equal only for same-train continuations). Hence the arc graph is a DAG ordered by pickup time. Any feasible chain is a path in this DAG, so cycles are impossible and no MTZ / DFJ subtour constraints are required.

---

## 2. Variant 1 — Arc-based flow formulation with big-M cumulatives (RECOMMENDED)

### 2.1 Decision variables
| Variable | Domain | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| x[i,j] | {0,1} | 1 if task j is performed immediately after task i by the same driver |
| s[i] | {0,1} | 1 if task i is the **start** of a driver duty |
| e[i] | {0,1} | 1 if task i is the **end** of a driver duty |
| f[i] | [0, T_c] | continuous driving time accumulated since the last real break, measured at the **drop-off** of task i |
| m[i] | [0, D_max] | total mileage in the duty up to and including task i |
| b[i] | ℝ | pickup time of the **first** task in the duty that ends at task i |

### 2.2 Objective
```
(OBJ)   minimize  Σ_{i∈I} s[i]
```
(Number of drivers = number of chain starts = number of chain ends.)

### 2.3 Constraints

**(C1) Coverage — every task is performed exactly once**
```
Σ_{j:(i,j)∈A} x[i,j] + e[i] = 1        ∀ i ∈ I
```
Each task has exactly one successor or is a chain end.

**(C2) Predecessor — at most one predecessor**
```
Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i] + s[i] = 1        ∀ i ∈ I
```
Each task has exactly one predecessor or is a chain start.

**(C3) Arc feasibility (implicit)**
Variables x[i,j] are only created for (i,j) ∈ A; for all other pairs the variable does not exist (equivalent to fixing it to 0).

**(C4) Number of drivers consistency**
```
Σ_{i∈I} s[i] = Σ_{i∈I} e[i]
```
(Automatically satisfied by (C1)+(C2) and flow conservation; stated explicitly for clarity.)

**(C5) Continuous driving time — start case**
```
f[i] ≤ dur(i) + M₁ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]        ∀ i ∈ I
f[i] ≥ dur(i) − M₁ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]        ∀ i ∈ I
```
If i has no predecessor (chain start) the RHS collapses to dur(i), forcing f[i] = dur(i). If i has a predecessor the constraint is non-binding (M₁ large enough).

**(C6) Continuous driving time — carry-over arc (no reset, reset(i,j)=0)**
```
f[i] ≤ f[j] + dur(i) + M₁·(1 − x[i,j])           ∀ (i,j) ∈ A with reset(i,j)=0
f[i] ≥ f[j] + dur(i) − M₁·(1 − x[i,j])           ∀ (i,j) ∈ A with reset(i,j)=0
```
When x[i,j]=1 this forces f[j] = f[i] + dur(j).

**(C7) Continuous driving time — reset arc (reset(i,j)=1)**
```
f[i] ≤ dur(i) + M₁·(1 − x[i,j])                  ∀ (i,j) ∈ A with reset(i,j)=1
f[i] ≥ dur(i) − M₁·(1 − x[i,j])                  ∀ (i,j) ∈ A with reset(i,j)=1
```
When x[i,j]=1 this forces f[j] = dur(j) (counter reset by the break).

**(C8) Continuous driving upper bound**
```
f[i] ≤ T_c                                        ∀ i ∈ I
```

**(C9) Mileage — start case**
```
m[i] ≤ dist(i) + M₂ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]       ∀ i ∈ I
m[i] ≥ dist(i) − M₂ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]       ∀ i ∈ I
```

**(C10) Mileage — carry-over**
```
m[i] ≤ m[j] + dist(i) + M₂·(1 − x[i,j])          ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
m[i] ≥ m[j] + dist(i) − M₂·(1 − x[i,j])          ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
```

**(C11) Mileage upper bound**
```
m[i] ≤ D_max                                      ∀ i ∈ I
```

**(C12) Duty span — start time of chain ending at i**
```
b[i] ≤ t_pu(i) + M₃ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]       ∀ i ∈ I
b[i] ≥ t_pu(i) − M₃ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]       ∀ i ∈ I
b[i] ≤ b[j] + M₃·(1 − x[i,j])                    ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
b[i] ≥ b[j] − M₃·(1 − x[i,j])                    ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
```

**(C13) Duty span upper bound**
```
t_do(i) − b[i] ≤ L_max                            ∀ i ∈ I
```

**(C14, optional) Fairness tie-breaker**
Introduce W = max workload (mileage) and minimize it lexicographically:
```
W ≥ m[i]                                          ∀ i ∈ I
```
Use W as a secondary objective after (OBJ). Equivalently minimize Σ m[i]² via piecewise-linear approximation, or impose `m[i] ≤ W` and minimize W.

### 2.4 Strengths / weaknesses of Variant 1
- **Strengths**: single MILP, no column generation, DAG makes subtour elimination unnecessary, big-M values are the natural resource bounds (tight), model size ~ |A| binary + 3|I| continuous.
- **Weaknesses**: LP relaxation can be marginally loose on the cumulative constraints (mitigated because M₁, M₂, M₃ are tight resource caps); for |I|=200 the number of arcs |A| is at most a few thousand — entirely tractable.

---

## 3. Variant 2 — Set-partitioning / column-generation formulation

### 3.1 Master problem
Let **P** = set of all **feasible chains** (paths in the DAG that satisfy C5–C13). For p ∈ P let `a[i,p] = 1` if task i ∈ p.

Variables: `y[p] ∈ {0,1}`, 1 if chain p is selected.

```
(OBJ-MP)   minimize  Σ_{p∈P} y[p]
(COVER)    Σ_{p∈P} a[i,p] · y[p] = 1                ∀ i ∈ I
```
(Number of drivers = Σ y[p] automatically.)

### 3.2 Pricing subproblem (resource-constrained shortest path on the DAG)
Find a feasible chain with negative reduced cost π[i] (dual of COVER):

```
minimize   Σ_{(i,j)∈A} c[i,j] · x[i,j] − Σ_{i∈I} π[i] · u[i]
s.t.       x, f, m, b, s, e satisfy C1–C13 (single-chain version)
```
This is a **label-setting shortest path** with resources (continuous driving time, mileage, span). Solved by dynamic programming over the DAG with dominance pruning. Each iteration adds one or more columns with negative reduced cost.

### 3.3 Equivalent compact arc formulation
Drop the chain variables, keep x[i,j], s[i], e[i] and add **one** cumulative variable per resource that is **scoped to a single chain** (use acommodity flow with |D| copies, one per driver). For 200 tasks this is impractical without D being endogenous — hence column generation.

### 3.4 Strengths / weaknesses
- **Strengths**: LP relaxation of the master is typically very tight; standard in crew scheduling literature.
- **Weaknesses**: requires an LP solver + a custom pricing oracle; convergence can be slow when many resources interact; integer round-off after column generation often needs a final MIP solve (branch-and-price).

---

## 4. Variant 3 — Time-indexed / time-discretized formulation

### 4.1 Discretization
Time grid T = {0, 1, …, T_max} minutes (T_max = 360, covering 10:03–15:58 + buffer). Let D = {1, …, D_ub} be a sufficient upper bound on drivers (e.g. D_ub = 200).

### 4.2 Variables
- `z[d,i] ∈ {0,1}` — driver d performs task i.
- `on[d,t] ∈ {0,1}` — driver d is on duty at minute t.
- `drv[d,t] ∈ {0,1}` — driver d is actively driving at minute t.
- `brk[d,t] ∈ {0,1}` — driver d is on a real break (gap ≥ 30 min) at minute t.
- `s_duty[d] ∈ {0,1}`, `e_duty[d] ∈ {0,1}` — driver d has any duty / has finished.

### 4.3 Key constraints (sketch)
```
Σ_{d∈D} z[d,i] = 1                                   ∀ i ∈ I
Σ_{i: t∈[t_pu(i),t_do(i))} z[d,i] = drv[d,t]         ∀ d,t
drv[d,t] ≤ on[d,t]                                   ∀ d,t
Σ_{τ=t−29}^{t} drv[d,τ] ≥ 30·brk[d,t]                ∀ d,t   (break detection)
f[d,t] = Σ_{τ=t−119}^{t} drv[d,τ] − 120·brk[d,t]     ∀ d,t
f[d,t] ≤ 120                                          ∀ d,t
Σ_{i} dist(i)·z[d,i] ≤ 150                           ∀ d
Σ_{t} on[d,t]·(last−first) ≤ 480                     ∀ d
```

### 4.4 Strengths / weaknesses
- **Strengths**: very general, easy to add shift pay, overtime, breaks of arbitrary length.
- **Weaknesses**: model size is O(|D|·T) ≈ 200·360 = 72 000 binary variables even before tasks; LP relaxation is extremely loose; impractical for 200 tasks without aggressive aggregation.

---

## 5. Variant 4 — Time-expanded network + flow-based formulation

### 5.1 Network
- Source σ, sink τ.
- For each task i: node i with capacity 1 (split i⁻ → i⁺ with arc of capacity 1, cost 0).
- Arc σ → i with capacity 1, cost 0 (start a duty at i).
- Arc i → τ with capacity 1, cost 0 (end a duty at i).
- Arc i → j for every (i,j) ∈ A with capacity 1, cost 0.

### 5.2 Variables and objective
- `flow[arc]` ≥ 0 integer.
- `x[i,j]`, `s[i]`, `e[i]` derived from flow values.
- Cumulative variables f[i], m[i], b[i] as in Variant 1.

```
minimize  Σ_{i∈I} flow[σ → i]
s.t.      flow conservation at every i⁻ and i⁺
          capacity 1 on every task node
          C5–C13 on the chosen arcs
```

### 5.3 Strengths / weaknesses
- **Strengths**: elegant; the number of drivers is the value of the σ→τ flow; subtour prevention is unnecessary because of the DAG.
- **Weaknesses**: cumulative resource constraints still need big-M (or resource-constrained shortest-path subproblem); essentially equivalent to Variant 1 in modelling power, slightly more variables (σ, τ nodes).

## 6. Comparison

| Criterion | V1 Arc-big-M | V2 Set-partitioning | V3 Time-indexed | V4 Flow |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Variables (200 tasks) | ~3 000 bin + 600 cont | exponential in |P| | ~70 000 bin | ~3 000 bin + 600 cont |
| Constraints | ~10·|A| | |cover| + pricing | O(|D|·T) | ~10·|A| |
| LP relaxation tightness | tight (M = resource cap) | very tight | very loose | tight |
| Solver needed | MILP (CPLEX/Gurobi/HiGHS) | LP + pricing + branch-and-price | MILP | MILP |
| Implementation effort | low | high | medium | low |
| Scalability to 200 tasks | excellent | excellent | poor | excellent |
| Handles all constraints (1)–(8) | yes | yes | yes | yes |

**Recommendation: Variant 1.** It is a single, compact MILP that any modern solver will solve to proven optimality in seconds for 200 tasks, the big-M values are the natural resource caps (so the LP relaxation is essentially tight), and the DAG structure removes the need for subtour elimination. Variants 2 and 4 are equivalent in modelling power but require more machinery; Variant 3 does not scale.

## 7. Recommended formulation — complete final specification

### 7.1 Sets
```
I = {1, …, 200}
A = {(i,j) ∈ I×I : feasible(i,j)}            (rule in §7.2)
```

### 7.2 Feasible-arc generation rule
For each pair (i, j) with i ≠ j, include (i, j) ∈ A **iff** all of:
1. `s_do(i) = s_pu(j)` (handover station match, both in {A, M, Z}).
2. `t_pu(j) ≥ t_do(i)` (time-forward).
3. Either
   - `same(i,j) = 1` (same train ID and `t_pu(j) = t_do(i)`), **or**
   - `t_pu(j) − t_do(i) ≥ τ_min = 30`.

Set `reset(i,j) = 1` if `t_pu(j) − t_do(i) ≥ R_min = 30`, else `0`. Note: for same-train continuations `gap = 0`, so `reset = 0` and continuous driving accumulates — which is correct, the driver never left the cab.

**Expected size of A**: with ~200 tasks uniformly spread over ~360 minutes and average successor window of ~30–60 minutes, |A| is in the range 1 500–4 000.

### 7.3 Parameters (numeric values)

```
τ_min = 30          R_min = 30          T_c = 120
D_max = 150         L_max = 480
M₁ = 120            M₂ = 150            M₃ = 480
mileage(A,M) = mileage(M,A) = 17.1
mileage(M,Z) = mileage(Z,M) = 26.4
```

### 7.4 Variables

```
x[i,j]  ∈ {0,1}     ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
s[i]    ∈ {0,1}     ∀ i ∈ I
e[i]    ∈ {0,1}     ∀ i ∈ I
f[i]    ∈ [0, 120]  ∀ i ∈ I
m[i]    ∈ [0, 150]  ∀ i ∈ I
b[i]    ∈ ℝ         ∀ i ∈ I          (free, but bounded by (C13))
```

### 7.5 Objective
```
minimize  Σ_{i∈I} s[i]
```

### 7.6 Constraints (numbered, complete)

```
(C1)  Σ_{j:(i,j)∈A} x[i,j] + e[i] = 1                  ∀ i ∈ I
(C2)  Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i] + s[i] = 1                  ∀ i ∈ I
(C3)  (implicit) x[i,j] exists only for (i,j) ∈ A

(C5a) f[i] ≤ dur(i) + 120·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]          ∀ i ∈ I
(C5b) f[i] ≥ dur(i) − 120·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]          ∀ i ∈ I
(C6a) f[i] ≤ f[j] + dur(i) + 120·(1 − x[i,j])           ∀ (i,j)∈A, reset(i,j)=0
(C6b) f[i] ≥ f[j] + dur(i) − 120·(1 − x[i,j])           ∀ (i,j)∈A, reset(i,j)=0
(C7a) f[i] ≤ dur(i) + 120·(1 − x[i,j])                  ∀ (i,j)∈A, reset(i,j)=1
(C7b) f[i] ≥ dur(i) − 120·(1 − x[i,j])                  ∀ (i,j)∈A, reset(i,j)=1
(C8)  f[i] ≤ 120                                        ∀ i ∈ I

(C9a) m[i] ≤ dist(i) + 150·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]         ∀ i ∈ I
(C9b) m[i] ≥ dist(i) − 150·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]         ∀ i ∈ I
(C10a) m[i] ≤ m[j] + dist(i) + 150·(1 − x[i,j])         ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
(C10b) m[i] ≥ m[j] + dist(i) − 150·(1 − x[i,j])         ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
(C11)  m[i] ≤ 150                                       ∀ i ∈ I

(C12a) b[i] ≤ t_pu(i) + 480·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]        ∀ i ∈ I
(C12b) b[i] ≥ t_pu(i) − 480·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]        ∀ i ∈ I
(C12c) b[i] ≤ b[j] + 480·(1 − x[i,j])                   ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
(C12d) b[i] ≥ b[j] − 480·(1 − x[i,j])                   ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
(C13)  t_do(i) − b[i] ≤ 480                             ∀ i ∈ I

(C14, optional fairness)  W ≥ m[i]                       ∀ i ∈ I
                          minimize W secondarily
```

### 7.7 Algorithm to extract the optimal task chains

Given the optimal solution (x*, s*, e*, f*, m*, b*):

```
chains ← empty list
starts ← { i ∈ I : s*[i] = 1 }
for each i ∈ starts do
    chain ← [i]
    cur ← i
    while e*[cur] = 0 do
        nxt ← the unique j with x*[cur, j] = 1
        chain.append(nxt)
        cur ← nxt
    end while
    chains.append(chain)
end for

# Sanity checks
assert every task appears in exactly one chain
assert len(chains) = Σ s*[i] = objective value
for each chain c:
    assert continuous driving rule respected (use f*)
    assert Σ_{i∈c} dist(i) ≤ 150
    assert t_do(last) − t_pu(first) ≤ 480
    assert handover station rule respected
```

### 7.8 Connection table output
For each chain c = (i₁, i₂, …, i_k) emit a row:

| chain_id | task_id | train | t_pu | s_pu | t_do | s_do | gap_to_next | reset? | cum_drive | cum_km | duty_span |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 331 | M16 | 10:03 | M | 10:57 | Z | 0:06:21 | no | 54.5 | 26.4 | 0:54 |
| 1 | 332 | N27 | 11:04 | Z | 11:40 | A | … | … | … | … | … |

This table is the direct deliverable for the dispatcher.

---

Variant 1 is the formulation to implement. It is a single MILP with ~3 000 binary variables and ~600 continuous variables, ~10·|A| constraints, tight big-M values equal to the resource caps, and a DAG that makes subtour elimination unnecessary. Any modern MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, HiGHS, SCIP) will return a proven-optimal crew plan in well under a minute for the 200-task instance, and the chain-extraction algorithm in §7.7 turns the solution directly into the dispatcher’s connection table.

response.content:
# Subway Crew Scheduling — MILP Formulations

Below I give a complete, self-contained treatment. Section 1 fixes the data, parameters and the feasible-arc generation rule shared by every variant. Sections 2–5 develop the four requested variants. Section 6 compares them. Section 7 gives the recommended formulation in full, ready to be coded. Section 8 gives the chain-extraction algorithm.

---

## 1. Common data, parameters and feasible arcs

### 1.1 Sets

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $T=\{1,\dots,200\}$ | Driving tasks |
| $S=\{A,M,Z\}$ | Handover stations |
| $\mathcal{A}\subseteq T\times T$ | Feasible precedence arcs (defined in §1.4) |

### 1.2 Task data (given)

For every task $i\in T$:

| Symbol | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{trn}(i)$ | train number | 331 |
| $\mathrm{tid}(i)$ | physical train ID | M16 |
| $p_s(i)\in S$ | pickup station | M |
| $d_s(i)\in S$ | drop-off station | Z |
| $p_t(i)$ | pickup time (min from 10:00) | 3.18 |
| $d_t(i)$ | drop-off time | 57.72 |
| $\delta(i)=d_t(i)-p_t(i)$ | task duration (min) | 54.53 |
| $m(i)$ | mileage (km) | 26.4 |

Mileage table: $m(A\!\to\!M)=m(M\!\to\!A)=17.1$; $m(M\!\to\!Z)=m(Z\!\to\!M)=26.4$. The line is bidirectional, so $m(i)\in\{17.1,26.4\}$.

### 1.3 Numerical parameters

| Symbol | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $\tau_{\min}$ | 30 min | minimum changeover gap |
| $R_{\min}$ | 30 min | break threshold (gap $\ge R_{\min}$ resets continuous-driving counter) |
| $T_c$ | 120 min | max continuous driving |
| $D_{\max}$ | 150 km | max duty mileage |
| $L_{\max}$ | 480 min | max duty span |
| $M_1$ | $T_c$ | big-M for continuous-driving |
| $M_2$ | $D_{\max}$ | big-M for mileage |
| $M_3$ | $L_{\max}$ | big-M for span |

### 1.4 Feasible-arc generation rule

An arc $(i,j)$ is feasible (write $j\in P(i)$ and $i\in S(j)$) iff

$$
d_s(i)=p_s(j)\in S,\qquad p_t(j)\ge d_t(i),
$$

and one of

$$
\bigl[\mathrm{tid}(i)=\mathrm{tid}(j)\ \wedge\ p_t(j)=d_t(i)\bigr]\ \ \vee\ \ \bigl[p_t(j)-d_t(i)\ge\tau_{\min}\bigr].
$$

Define the break indicator

$$
\beta_{ij}=\begin{cases}0 & \text{if }\mathrm{tid}(i)=\mathrm{tid}(j)\text{ and }p_t(j)=d_t(i)\\[2pt] 1 & \text{if }p_t(j)-d_t(i)\ge R_{\min}\\[2pt] \text{undefined} & \text{otherwise (infeasible)}\end{cases}
$$

For every feasible arc $\beta_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$. (Same-train continuation has $\beta=0$; any changeover has $\beta=1$.)

### 1.5 Why subtour elimination is unnecessary

All feasible arcs satisfy $p_t(j)\ge d_t(i)$. Hence the digraph $(T,\mathcal{A})$ is a DAG ordered by pickup time. Any chain (path in this DAG) is automatically acyclic and time-ordered. The standard MTZ / DFJ subtour elimination is therefore not required.

---

## 2. Variant 1 — Arc-based flow with big-M cumulatives

### 2.1 Decision variables

| Variable | Domain | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$ | $(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}$ | 1 if task $j$ immediately follows $i$ in the same duty |
| $s_i\in\{0,1\}$ | $i\in T$ | 1 if task $i$ is a chain start |
| $e_i\in\{0,1\}$ | $i\in T$ | 1 if task $i$ is a chain end |
| $u_i\ge 0$ | $i\in T$ | continuous-driving minutes accumulated since the last real break, ending with task $i$ |
| $v_i\ge 0$ | $i\in T$ | cumulative mileage in the duty ending with task $i$ |
| $w_i\ge 0$ | $i\in T$ | duty start time (pickup time of first task) of the chain containing $i$ |

### 2.2 Objective

$$
\min\ \sum_{i\in T}s_i \qquad\Bigl(=\sum_{i\in T}e_i\Bigr) \tag{V1-OBJ}
$$

### 2.3 Constraints

**Coverage and chaining (flow conservation).**

$$
\sum_{j\in S(i)} x_{ij} + e_i = 1 \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-C1}
$$

$$
\sum_{j\in P(i)} x_{ji} + s_i = 1 \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-C2}
$$

$$
s_i + e_i \le 2 \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-C3}
$$

(C3 allows a single-task duty to be both start and end.)

**Continuous-driving time with break reset.** For each task $i$ and each feasible predecessor $j\in P(i)$:

$$
u_i \ge u_j + \delta(i) - M_1(1-x_{ji}) - M_1(1-\beta_{ji}) \tag{V1-U1}
$$

$$
u_i \ge \delta(i) - M_1(1-x_{ji}) - M_1\,\beta_{ji} \tag{V1-U2}
$$

$$
u_i \le u_j + \delta(i) + M_1(1-x_{ji}) + M_1(1-\beta_{ji}) \tag{V1-U3}
$$

$$
u_i \le \delta(i) + M_1(1-x_{ji}) + M_1\,\beta_{ji} \tag{V1-U4}
$$

$$
u_i \ge \delta(i) - M_1(1-s_i) \tag{V1-U5}
$$

$$
u_i \le \delta(i) + M_1(1-s_i) \tag{V1-U6}
$$

$$
u_i \le T_c \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-U7}
$$

Logic: (U1,U3) activate when $x_{ji}=1,\beta_{ji}=0$ (no break) and force $u_i=u_j+\delta(i)$. (U2,U4) activate when $x_{ji}=1,\beta_{ji}=1$ (break) and force $u_i=\delta(i)$. (U5,U6) activate when $s_i=1$ and force $u_i=\delta(i)$.

**Cumulative mileage.** For each $j\in P(i)$:

$$
v_i \ge v_j + m(i) - M_2(1-x_{ji}) \tag{V1-V1}
$$

$$
v_i \le v_j + m(i) + M_2(1-x_{ji}) \tag{V1-V2}
$$

$$
v_i \ge m(i) - M_2(1-s_i) \tag{V1-V3}
$$

$$
v_i \le m(i) + M_2(1-s_i) \tag{V1-V4}
$$

$$
v_i \le D_{\max} \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-V5}
$$

**Duty span.** Let $\sigma_i = p_t(i)$ (start of task $i$) and $\eta_i = d_t(i)$ (end of task $i$). For each $j\in P(i)$:

$$
w_i \ge w_j - M_3(1-x_{ji}) \tag{V1-W1}
$$

$$
w_i \le w_j + M_3(1-x_{ji}) \tag{V1-W2}
$$

$$
w_i \ge p_t(i) - M_3(1-s_i) \tag{V1-W3}
$$

$$
w_i \le p_t(i) + M_3(1-s_i) \tag{V1-W4}
$$

$$
d_t(i) - w_i \le L_{\max} \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-W5}
$$

### 2.4 Discussion

* **Strengths.** Single MILP, no column generation, DAG makes it cycle-free, big-M values are tight ($T_c,D_{\max},L_{\max}$).
* **Weaknesses.** Each arc generates 4 big-M inequalities for $u$, 2 for $v$, 2 for $w$. With $|\mathcal{A}|\sim 10^4$ this is $\sim 8\times 10^4$ rows; LP relaxation is moderately weak because of the big-M links, but integrality is excellent in practice because the DAG forces a topological ordering.
* **Size.** $\sim 200$ binaries for $s,e$, $\sim 10^4$ binaries for $x$, $\sim 600$ continuous cumulatives. Solves in seconds with CPLEX/Gurobi.

---

## 3. Variant 2 — Set-partitioning with column generation

### 3.1 Master problem (MP)

Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the (exponentially large) set of feasible chains. A *feasible chain* is a path $p=(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_k)$ in the DAG such that

* every consecutive pair is in $\mathcal{A}$,
* $\sum_{r=1}^k \delta(i_r)\le T_c$ between any two consecutive real breaks (i.e. cumulative driving between $\beta=1$ arcs $\le T_c$),
* $\sum_{r=1}^k m(i_r)\le D_{\max}$,
* $d_t(i_k)-p_t(i_1)\le L_{\max}$.

Variables $y_p\in\{0,1\}$ for $p\in\mathcal{P}$.

$$
\min \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}} y_p \tag{V2-OBJ}
$$

$$
\sum_{p\ni i} y_p = 1 \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V2-COV}
$$

### 3.2 Pricing subproblem (PSP)

For dual prices $\pi_i$ (one per task), find a feasible chain $p$ with negative reduced cost $1-\sum_{i\in p}\pi_i$. This is a *shortest path with resource constraints* on the DAG with resources

* cumulative duration $\Delta$ (reset to $\delta(i)$ on every break arc, $\le T_c$),
* cumulative mileage $M$ (no reset, $\le D_{\max}$),
* duty span $L$ (no reset, $\le L_{\max}$).

Solve by dynamic programming or label-setting with dominance. Each generated column is appended to $\mathcal{P}$ until no negative-reduced-cost column exists; then solve the integer MP (or branch-and-price).

### 3.3 Equivalent compact arc formulation

By Dantzig–Wolfe decomposition, the LP relaxation of (V2) equals the LP relaxation of (V1). The integer versions are equivalent because the DAG forbids cycles, so the convexity constraints are not needed.

### 3.4 Discussion

* **Strengths.** Tightest LP relaxation (often integral for this problem class); scales to millions of tasks.
* **Weaknesses.** Requires implementing a pricing solver, branching strategy, and column management. Overkill for 200 tasks.

---

## 4. Variant 3 — Driver-indexed / time-indexed formulation

Let $K$ be an upper bound on the number of drivers (e.g. $K=200$). Discretise time in 1-minute slots $t\in\{0,1,\dots,T_{\max}\}$ with $T_{\max}=360$.

### 4.1 Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $a_{ki}\in\{0,1\}$ | driver $k$ performs task $i$ |
| $z_{kt}\in\{0,1\}$ | driver $k$ is on duty at minute $t$ |
| $g_{kt}\in\{0,1\}$ | driver $k$ is driving at minute $t$ |
| $b_k\in\{0,1\}$ | driver $k$ is used |

### 4.2 Constraints

**Coverage:**

$$
\sum_{k=1}^K a_{ki}=1 \quad \forall i \tag{V3-COV}
$$

**Driving implies on-duty:**

$$
g_{kt}\le z_{kt} \quad \forall k,t \tag{V3-DOD}
$$

**Task coverage in time:**

$$
\sum_{t=p_t(i)}^{d_t(i)-1} g_{kt} \ge \delta(i)\,a_{ki} \quad \forall k,i \tag{V3-TIME}
$$

(Forces driver $k$ to be driving during the whole task if assigned.)

**Continuous driving ≤ $T_c$:** for every $t$ and every window of length $T_c$,

$$
\sum_{s=t}^{t+T_c-1} g_{ks} \le T_c + M_1(1-b_k) \quad \forall k,t \tag{V3-CD}
$$

(Trivially satisfied if driver $k$ unused.)

**Break reset:** if gap between consecutive tasks of driver $k$ is $\ge R_{\min}$, the counter resets. This is enforced implicitly by (V3-CD) only if we ensure that "non-driving on-duty" minutes are excluded. Replace $g_{ks}$ by a *driving-since-last-break* counter $c_{kt}$ with $c_{kt+1}=(c_{kt}+1)\cdot g_{kt}$ and $c_{kt+1}\le g_{kt}\cdot T_c$ etc.

**Mileage:** $\sum_i m(i)\,a_{ki}\le D_{\max}$ for all $k$.

**Span:** for each driver $k$, $\max_i\{d_t(i):a_{ki}=1\}-\min_i\{p_t(i):a_{ki}=1\}\le L_{\max}$.

**Driver-count linkage:**

$$
\sum_{k=1}^K b_k \le \sum_{k=1}^K a_{ki}\ \text{(any }i\text{)};\quad b_k\ge a_{ki}\ \forall k,i \tag{V3-LINK}
$$

### 4.3 Objective

$$
\min \sum_{k=1}^K b_k \tag{V3-OBJ}
$$

### 4.4 Discussion

* **Strengths.** Very flexible; can encode complex labour rules (overtime, breaks, days off) by adding columns of $z_{kt},g_{kt}$.
* **Weaknesses.** Huge: $K\cdot T_{\max}\approx 200\cdot 360=72{,}000$ binaries for $z$ alone, plus $K\cdot |T|=40{,}000$ for $a$. Symmetry between drivers requires ordering constraints or driver-indexed branching. LP relaxation is weak due to time-indexing.
* **Verdict.** Not recommended for this problem size.

---

## 5. Variant 4 — Time-expanded network + flow-based

Build a time-expanded DAG whose nodes are the 200 tasks plus a source $\alpha$ and sink $\omega$.

### 5.1 Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $f_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$ | one driver flows from task $i$ to task $j$ |
| $f_{\alpha i}\in\{0,1\}$ | task $i$ is a chain start |
| $f_{i\omega}\in\{0,1\}$ | task $i$ is a chain end |

### 5.2 Constraints

**Flow conservation at every task node:**

$$
f_{\alpha i} + \sum_{j\in P(i)} f_{ji} = \sum_{j\in S(i)} f_{ij} + f_{i\omega} = 1 \quad \forall i \tag{V4-FC}
$$

**Resource cumulatives** carried on each arc, identical in form to (V1-U/V/W) but with $f$ replacing $x$ and $f_{\alpha i}$ replacing $s_i$.

**Objective:**

$$
\min \sum_{i\in T} f_{\alpha i} \tag{V4-OBJ}
$$

### 5.3 Discussion

* Mathematically equivalent to Variant 1 (the $f$ variables are just a re-labelling of $x,s,e$).
* Useful pedagogically: it makes the "one unit of flow = one driver" interpretation explicit.
* Same size and LP strength as V1.

---

## 6. Comparison

| Criterion | V1 Arc-bigM | V2 Set-partition | V3 Driver-indexed | V4 Flow |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Variables | $\sim 10^4$ bin + 600 cont | columns (unbounded) | $\sim 10^5$ bin | $\sim 10^4$ bin |
| Constraints | $\sim 8\cdot 10^4$ | $|\mathcal{P}|$ columns + 200 cover | $\sim 10^6$ | $\sim 8\cdot 10^4$ |
| LP relaxation | moderate (big-M) | tightest | weak | moderate |
| Integrality | excellent (DAG) | excellent | needs symmetry breaking | excellent |
| Implementation effort | low | high (pricing) | medium | low |
| Scales to 200 tasks | **yes, seconds** | yes, but overkill | heavy | yes |

---

## 7. Recommendation: Variant 1

For 200 tasks the arc-based big-M formulation is the right tool: a single MILP, tight big-M values, DAG structure, and standard solvers handle it in seconds. The set-partitioning variant would dominate only at thousands of tasks. I now give the **complete final model** with all numeric parameters.

### 7.1 Sets and parameters

$$
\begin{aligned}
T&=\{1,\dots,200\},\quad S=\{A,M,Z\},\quad \mathcal{A}\subseteq T\times T \text{ (from §1.4)}\\[2pt]
\tau_{\min}&=30,\ R_{\min}=30,\ T_c=120,\ D_{\max}=150,\ L_{\max}=480\\[2pt]
M_1&=120,\ M_2=150,\ M_3=480\\[2pt]
\delta(i)&=d_t(i)-p_t(i),\quad m(i)\in\{17.1,26.4\}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 7.2 Variables

$$
\begin{aligned}
&x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\ \ (i,j)\in\mathcal{A}\\
&s_i,\,e_i\in\{0,1\}\ \ i\in T\\
&u_i\ge 0,\ v_i\ge 0,\ w_i\ge 0\ \ i\in T
\end{aligned}
$$

### 7.3 Objective

$$
\boxed{\min\ \sum_{i\in T} s_i}
$$

### 7.4 Constraints

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\textbf{(1) Coverage — exactly one predecessor or a start:}\\
&\sum_{j\in P(i)} x_{ji} + s_i = 1 &&\forall i\in T\\[4pt]
&\textbf{(2) Coverage — exactly one successor or an end:}\\
&\sum_{j\in S(i)} x_{ij} + e_i = 1 &&\forall i\in T\\[4pt]
&\textbf{(3) Single-task duties allowed:}\\
&s_i + e_i \le 2 &&\forall i\in T\\[4pt]
&\textbf{(4) Continuous driving (reset on break):}\\
&u_i \ge u_j + \delta(i) - 120(1-x_{ji}) - 120(1-\beta_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&u_i \ge \delta(i) - 120(1-x_{ji}) - 120\,\beta_{ji} &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&u_i \le u_j + \delta(i) + 120(1-x_{ji}) + 120(1-\beta_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&u_i \le \delta(i) + 120(1-x_{ji}) + 120\,\beta_{ji} &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&u_i \ge \delta(i) - 120(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&u_i \le \delta(i) + 120(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&u_i \le 120 &&\forall i\\[4pt]
&\textbf{(5) Cumulative mileage:}\\
&v_i \ge v_j + m(i) - 150(1-x_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&v_i \le v_j + m(i) + 150(1-x_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&v_i \ge m(i) - 150(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&v_i \le m(i) + 150(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&v_i \le 150 &&\forall i\\[4pt]
&\textbf{(6) Duty span:}\\
&w_i \ge w_j - 480(1-x_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&w_i \le w_j + 480(1-x_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&w_i \ge p_t(i) - 480(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&w_i \le p_t(i) + 480(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&d_t(i) - w_i \le 480 &&\forall i
\end{aligned}
$$

### 7.5 Optional fairness tie-breaker

Add a second objective (lexicographic) or a max-min workload term:

$$
\max\ \min_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\Bigl(\sum_{i\in c}\delta(i)\Bigr)
$$

or equivalently, with $W$ a scalar and $\theta$ an auxiliary variable,

$$
\max\ \theta\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \theta \le \sum_{i\in T}\delta(i)\,a_{ci}\ \forall c
$$

where $a_{ci}$ is the indicator of task $i$ belonging to chain $c$. In practice, since the chains are not pre-computed, encode this with chain-start variables: $\theta\le \sum_{i\in T}\delta(i)\,s_i\cdot K - \sum_i \delta(i)\,s_i$ … a simpler proxy is to add a small penalty $\varepsilon\sum_i v_i$ to the objective so the solver spreads mileage across drivers.

### 7.6 Parameter table for the implementer

| Name | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| $\tau_{\min}$ | 30 min | given |
| $R_{\min}$ | 30 min | given |
| $T_c$ | 120 min | given |
| $D_{\max}$ | 150 km | given |
| $L_{\max}$ | 480 min | given |
| $M_1$ | 120 | $=T_c$ |
| $M_2$ | 150 | $=D_{\max}$ |
| $M_3$ | 480 | $=L_{\max}$ |
| $m(A\!\leftrightarrow\!M)$ | 17.1 km | given |
| $m(M\!\leftrightarrow\!Z)$ | 26.4 km | given |

---

## 8. Chain-extraction algorithm

After the MILP is solved (binary variables fixed):

```
Input:  x*, s*, e*, u*, v*, w*
Output: list of chains C = {c_1,...,c_K}; K = number of drivers

1.  K := sum(s*)                              # number of drivers
2.  Build adjacency list Adj(i) := {j : x*_{ij} = 1}
3.  Starts := {i : s*_i = 1}
4.  For each i in Starts:
        chain := []
        cur := i
        while cur is not None:
            chain.append(cur)
            nxt := the unique j in Adj(cur)   # at most one by (V1-C1)
            cur := nxt
        C.append(chain)
5.  Sanity checks:
        - every task appears in exactly one chain
        - |C| = K
        - for each chain c: sum(m(i)) ≤ 150, d_t(last)-p_t(first) ≤ 480,
          and for every pair of consecutive tasks the break rule holds
6.  Print connection table: rows = (chain_id, task_index, position,
        task_id, train, pu_station, pu_time, do_station, do_time,
        gap_to_next_min, same_train_as_next, break_after)
```

The connection table row for task $i$ contains:

| Column | Value |
|---|---|
| chain | $\#c$ such that $i\in c$ |
| pos | position within chain (1-based) |
| task | $i$ |
| train | $\mathrm{trn}(i)$ |
| tid | $\mathrm{tid}(i)$ |
| pu_st, pu_t | $p_s(i), p_t(i)$ |
| do_st, do_t | $d_s(i), d_t(i)$ |
| next_task | $j$ with $x^*_{ij}=1$, or `END` |
| gap_min | $p_t(j)-d_t(i)$ |
| same_train | $\mathrm{tid}(i)=\mathrm{tid}(j)$ |
| break | $\beta_{ij}$ |
| cum_u | $u^*_i$ |
| cum_v | $v^*_i$ |
| cum_w | $w^*_i$ |

This table is the deliverable: it gives the optimal task chains (one row per task, grouped by chain), the number of drivers $K=\sum s_i^*$, and a complete audit trail showing where every break, every same-train continuation, and every resource cumulative stands.

---

### Final notes

* The DAG property (all arcs go forward in pickup time) is what makes subtour elimination unnecessary and what guarantees that the chain-extraction algorithm terminates and is unique.
* Big-M values are tight because they equal the natural upper bounds of the cumulatives; this keeps the LP relaxation close to integer.
* For 200 tasks and $|\mathcal A|\approx 10^4$, modern MILP solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi, HiGHS) return the proven optimum in well under a minute on a laptop.
* If the instance grows (e.g. a full day with 1500 tasks), switch to Variant 2 with column generation; the pricing subproblem is a label-setting shortest path with three resources (continuous driving, mileage, span) and runs in milliseconds.

response.content:
# Subway Crew (Driver) Scheduling — MILP Formulations

Below I give a complete treatment. Section 1 fixes the common data model; Sections 2–5 give the four variants you asked for; Section 6 compares them; Section 7 is the recommended formulation with every equation, every parameter value, the arc-generation rule, and the chain-extraction algorithm.

---

## 1. Common data model (used by every variant)

### 1.1 Sets
- **I** = {1, …, 200} — driving tasks.
- **S** = {A, M, Z} — attendance / handover stations.
- **A ⊆ I × I** — feasible predecessor→successor arcs (rule in §7.2).

### 1.2 Task parameters (read directly from the task table)
For every i ∈ I:
- `t_pu(i)` — pickup clock time (minutes from 10:03, i.e. integer minutes).
- `t_do(i)` — drop-off clock time.
- `s_pu(i), s_do(i) ∈ S` — pickup / drop-off station.
- `trainID(i)` — physical train (e.g. M16, N23, L06, …).
- `dur(i) = t_do(i) − t_pu(i)` — driving time of the task (35–55 min).
- `dist(i)` — mileage of the task = mileage(s_pu(i), s_do(i)) ∈ {17.1, 26.4}.

### 1.3 Mileage table (km, symmetric)
| from \ to | A | M | Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 0 | 17.1 | — |
| **M** | 17.1 | 0 | 26.4 |
| **Z** | — | 26.4 | 0 |

### 1.4 Global parameters (numeric)
| Symbol | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| τ_min | 30 min | minimum changeover / walking time |
| R_min | 30 min | gap that counts as a real break |
| T_c | 120 min | max continuous driving before a break |
| D_max | 150 km | max duty mileage |
| L_max | 480 min | max duty span |
| M₁ | T_c = 120 | big-M for continuous-driving |
| M₂ | D_max = 150 | big-M for mileage |
| M₃ | L_max = 480 | big-M for duty span |

### 1.5 Derived arc parameters (constants, not variables)
For every (i, j) ∈ A:
- `gap(i,j) = t_pu(j) − t_do(i)`.
- `reset(i,j) = 1` if `gap(i,j) ≥ R_min`, else `0`.
- `same(i,j) = 1` if `trainID(i) = trainID(j)` and `t_pu(j) = t_do(i)`, else `0`.

### 1.6 DAG justification (no subtour elimination needed)
Every feasible arc (i, j) satisfies `t_pu(j) ≥ t_do(i)` (strict for normal changeovers, equal only for same-train continuations). Hence the arc graph is a DAG ordered by pickup time. Any feasible chain is a path in this DAG, so cycles are impossible and no MTZ / DFJ subtour constraints are required.

---

## 2. Variant 1 — Arc-based flow formulation with big-M cumulatives (RECOMMENDED)

### 2.1 Decision variables
| Variable | Domain | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| x[i,j] | {0,1} | 1 if task j is performed immediately after task i by the same driver |
| s[i] | {0,1} | 1 if task i is the **start** of a driver duty |
| e[i] | {0,1} | 1 if task i is the **end** of a driver duty |
| f[i] | [0, T_c] | continuous driving time accumulated since the last real break, measured at the **drop-off** of task i |
| m[i] | [0, D_max] | total mileage in the duty up to and including task i |
| b[i] | ℝ | pickup time of the **first** task in the duty that ends at task i |

### 2.2 Objective
```
(OBJ)   minimize  Σ_{i∈I} s[i]
```
(Number of drivers = number of chain starts = number of chain ends.)

### 2.3 Constraints

**(C1) Coverage — every task is performed exactly once**
```
Σ_{j:(i,j)∈A} x[i,j] + e[i] = 1        ∀ i ∈ I
```
Each task has exactly one successor or is a chain end.

**(C2) Predecessor — at most one predecessor**
```
Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i] + s[i] = 1        ∀ i ∈ I
```
Each task has exactly one predecessor or is a chain start.

**(C3) Arc feasibility (implicit)**
Variables x[i,j] are only created for (i,j) ∈ A; for all other pairs the variable does not exist (equivalent to fixing it to 0).

**(C4) Number of drivers consistency**
```
Σ_{i∈I} s[i] = Σ_{i∈I} e[i]
```
(Automatically satisfied by (C1)+(C2) and flow conservation; stated explicitly for clarity.)

**(C5) Continuous driving time — start case**
```
f[i] ≤ dur(i) + M₁ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]        ∀ i ∈ I
f[i] ≥ dur(i) − M₁ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]        ∀ i ∈ I
```
If i has no predecessor (chain start) the RHS collapses to dur(i), forcing f[i] = dur(i). If i has a predecessor the constraint is non-binding (M₁ large enough).

**(C6) Continuous driving time — carry-over arc (no reset, reset(i,j)=0)**
```
f[i] ≤ f[j] + dur(i) + M₁·(1 − x[i,j])           ∀ (i,j) ∈ A with reset(i,j)=0
f[i] ≥ f[j] + dur(i) − M₁·(1 − x[i,j])           ∀ (i,j) ∈ A with reset(i,j)=0
```
When x[i,j]=1 this forces f[j] = f[i] + dur(j).

**(C7) Continuous driving time — reset arc (reset(i,j)=1)**
```
f[i] ≤ dur(i) + M₁·(1 − x[i,j])                  ∀ (i,j) ∈ A with reset(i,j)=1
f[i] ≥ dur(i) − M₁·(1 − x[i,j])                  ∀ (i,j) ∈ A with reset(i,j)=1
```
When x[i,j]=1 this forces f[j] = dur(j) (counter reset by the break).

**(C8) Continuous driving upper bound**
```
f[i] ≤ T_c                                        ∀ i ∈ I
```

**(C9) Mileage — start case**
```
m[i] ≤ dist(i) + M₂ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]       ∀ i ∈ I
m[i] ≥ dist(i) − M₂ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]       ∀ i ∈ I
```

**(C10) Mileage — carry-over**
```
m[i] ≤ m[j] + dist(i) + M₂·(1 − x[i,j])          ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
m[i] ≥ m[j] + dist(i) − M₂·(1 − x[i,j])          ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
```

**(C11) Mileage upper bound**
```
m[i] ≤ D_max                                      ∀ i ∈ I
```

**(C12) Duty span — start time of chain ending at i**
```
b[i] ≤ t_pu(i) + M₃ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]       ∀ i ∈ I
b[i] ≥ t_pu(i) − M₃ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]       ∀ i ∈ I
b[i] ≤ b[j] + M₃·(1 − x[i,j])                    ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
b[i] ≥ b[j] − M₃·(1 − x[i,j])                    ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
```

**(C13) Duty span upper bound**
```
t_do(i) − b[i] ≤ L_max                            ∀ i ∈ I
```

**(C14, optional) Fairness tie-breaker**
Introduce W = max workload (mileage) and minimize it lexicographically:
```
W ≥ m[i]                                          ∀ i ∈ I
```
Use W as a secondary objective after (OBJ). Equivalently minimize Σ m[i]² via piecewise-linear approximation, or impose `m[i] ≤ W` and minimize W.

### 2.4 Strengths / weaknesses of Variant 1
- **Strengths**: single MILP, no column generation, DAG makes subtour elimination unnecessary, big-M values are the natural resource bounds (tight), model size ~ |A| binary + 3|I| continuous.
- **Weaknesses**: LP relaxation can be marginally loose on the cumulative constraints (mitigated because M₁, M₂, M₃ are tight resource caps); for |I|=200 the number of arcs |A| is at most a few thousand — entirely tractable.

---

## 3. Variant 2 — Set-partitioning / column-generation formulation

### 3.1 Master problem
Let **P** = set of all **feasible chains** (paths in the DAG that satisfy C5–C13). For p ∈ P let `a[i,p] = 1` if task i ∈ p.

Variables: `y[p] ∈ {0,1}`, 1 if chain p is selected.

```
(OBJ-MP)   minimize  Σ_{p∈P} y[p]
(COVER)    Σ_{p∈P} a[i,p] · y[p] = 1                ∀ i ∈ I
```
(Number of drivers = Σ y[p] automatically.)

### 3.2 Pricing subproblem (resource-constrained shortest path on the DAG)
Find a feasible chain with negative reduced cost π[i] (dual of COVER):

```
minimize   Σ_{(i,j)∈A} c[i,j] · x[i,j] − Σ_{i∈I} π[i] · u[i]
s.t.       x, f, m, b, s, e satisfy C1–C13 (single-chain version)
```
This is a **label-setting shortest path** with resources (continuous driving time, mileage, span). Solved by dynamic programming over the DAG with dominance pruning. Each iteration adds one or more columns with negative reduced cost.

### 3.3 Equivalent compact arc formulation
Drop the chain variables, keep x[i,j], s[i], e[i] and add **one** cumulative variable per resource that is **scoped to a single chain** (use acommodity flow with |D| copies, one per driver). For 200 tasks this is impractical without D being endogenous — hence column generation.

### 3.4 Strengths / weaknesses
- **Strengths**: LP relaxation of the master is typically very tight; standard in crew scheduling literature.
- **Weaknesses**: requires an LP solver + a custom pricing oracle; convergence can be slow when many resources interact; integer round-off after column generation often needs a final MIP solve (branch-and-price).

---

## 4. Variant 3 — Time-indexed / time-discretized formulation

### 4.1 Discretization
Time grid T = {0, 1, …, T_max} minutes (T_max = 360, covering 10:03–15:58 + buffer). Let D = {1, …, D_ub} be a sufficient upper bound on drivers (e.g. D_ub = 200).

### 4.2 Variables
- `z[d,i] ∈ {0,1}` — driver d performs task i.
- `on[d,t] ∈ {0,1}` — driver d is on duty at minute t.
- `drv[d,t] ∈ {0,1}` — driver d is actively driving at minute t.
- `brk[d,t] ∈ {0,1}` — driver d is on a real break (gap ≥ 30 min) at minute t.
- `s_duty[d] ∈ {0,1}`, `e_duty[d] ∈ {0,1}` — driver d has any duty / has finished.

### 4.3 Key constraints (sketch)
```
Σ_{d∈D} z[d,i] = 1                                   ∀ i ∈ I
Σ_{i: t∈[t_pu(i),t_do(i))} z[d,i] = drv[d,t]         ∀ d,t
drv[d,t] ≤ on[d,t]                                   ∀ d,t
Σ_{τ=t−29}^{t} drv[d,τ] ≥ 30·brk[d,t]                ∀ d,t   (break detection)
f[d,t] = Σ_{τ=t−119}^{t} drv[d,τ] − 120·brk[d,t]     ∀ d,t
f[d,t] ≤ 120                                          ∀ d,t
Σ_{i} dist(i)·z[d,i] ≤ 150                           ∀ d
Σ_{t} on[d,t]·(last−first) ≤ 480                     ∀ d
```

### 4.4 Strengths / weaknesses
- **Strengths**: very general, easy to add shift pay, overtime, breaks of arbitrary length.
- **Weaknesses**: model size is O(|D|·T) ≈ 200·360 = 72 000 binary variables even before tasks; LP relaxation is extremely loose; impractical for 200 tasks without aggressive aggregation.

---

## 5. Variant 4 — Time-expanded network + flow-based formulation

### 5.1 Network
- Source σ, sink τ.
- For each task i: node i with capacity 1 (split i⁻ → i⁺ with arc of capacity 1, cost 0).
- Arc σ → i with capacity 1, cost 0 (start a duty at i).
- Arc i → τ with capacity 1, cost 0 (end a duty at i).
- Arc i → j for every (i,j) ∈ A with capacity 1, cost 0.

### 5.2 Variables and objective
- `flow[arc]` ≥ 0 integer.
- `x[i,j]`, `s[i]`, `e[i]` derived from flow values.
- Cumulative variables f[i], m[i], b[i] as in Variant 1.

```
minimize  Σ_{i∈I} flow[σ → i]
s.t.      flow conservation at every i⁻ and i⁺
          capacity 1 on every task node
          C5–C13 on the chosen arcs
```

### 5.3 Strengths / weaknesses
- **Strengths**: elegant; the number of drivers is the value of the σ→τ flow; subtour prevention is unnecessary because of the DAG.
- **Weaknesses**: cumulative resource constraints still need big-M (or resource-constrained shortest-path subproblem); essentially equivalent to Variant 1 in modelling power, slightly more variables (σ, τ nodes).

---

## 6. Comparison

| Criterion | V1 Arc-big-M | V2 Set-partitioning | V3 Time-indexed | V4 Flow |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Variables (200 tasks) | ~3 000 bin + 600 cont | exponential in |P| | ~70 000 bin | ~3 000 bin + 600 cont |
| Constraints | ~10·|A| | |cover| + pricing | O(|D|·T) | ~10·|A| |
| LP relaxation tightness | tight (M = resource cap) | very tight | very loose | tight |
| Solver needed | MILP (CPLEX/Gurobi/HiGHS) | LP + pricing + branch-and-price | MILP | MILP |
| Implementation effort | low | high | medium | low |
| Scalability to 200 tasks | excellent | excellent | poor | excellent |
| Handles all constraints (1)–(8) | yes | yes | yes | yes |

**Recommendation: Variant 1.** It is a single, compact MILP that any modern solver will solve to proven optimality in seconds for 200 tasks, the big-M values are the natural resource caps (so the LP relaxation is essentially tight), and the DAG structure removes the need for subtour elimination. Variants 2 and 4 are equivalent in modelling power but require more machinery; Variant 3 does not scale.

---

## 7. Recommended formulation — complete final specification

### 7.1 Sets
```
I = {1, …, 200}
A = {(i,j) ∈ I×I : feasible(i,j)}            (rule in §7.2)
```

### 7.2 Feasible-arc generation rule
For each pair (i, j) with i ≠ j, include (i, j) ∈ A **iff** all of:
1. `s_do(i) = s_pu(j)` (handover station match, both in {A, M, Z}).
2. `t_pu(j) ≥ t_do(i)` (time-forward).
3. Either
   - `same(i,j) = 1` (same train ID and `t_pu(j) = t_do(i)`), **or**
   - `t_pu(j) − t_do(i) ≥ τ_min = 30`.

Set `reset(i,j) = 1` if `t_pu(j) − t_do(i) ≥ R_min = 30`, else `0`. Note: for same-train continuations `gap = 0`, so `reset = 0` and continuous driving accumulates — which is correct, the driver never left the cab.

**Expected size of A**: with ~200 tasks uniformly spread over ~360 minutes and average successor window of ~30–60 minutes, |A| is in the range 1 500–4 000.

### 7.3 Parameters (numeric values)

```
τ_min = 30          R_min = 30          T_c = 120
D_max = 150         L_max = 480
M₁ = 120            M₂ = 150            M₃ = 480
mileage(A,M) = mileage(M,A) = 17.1
mileage(M,Z) = mileage(Z,M) = 26.4
```

### 7.4 Variables

```
x[i,j]  ∈ {0,1}     ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
s[i]    ∈ {0,1}     ∀ i ∈ I
e[i]    ∈ {0,1}     ∀ i ∈ I
f[i]    ∈ [0, 120]  ∀ i ∈ I
m[i]    ∈ [0, 150]  ∀ i ∈ I
b[i]    ∈ ℝ         ∀ i ∈ I          (free, but bounded by (C13))
```

### 7.5 Objective
```
minimize  Σ_{i∈I} s[i]
```

### 7.6 Constraints (numbered, complete)

```
(C1)  Σ_{j:(i,j)∈A} x[i,j] + e[i] = 1                  ∀ i ∈ I
(C2)  Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i] + s[i] = 1                  ∀ i ∈ I
(C3)  (implicit) x[i,j] exists only for (i,j) ∈ A

(C5a) f[i] ≤ dur(i) + 120·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]          ∀ i ∈ I
(C5b) f[i] ≥ dur(i) − 120·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]          ∀ i ∈ I
(C6a) f[i] ≤ f[j] + dur(i) + 120·(1 − x[i,j])           ∀ (i,j)∈A, reset(i,j)=0
(C6b) f[i] ≥ f[j] + dur(i) − 120·(1 − x[i,j])           ∀ (i,j)∈A, reset(i,j)=0
(C7a) f[i] ≤ dur(i) + 120·(1 − x[i,j])                  ∀ (i,j)∈A, reset(i,j)=1
(C7b) f[i] ≥ dur(i) − 120·(1 − x[i,j])                  ∀ (i,j)∈A, reset(i,j)=1
(C8)  f[i] ≤ 120                                        ∀ i ∈ I

(C9a) m[i] ≤ dist(i) + 150·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]         ∀ i ∈ I
(C9b) m[i] ≥ dist(i) − 150·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]         ∀ i ∈ I
(C10a) m[i] ≤ m[j] + dist(i) + 150·(1 − x[i,j])         ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
(C10b) m[i] ≥ m[j] + dist(i) − 150·(1 − x[i,j])         ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
(C11)  m[i] ≤ 150                                       ∀ i ∈ I

(C12a) b[i] ≤ t_pu(i) + 480·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]        ∀ i ∈ I
(C12b) b[i] ≥ t_pu(i) − 480·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]        ∀ i ∈ I
(C12c) b[i] ≤ b[j] + 480·(1 − x[i,j])                   ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
(C12d) b[i] ≥ b[j] − 480·(1 − x[i,j])                   ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
(C13)  t_do(i) − b[i] ≤ 480                             ∀ i ∈ I

(C14, optional fairness)  W ≥ m[i]                       ∀ i ∈ I
                          minimize W secondarily
```

### 7.7 Algorithm to extract the optimal task chains

Given the optimal solution (x*, s*, e*, f*, m*, b*):

```
chains ← empty list
starts ← { i ∈ I : s*[i] = 1 }
for each i ∈ starts do
    chain ← [i]
    cur ← i
    while e*[cur] = 0 do
        nxt ← the unique j with x*[cur, j] = 1
        chain.append(nxt)
        cur ← nxt
    end while
    chains.append(chain)
end for

# Sanity checks
assert every task appears in exactly one chain
assert len(chains) = Σ s*[i] = objective value
for each chain c:
    assert continuous driving rule respected (use f*)
    assert Σ_{i∈c} dist(i) ≤ 150
    assert t_do(last) − t_pu(first) ≤ 480
    assert handover station rule respected
```

  f[i] = dur(i) + sum_{j} x[j,i] * f_continuation[j,i]

where f_continuation[j,i] is an auxiliary variable. This gets complex.

Let me stick with the big-M approach:

For each task i:
  f[i] <= T_c
  f[i] >= dur(i)  [since at least dur(i) of driving]
  
  f[i] <= dur(i) + M1 * sum_j x[j,i]  [if start, f[i] = dur(i)]
  
  For each j with (j,i) ∈ A:
    If reset(j,i) = 1:
      f[i] <= dur(i) + M1*(1 - x[j,i])
      f[i] >= dur(i) - M1*(1 - x[j,i])
    Else (reset = 0):
      f[i] <= f[j] + dur(i) + M1*(1 - x[j,i])
      f[i] >= f[j] + dur(i) - M1*(1 - x[j,i])

Wait, the "if start" constraint f[i] <= dur(i) + M1*sum_j x[j,i] is redundant with the per-arc constraints when there's a predecessor. Let me think again.

If i has predecessor j (x[j,i] = 1):
- Per-arc constraint: f[i] <= f[j] + dur(i) + M1*0 = f[j] + dur(i) (if no reset)
  or f[i] <= dur(i) + M1*0 = dur(i) (if reset)
- "If start" constraint: f[i] <= dur(i) + M1*1 = dur(i) + M1 (non-binding)

So the "if start" constraint is non-binding when there's a predecessor. Good.

If i has no predecessor (sum_j x[j,i] = 0):
- Per-arc constraints: don't apply (x[j,i] = 0 for all j)
- "If start" constraint: f[i] <= dur(i) + M1*0 = dur(i)
- Combined with f[i] >= dur(i): f[i] = dur(i). Good.

So we need the "if start" constraint to handle the case when i is a chain start.

Similarly for lower bound:
  f[i] >= dur(i) - M1 * sum_j x[j,i]

If sum_j x[j,i] = 0: f[i] >= dur(i). Combined with f[i] <= dur(i): f[i] = dur(i). Good.
If sum_j x[j,i] = 1: f[i] >= dur(i) - M1 (non-binding).

OK so the formulation is:

  f[i] <= T_c, ∀i
  f[i] <= dur(i) + M1 * sum_{j: (j,i)∈A} x[j,i], ∀i  [start constraint]
  f[i] >= dur(i) - M1 * sum_{j: (j,i)∈A} x[j,i], ∀i  [start constraint]
  
  For each (j,i) ∈ A with reset(j,i) = 0:
    f[i] <= f[j] + dur(i) + M1*(1 - x[j,i])
    f[i] >= f[j] + dur(i) - M1*(1 - x[j,i])
  
  For each (j,i) ∈ A with reset(j,i) = 1:
    f[i] <= dur(i) + M1*(1 - x[j,i])
    f[i] >= dur(i) - M1*(1 - x[j,i])

This is correct.

Similarly for m[i] and b[i].

1. s_do(i) = s_pu(j) (handover at same station, which is in {A, M, Z})
2. Either:
   a. same_train(i,j) AND t_pu(j) = t_do(i) (continuation, tau_min = 0)
   b. t_pu(j) >= t_do(i) + tau_min (normal changeover)

And reset(i,j) = 1 if t_pu(j) - t_do(i) >= R_min, else 0.
