messages.content:
Model 1:
# Subway Crew Scheduling — MILP Formulations

Below I give a complete, self-contained treatment. Section 1 fixes the data, parameters and the feasible-arc generation rule shared by every variant. Sections 2–5 develop the four requested variants. Section 6 compares them. Section 7 gives the recommended formulation in full, ready to be coded. Section 8 gives the chain-extraction algorithm.

---

## 1. Common data, parameters and feasible arcs

### 1.1 Sets

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $T=\{1,\dots,200\}$ | Driving tasks |
| $S=\{A,M,Z\}$ | Handover stations |
| $\mathcal{A}\subseteq T\times T$ | Feasible precedence arcs (defined in §1.4) |

### 1.2 Task data (given)

For every task $i\in T$:

| Symbol | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{trn}(i)$ | train number | 331 |
| $\mathrm{tid}(i)$ | physical train ID | M16 |
| $p_s(i)\in S$ | pickup station | M |
| $d_s(i)\in S$ | drop-off station | Z |
| $p_t(i)$ | pickup time (min from 10:00) | 3.18 |
| $d_t(i)$ | drop-off time | 57.72 |
| $\delta(i)=d_t(i)-p_t(i)$ | task duration (min) | 54.53 |
| $m(i)$ | mileage (km) | 26.4 |

Mileage table: $m(A\!\to\!M)=m(M\!\to\!A)=17.1$; $m(M\!\to\!Z)=m(Z\!\to\!M)=26.4$. The line is bidirectional, so $m(i)\in\{17.1,26.4\}$.

### 1.3 Numerical parameters

| Symbol | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $\tau_{\min}$ | 30 min | minimum changeover gap |
| $R_{\min}$ | 30 min | break threshold (gap $\ge R_{\min}$ resets continuous-driving counter) |
| $T_c$ | 120 min | max continuous driving |
| $D_{\max}$ | 150 km | max duty mileage |
| $L_{\max}$ | 480 min | max duty span |
| $M_1$ | $T_c$ | big-M for continuous-driving |
| $M_2$ | $D_{\max}$ | big-M for mileage |
| $M_3$ | $L_{\max}$ | big-M for span |

### 1.4 Feasible-arc generation rule

An arc $(i,j)$ is feasible (write $j\in P(i)$ and $i\in S(j)$) iff

$$
d_s(i)=p_s(j)\in S,\qquad p_t(j)\ge d_t(i),
$$

and one of

$$
\bigl[\mathrm{tid}(i)=\mathrm{tid}(j)\ \wedge\ p_t(j)=d_t(i)\bigr]\ \ \vee\ \ \bigl[p_t(j)-d_t(i)\ge\tau_{\min}\bigr].
$$

Define the break indicator

$$
\beta_{ij}=\begin{cases}0 & \text{if }\mathrm{tid}(i)=\mathrm{tid}(j)\text{ and }p_t(j)=d_t(i)\\[2pt] 1 & \text{if }p_t(j)-d_t(i)\ge R_{\min}\\[2pt] \text{undefined} & \text{otherwise (infeasible)}\end{cases}
$$

For every feasible arc $\beta_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$. (Same-train continuation has $\beta=0$; any changeover has $\beta=1$.)

### 1.5 Why subtour elimination is unnecessary

All feasible arcs satisfy $p_t(j)\ge d_t(i)$. Hence the digraph $(T,\mathcal{A})$ is a DAG ordered by pickup time. Any chain (path in this DAG) is automatically acyclic and time-ordered. The standard MTZ / DFJ subtour elimination is therefore not required.

---

## 2. Variant 1 — Arc-based flow with big-M cumulatives

### 2.1 Decision variables

| Variable | Domain | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$ | $(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}$ | 1 if task $j$ immediately follows $i$ in the same duty |
| $s_i\in\{0,1\}$ | $i\in T$ | 1 if task $i$ is a chain start |
| $e_i\in\{0,1\}$ | $i\in T$ | 1 if task $i$ is a chain end |
| $u_i\ge 0$ | $i\in T$ | continuous-driving minutes accumulated since the last real break, ending with task $i$ |
| $v_i\ge 0$ | $i\in T$ | cumulative mileage in the duty ending with task $i$ |
| $w_i\ge 0$ | $i\in T$ | duty start time (pickup time of first task) of the chain containing $i$ |

### 2.2 Objective

$$
\min\ \sum_{i\in T}s_i \qquad\Bigl(=\sum_{i\in T}e_i\Bigr) \tag{V1-OBJ}
$$

### 2.3 Constraints

**Coverage and chaining (flow conservation).**

$$
\sum_{j\in S(i)} x_{ij} + e_i = 1 \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-C1}
$$

$$
\sum_{j\in P(i)} x_{ji} + s_i = 1 \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-C2}
$$

$$
s_i + e_i \le 2 \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-C3}
$$

(C3 allows a single-task duty to be both start and end.)

**Continuous-driving time with break reset.** For each task $i$ and each feasible predecessor $j\in P(i)$:

$$
u_i \ge u_j + \delta(i) - M_1(1-x_{ji}) - M_1(1-\beta_{ji}) \tag{V1-U1}
$$

$$
u_i \ge \delta(i) - M_1(1-x_{ji}) - M_1\,\beta_{ji} \tag{V1-U2}
$$

$$
u_i \le u_j + \delta(i) + M_1(1-x_{ji}) + M_1(1-\beta_{ji}) \tag{V1-U3}
$$

$$
u_i \le \delta(i) + M_1(1-x_{ji}) + M_1\,\beta_{ji} \tag{V1-U4}
$$

$$
u_i \ge \delta(i) - M_1(1-s_i) \tag{V1-U5}
$$

$$
u_i \le \delta(i) + M_1(1-s_i) \tag{V1-U6}
$$

$$
u_i \le T_c \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-U7}
$$

Logic: (U1,U3) activate when $x_{ji}=1,\beta_{ji}=0$ (no break) and force $u_i=u_j+\delta(i)$. (U2,U4) activate when $x_{ji}=1,\beta_{ji}=1$ (break) and force $u_i=\delta(i)$. (U5,U6) activate when $s_i=1$ and force $u_i=\delta(i)$.

**Cumulative mileage.** For each $j\in P(i)$:

$$
v_i \ge v_j + m(i) - M_2(1-x_{ji}) \tag{V1-V1}
$$

$$
v_i \le v_j + m(i) + M_2(1-x_{ji}) \tag{V1-V2}
$$

$$
v_i \ge m(i) - M_2(1-s_i) \tag{V1-V3}
$$

$$
v_i \le m(i) + M_2(1-s_i) \tag{V1-V4}
$$

$$
v_i \le D_{\max} \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-V5}
$$

**Duty span.** Let $\sigma_i = p_t(i)$ (start of task $i$) and $\eta_i = d_t(i)$ (end of task $i$). For each $j\in P(i)$:

$$
w_i \ge w_j - M_3(1-x_{ji}) \tag{V1-W1}
$$

$$
w_i \le w_j + M_3(1-x_{ji}) \tag{V1-W2}
$$

$$
w_i \ge p_t(i) - M_3(1-s_i) \tag{V1-W3}
$$

$$
w_i \le p_t(i) + M_3(1-s_i) \tag{V1-W4}
$$

$$
d_t(i) - w_i \le L_{\max} \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V1-W5}
$$

### 2.4 Discussion

* **Strengths.** Single MILP, no column generation, DAG makes it cycle-free, big-M values are tight ($T_c,D_{\max},L_{\max}$).
* **Weaknesses.** Each arc generates 4 big-M inequalities for $u$, 2 for $v$, 2 for $w$. With $|\mathcal{A}|\sim 10^4$ this is $\sim 8\times 10^4$ rows; LP relaxation is moderately weak because of the big-M links, but integrality is excellent in practice because the DAG forces a topological ordering.
* **Size.** $\sim 200$ binaries for $s,e$, $\sim 10^4$ binaries for $x$, $\sim 600$ continuous cumulatives. Solves in seconds with CPLEX/Gurobi.

---

## 3. Variant 2 — Set-partitioning with column generation

### 3.1 Master problem (MP)

Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the (exponentially large) set of feasible chains. A *feasible chain* is a path $p=(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_k)$ in the DAG such that

* every consecutive pair is in $\mathcal{A}$,
* $\sum_{r=1}^k \delta(i_r)\le T_c$ between any two consecutive real breaks (i.e. cumulative driving between $\beta=1$ arcs $\le T_c$),
* $\sum_{r=1}^k m(i_r)\le D_{\max}$,
* $d_t(i_k)-p_t(i_1)\le L_{\max}$.

Variables $y_p\in\{0,1\}$ for $p\in\mathcal{P}$.

$$
\min \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}} y_p \tag{V2-OBJ}
$$

$$
\sum_{p\ni i} y_p = 1 \quad \forall i\in T \tag{V2-COV}
$$

### 3.2 Pricing subproblem (PSP)

For dual prices $\pi_i$ (one per task), find a feasible chain $p$ with negative reduced cost $1-\sum_{i\in p}\pi_i$. This is a *shortest path with resource constraints* on the DAG with resources

* cumulative duration $\Delta$ (reset to $\delta(i)$ on every break arc, $\le T_c$),
* cumulative mileage $M$ (no reset, $\le D_{\max}$),
* duty span $L$ (no reset, $\le L_{\max}$).

Solve by dynamic programming or label-setting with dominance. Each generated column is appended to $\mathcal{P}$ until no negative-reduced-cost column exists; then solve the integer MP (or branch-and-price).

### 3.3 Equivalent compact arc formulation

By Dantzig–Wolfe decomposition, the LP relaxation of (V2) equals the LP relaxation of (V1). The integer versions are equivalent because the DAG forbids cycles, so the convexity constraints are not needed.

### 3.4 Discussion

* **Strengths.** Tightest LP relaxation (often integral for this problem class); scales to millions of tasks.
* **Weaknesses.** Requires implementing a pricing solver, branching strategy, and column management. Overkill for 200 tasks.

---

## 4. Variant 3 — Driver-indexed / time-indexed formulation

Let $K$ be an upper bound on the number of drivers (e.g. $K=200$). Discretise time in 1-minute slots $t\in\{0,1,\dots,T_{\max}\}$ with $T_{\max}=360$.

### 4.1 Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $a_{ki}\in\{0,1\}$ | driver $k$ performs task $i$ |
| $z_{kt}\in\{0,1\}$ | driver $k$ is on duty at minute $t$ |
| $g_{kt}\in\{0,1\}$ | driver $k$ is driving at minute $t$ |
| $b_k\in\{0,1\}$ | driver $k$ is used |

### 4.2 Constraints

**Coverage:**

$$
\sum_{k=1}^K a_{ki}=1 \quad \forall i \tag{V3-COV}
$$

**Driving implies on-duty:**

$$
g_{kt}\le z_{kt} \quad \forall k,t \tag{V3-DOD}
$$

**Task coverage in time:**

$$
\sum_{t=p_t(i)}^{d_t(i)-1} g_{kt} \ge \delta(i)\,a_{ki} \quad \forall k,i \tag{V3-TIME}
$$

(Forces driver $k$ to be driving during the whole task if assigned.)

**Continuous driving ≤ $T_c$:** for every $t$ and every window of length $T_c$,

$$
\sum_{s=t}^{t+T_c-1} g_{ks} \le T_c + M_1(1-b_k) \quad \forall k,t \tag{V3-CD}
$$

(Trivially satisfied if driver $k$ unused.)

**Break reset:** if gap between consecutive tasks of driver $k$ is $\ge R_{\min}$, the counter resets. This is enforced implicitly by (V3-CD) only if we ensure that "non-driving on-duty" minutes are excluded. Replace $g_{ks}$ by a *driving-since-last-break* counter $c_{kt}$ with $c_{kt+1}=(c_{kt}+1)\cdot g_{kt}$ and $c_{kt+1}\le g_{kt}\cdot T_c$ etc.

**Mileage:** $\sum_i m(i)\,a_{ki}\le D_{\max}$ for all $k$.

**Span:** for each driver $k$, $\max_i\{d_t(i):a_{ki}=1\}-\min_i\{p_t(i):a_{ki}=1\}\le L_{\max}$.

**Driver-count linkage:**

$$
\sum_{k=1}^K b_k \le \sum_{k=1}^K a_{ki}\ \text{(any }i\text{)};\quad b_k\ge a_{ki}\ \forall k,i \tag{V3-LINK}
$$

### 4.3 Objective

$$
\min \sum_{k=1}^K b_k \tag{V3-OBJ}
$$

### 4.4 Discussion

* **Strengths.** Very flexible; can encode complex labour rules (overtime, breaks, days off) by adding columns of $z_{kt},g_{kt}$.
* **Weaknesses.** Huge: $K\cdot T_{\max}\approx 200\cdot 360=72{,}000$ binaries for $z$ alone, plus $K\cdot |T|=40{,}000$ for $a$. Symmetry between drivers requires ordering constraints or driver-indexed branching. LP relaxation is weak due to time-indexing.
* **Verdict.** Not recommended for this problem size.

---

## 5. Variant 4 — Time-expanded network + flow-based

Build a time-expanded DAG whose nodes are the 200 tasks plus a source $\alpha$ and sink $\omega$.

### 5.1 Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $f_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$ | one driver flows from task $i$ to task $j$ |
| $f_{\alpha i}\in\{0,1\}$ | task $i$ is a chain start |
| $f_{i\omega}\in\{0,1\}$ | task $i$ is a chain end |

### 5.2 Constraints

**Flow conservation at every task node:**

$$
f_{\alpha i} + \sum_{j\in P(i)} f_{ji} = \sum_{j\in S(i)} f_{ij} + f_{i\omega} = 1 \quad \forall i \tag{V4-FC}
$$

**Resource cumulatives** carried on each arc, identical in form to (V1-U/V/W) but with $f$ replacing $x$ and $f_{\alpha i}$ replacing $s_i$.

**Objective:**

$$
\min \sum_{i\in T} f_{\alpha i} \tag{V4-OBJ}
$$

### 5.3 Discussion

* Mathematically equivalent to Variant 1 (the $f$ variables are just a re-labelling of $x,s,e$).
* Useful pedagogically: it makes the "one unit of flow = one driver" interpretation explicit.
* Same size and LP strength as V1.

---

## 6. Comparison

| Criterion | V1 Arc-bigM | V2 Set-partition | V3 Driver-indexed | V4 Flow |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Variables | $\sim 10^4$ bin + 600 cont | columns (unbounded) | $\sim 10^5$ bin | $\sim 10^4$ bin |
| Constraints | $\sim 8\cdot 10^4$ | $|\mathcal{P}|$ columns + 200 cover | $\sim 10^6$ | $\sim 8\cdot 10^4$ |
| LP relaxation | moderate (big-M) | tightest | weak | moderate |
| Integrality | excellent (DAG) | excellent | needs symmetry breaking | excellent |
| Implementation effort | low | high (pricing) | medium | low |
| Scales to 200 tasks | **yes, seconds** | yes, but overkill | heavy | yes |

---

## 7. Recommendation: Variant 1

For 200 tasks the arc-based big-M formulation is the right tool: a single MILP, tight big-M values, DAG structure, and standard solvers handle it in seconds. The set-partitioning variant would dominate only at thousands of tasks. I now give the **complete final model** with all numeric parameters.

### 7.1 Sets and parameters

$$
\begin{aligned}
T&=\{1,\dots,200\},\quad S=\{A,M,Z\},\quad \mathcal{A}\subseteq T\times T \text{ (from §1.4)}\\[2pt]
\tau_{\min}&=30,\ R_{\min}=30,\ T_c=120,\ D_{\max}=150,\ L_{\max}=480\\[2pt]
M_1&=120,\ M_2=150,\ M_3=480\\[2pt]
\delta(i)&=d_t(i)-p_t(i),\quad m(i)\in\{17.1,26.4\}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 7.2 Variables

$$
\begin{aligned}
&x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\ \ (i,j)\in\mathcal{A}\\
&s_i,\,e_i\in\{0,1\}\ \ i\in T\\
&u_i\ge 0,\ v_i\ge 0,\ w_i\ge 0\ \ i\in T
\end{aligned}
$$

### 7.3 Objective

$$
\boxed{\min\ \sum_{i\in T} s_i}
$$

### 7.4 Constraints

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\textbf{(1) Coverage — exactly one predecessor or a start:}\\
&\sum_{j\in P(i)} x_{ji} + s_i = 1 &&\forall i\in T\\[4pt]
&\textbf{(2) Coverage — exactly one successor or an end:}\\
&\sum_{j\in S(i)} x_{ij} + e_i = 1 &&\forall i\in T\\[4pt]
&\textbf{(3) Single-task duties allowed:}\\
&s_i + e_i \le 2 &&\forall i\in T\\[4pt]
&\textbf{(4) Continuous driving (reset on break):}\\
&u_i \ge u_j + \delta(i) - 120(1-x_{ji}) - 120(1-\beta_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&u_i \ge \delta(i) - 120(1-x_{ji}) - 120\,\beta_{ji} &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&u_i \le u_j + \delta(i) + 120(1-x_{ji}) + 120(1-\beta_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&u_i \le \delta(i) + 120(1-x_{ji}) + 120\,\beta_{ji} &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&u_i \ge \delta(i) - 120(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&u_i \le \delta(i) + 120(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&u_i \le 120 &&\forall i\\[4pt]
&\textbf{(5) Cumulative mileage:}\\
&v_i \ge v_j + m(i) - 150(1-x_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&v_i \le v_j + m(i) + 150(1-x_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&v_i \ge m(i) - 150(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&v_i \le m(i) + 150(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&v_i \le 150 &&\forall i\\[4pt]
&\textbf{(6) Duty span:}\\
&w_i \ge w_j - 480(1-x_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&w_i \le w_j + 480(1-x_{ji}) &&\forall i,\ \forall j\in P(i)\\
&w_i \ge p_t(i) - 480(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&w_i \le p_t(i) + 480(1-s_i) &&\forall i\\
&d_t(i) - w_i \le 480 &&\forall i
\end{aligned}
$$

### 7.5 Optional fairness tie-breaker

Add a second objective (lexicographic) or a max-min workload term:

$$
\max\ \min_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\Bigl(\sum_{i\in c}\delta(i)\Bigr)
$$

or equivalently, with $W$ a scalar and $\theta$ an auxiliary variable,

$$
\max\ \theta\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \theta \le \sum_{i\in T}\delta(i)\,a_{ci}\ \forall c
$$

where $a_{ci}$ is the indicator of task $i$ belonging to chain $c$. In practice, since the chains are not pre-computed, encode this with chain-start variables: $\theta\le \sum_{i\in T}\delta(i)\,s_i\cdot K - \sum_i \delta(i)\,s_i$ … a simpler proxy is to add a small penalty $\varepsilon\sum_i v_i$ to the objective so the solver spreads mileage across drivers.

### 7.6 Parameter table for the implementer

| Name | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| $\tau_{\min}$ | 30 min | given |
| $R_{\min}$ | 30 min | given |
| $T_c$ | 120 min | given |
| $D_{\max}$ | 150 km | given |
| $L_{\max}$ | 480 min | given |
| $M_1$ | 120 | $=T_c$ |
| $M_2$ | 150 | $=D_{\max}$ |
| $M_3$ | 480 | $=L_{\max}$ |
| $m(A\!\leftrightarrow\!M)$ | 17.1 km | given |
| $m(M\!\leftrightarrow\!Z)$ | 26.4 km | given |

---

## 8. Chain-extraction algorithm

After the MILP is solved (binary variables fixed):

```
Input:  x*, s*, e*, u*, v*, w*
Output: list of chains C = {c_1,...,c_K}; K = number of drivers

1.  K := sum(s*)                              # number of drivers
2.  Build adjacency list Adj(i) := {j : x*_{ij} = 1}
3.  Starts := {i : s*_i = 1}
4.  For each i in Starts:
        chain := []
        cur := i
        while cur is not None:
            chain.append(cur)
            nxt := the unique j in Adj(cur)   # at most one by (V1-C1)
            cur := nxt
        C.append(chain)
5.  Sanity checks:
        - every task appears in exactly one chain
        - |C| = K
        - for each chain c: sum(m(i)) ≤ 150, d_t(last)-p_t(first) ≤ 480,
          and for every pair of consecutive tasks the break rule holds
6.  Print connection table: rows = (chain_id, task_index, position,
        task_id, train, pu_station, pu_time, do_station, do_time,
        gap_to_next_min, same_train_as_next, break_after)
```

The connection table row for task $i$ contains:

| Column | Value |
|---|---|
| chain | $\#c$ such that $i\in c$ |
| pos | position within chain (1-based) |
| task | $i$ |
| train | $\mathrm{trn}(i)$ |
| tid | $\mathrm{tid}(i)$ |
| pu_st, pu_t | $p_s(i), p_t(i)$ |
| do_st, do_t | $d_s(i), d_t(i)$ |
| next_task | $j$ with $x^*_{ij}=1$, or `END` |
| gap_min | $p_t(j)-d_t(i)$ |
| same_train | $\mathrm{tid}(i)=\mathrm{tid}(j)$ |
| break | $\beta_{ij}$ |
| cum_u | $u^*_i$ |
| cum_v | $v^*_i$ |
| cum_w | $w^*_i$ |

This table is the deliverable: it gives the optimal task chains (one row per task, grouped by chain), the number of drivers $K=\sum s_i^*$, and a complete audit trail showing where every break, every same-train continuation, and every resource cumulative stands.

---

### Final notes

* The DAG property (all arcs go forward in pickup time) is what makes subtour elimination unnecessary and what guarantees that the chain-extraction algorithm terminates and is unique.
* Big-M values are tight because they equal the natural upper bounds of the cumulatives; this keeps the LP relaxation close to integer.
* For 200 tasks and $|\mathcal A|\approx 10^4$, modern MILP solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi, HiGHS) return the proven optimum in well under a minute on a laptop.
* If the instance grows (e.g. a full day with 1500 tasks), switch to Variant 2 with column generation; the pricing subproblem is a label-setting shortest path with three resources (continuous driving, mileage, span) and runs in milliseconds.

# Subway Crew (Driver) Scheduling — MILP Formulations

Below I give a complete treatment. Section 1 fixes the common data model; Sections 2–5 give the four variants you asked for; Section 6 compares them; Section 7 is the recommended formulation with every equation, every parameter value, the arc-generation rule, and the chain-extraction algorithm.

---

## 1. Common data model (used by every variant)

### 1.1 Sets
- **I** = {1, …, 200} — driving tasks.
- **S** = {A, M, Z} — attendance / handover stations.
- **A ⊆ I × I** — feasible predecessor→successor arcs (rule in §7.2).

### 1.2 Task parameters (read directly from the task table)
For every i ∈ I:
- `t_pu(i)` — pickup clock time (minutes from 10:03, i.e. integer minutes).
- `t_do(i)` — drop-off clock time.
- `s_pu(i), s_do(i) ∈ S` — pickup / drop-off station.
- `trainID(i)` — physical train (e.g. M16, N23, L06, …).
- `dur(i) = t_do(i) − t_pu(i)` — driving time of the task (35–55 min).
- `dist(i)` — mileage of the task = mileage(s_pu(i), s_do(i)) ∈ {17.1, 26.4}.

### 1.3 Mileage table (km, symmetric)
| from \ to | A | M | Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 0 | 17.1 | — |
| **M** | 17.1 | 0 | 26.4 |
| **Z** | — | 26.4 | 0 |

### 1.4 Global parameters (numeric)
| Symbol | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| τ_min | 30 min | minimum changeover / walking time |
| R_min | 30 min | gap that counts as a real break |
| T_c | 120 min | max continuous driving before a break |
| D_max | 150 km | max duty mileage |
| L_max | 480 min | max duty span |
| M₁ | T_c = 120 | big-M for continuous-driving |
| M₂ | D_max = 150 | big-M for mileage |
| M₃ | L_max = 480 | big-M for duty span |

### 1.5 Derived arc parameters (constants, not variables)
For every (i, j) ∈ A:
- `gap(i,j) = t_pu(j) − t_do(i)`.
- `reset(i,j) = 1` if `gap(i,j) ≥ R_min`, else `0`.
- `same(i,j) = 1` if `trainID(i) = trainID(j)` and `t_pu(j) = t_do(i)`, else `0`.

### 1.6 DAG justification (no subtour elimination needed)
Every feasible arc (i, j) satisfies `t_pu(j) ≥ t_do(i)` (strict for normal changeovers, equal only for same-train continuations). Hence the arc graph is a DAG ordered by pickup time. Any feasible chain is a path in this DAG, so cycles are impossible and no MTZ / DFJ subtour constraints are required.

---

## 2. Variant 1 — Arc-based flow formulation with big-M cumulatives (RECOMMENDED)

### 2.1 Decision variables
| Variable | Domain | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| x[i,j] | {0,1} | 1 if task j is performed immediately after task i by the same driver |
| s[i] | {0,1} | 1 if task i is the **start** of a driver duty |
| e[i] | {0,1} | 1 if task i is the **end** of a driver duty |
| f[i] | [0, T_c] | continuous driving time accumulated since the last real break, measured at the **drop-off** of task i |
| m[i] | [0, D_max] | total mileage in the duty up to and including task i |
| b[i] | ℝ | pickup time of the **first** task in the duty that ends at task i |

### 2.2 Objective
```
(OBJ)   minimize  Σ_{i∈I} s[i]
```
(Number of drivers = number of chain starts = number of chain ends.)

### 2.3 Constraints

**(C1) Coverage — every task is performed exactly once**
```
Σ_{j:(i,j)∈A} x[i,j] + e[i] = 1        ∀ i ∈ I
```
Each task has exactly one successor or is a chain end.

**(C2) Predecessor — at most one predecessor**
```
Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i] + s[i] = 1        ∀ i ∈ I
```
Each task has exactly one predecessor or is a chain start.

**(C3) Arc feasibility (implicit)**
Variables x[i,j] are only created for (i,j) ∈ A; for all other pairs the variable does not exist (equivalent to fixing it to 0).

**(C4) Number of drivers consistency**
```
Σ_{i∈I} s[i] = Σ_{i∈I} e[i]
```
(Automatically satisfied by (C1)+(C2) and flow conservation; stated explicitly for clarity.)

**(C5) Continuous driving time — start case**
```
f[i] ≤ dur(i) + M₁ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]        ∀ i ∈ I
f[i] ≥ dur(i) − M₁ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]        ∀ i ∈ I
```
If i has no predecessor (chain start) the RHS collapses to dur(i), forcing f[i] = dur(i). If i has a predecessor the constraint is non-binding (M₁ large enough).

**(C6) Continuous driving time — carry-over arc (no reset, reset(i,j)=0)**
```
f[i] ≤ f[j] + dur(i) + M₁·(1 − x[i,j])           ∀ (i,j) ∈ A with reset(i,j)=0
f[i] ≥ f[j] + dur(i) − M₁·(1 − x[i,j])           ∀ (i,j) ∈ A with reset(i,j)=0
```
When x[i,j]=1 this forces f[j] = f[i] + dur(j).

**(C7) Continuous driving time — reset arc (reset(i,j)=1)**
```
f[i] ≤ dur(i) + M₁·(1 − x[i,j])                  ∀ (i,j) ∈ A with reset(i,j)=1
f[i] ≥ dur(i) − M₁·(1 − x[i,j])                  ∀ (i,j) ∈ A with reset(i,j)=1
```
When x[i,j]=1 this forces f[j] = dur(j) (counter reset by the break).

**(C8) Continuous driving upper bound**
```
f[i] ≤ T_c                                        ∀ i ∈ I
```

**(C9) Mileage — start case**
```
m[i] ≤ dist(i) + M₂ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]       ∀ i ∈ I
m[i] ≥ dist(i) − M₂ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]       ∀ i ∈ I
```

**(C10) Mileage — carry-over**
```
m[i] ≤ m[j] + dist(i) + M₂·(1 − x[i,j])          ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
m[i] ≥ m[j] + dist(i) − M₂·(1 − x[i,j])          ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
```

**(C11) Mileage upper bound**
```
m[i] ≤ D_max                                      ∀ i ∈ I
```

**(C12) Duty span — start time of chain ending at i**
```
b[i] ≤ t_pu(i) + M₃ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]       ∀ i ∈ I
b[i] ≥ t_pu(i) − M₃ · Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]       ∀ i ∈ I
b[i] ≤ b[j] + M₃·(1 − x[i,j])                    ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
b[i] ≥ b[j] − M₃·(1 − x[i,j])                    ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
```

**(C13) Duty span upper bound**
```
t_do(i) − b[i] ≤ L_max                            ∀ i ∈ I
```

**(C14, optional) Fairness tie-breaker**
Introduce W = max workload (mileage) and minimize it lexicographically:
```
W ≥ m[i]                                          ∀ i ∈ I
```
Use W as a secondary objective after (OBJ). Equivalently minimize Σ m[i]² via piecewise-linear approximation, or impose `m[i] ≤ W` and minimize W.

### 2.4 Strengths / weaknesses of Variant 1
- **Strengths**: single MILP, no column generation, DAG makes subtour elimination unnecessary, big-M values are the natural resource bounds (tight), model size ~ |A| binary + 3|I| continuous.
- **Weaknesses**: LP relaxation can be marginally loose on the cumulative constraints (mitigated because M₁, M₂, M₃ are tight resource caps); for |I|=200 the number of arcs |A| is at most a few thousand — entirely tractable.

---

## 3. Variant 2 — Set-partitioning / column-generation formulation

### 3.1 Master problem
Let **P** = set of all **feasible chains** (paths in the DAG that satisfy C5–C13). For p ∈ P let `a[i,p] = 1` if task i ∈ p.

Variables: `y[p] ∈ {0,1}`, 1 if chain p is selected.

```
(OBJ-MP)   minimize  Σ_{p∈P} y[p]
(COVER)    Σ_{p∈P} a[i,p] · y[p] = 1                ∀ i ∈ I
```
(Number of drivers = Σ y[p] automatically.)

### 3.2 Pricing subproblem (resource-constrained shortest path on the DAG)
Find a feasible chain with negative reduced cost π[i] (dual of COVER):

```
minimize   Σ_{(i,j)∈A} c[i,j] · x[i,j] − Σ_{i∈I} π[i] · u[i]
s.t.       x, f, m, b, s, e satisfy C1–C13 (single-chain version)
```
This is a **label-setting shortest path** with resources (continuous driving time, mileage, span). Solved by dynamic programming over the DAG with dominance pruning. Each iteration adds one or more columns with negative reduced cost.

### 3.3 Equivalent compact arc formulation
Drop the chain variables, keep x[i,j], s[i], e[i] and add **one** cumulative variable per resource that is **scoped to a single chain** (use acommodity flow with |D| copies, one per driver). For 200 tasks this is impractical without D being endogenous — hence column generation.

### 3.4 Strengths / weaknesses
- **Strengths**: LP relaxation of the master is typically very tight; standard in crew scheduling literature.
- **Weaknesses**: requires an LP solver + a custom pricing oracle; convergence can be slow when many resources interact; integer round-off after column generation often needs a final MIP solve (branch-and-price).

---

## 4. Variant 3 — Time-indexed / time-discretized formulation

### 4.1 Discretization
Time grid T = {0, 1, …, T_max} minutes (T_max = 360, covering 10:03–15:58 + buffer). Let D = {1, …, D_ub} be a sufficient upper bound on drivers (e.g. D_ub = 200).

### 4.2 Variables
- `z[d,i] ∈ {0,1}` — driver d performs task i.
- `on[d,t] ∈ {0,1}` — driver d is on duty at minute t.
- `drv[d,t] ∈ {0,1}` — driver d is actively driving at minute t.
- `brk[d,t] ∈ {0,1}` — driver d is on a real break (gap ≥ 30 min) at minute t.
- `s_duty[d] ∈ {0,1}`, `e_duty[d] ∈ {0,1}` — driver d has any duty / has finished.

### 4.3 Key constraints (sketch)
```
Σ_{d∈D} z[d,i] = 1                                   ∀ i ∈ I
Σ_{i: t∈[t_pu(i),t_do(i))} z[d,i] = drv[d,t]         ∀ d,t
drv[d,t] ≤ on[d,t]                                   ∀ d,t
Σ_{τ=t−29}^{t} drv[d,τ] ≥ 30·brk[d,t]                ∀ d,t   (break detection)
f[d,t] = Σ_{τ=t−119}^{t} drv[d,τ] − 120·brk[d,t]     ∀ d,t
f[d,t] ≤ 120                                          ∀ d,t
Σ_{i} dist(i)·z[d,i] ≤ 150                           ∀ d
Σ_{t} on[d,t]·(last−first) ≤ 480                     ∀ d
```

### 4.4 Strengths / weaknesses
- **Strengths**: very general, easy to add shift pay, overtime, breaks of arbitrary length.
- **Weaknesses**: model size is O(|D|·T) ≈ 200·360 = 72 000 binary variables even before tasks; LP relaxation is extremely loose; impractical for 200 tasks without aggressive aggregation.

---

## 5. Variant 4 — Time-expanded network + flow-based formulation

### 5.1 Network
- Source σ, sink τ.
- For each task i: node i with capacity 1 (split i⁻ → i⁺ with arc of capacity 1, cost 0).
- Arc σ → i with capacity 1, cost 0 (start a duty at i).
- Arc i → τ with capacity 1, cost 0 (end a duty at i).
- Arc i → j for every (i,j) ∈ A with capacity 1, cost 0.

### 5.2 Variables and objective
- `flow[arc]` ≥ 0 integer.
- `x[i,j]`, `s[i]`, `e[i]` derived from flow values.
- Cumulative variables f[i], m[i], b[i] as in Variant 1.

```
minimize  Σ_{i∈I} flow[σ → i]
s.t.      flow conservation at every i⁻ and i⁺
          capacity 1 on every task node
          C5–C13 on the chosen arcs
```

### 5.3 Strengths / weaknesses
- **Strengths**: elegant; the number of drivers is the value of the σ→τ flow; subtour prevention is unnecessary because of the DAG.
- **Weaknesses**: cumulative resource constraints still need big-M (or resource-constrained shortest-path subproblem); essentially equivalent to Variant 1 in modelling power, slightly more variables (σ, τ nodes).

---

## 6. Comparison

| Criterion | V1 Arc-big-M | V2 Set-partitioning | V3 Time-indexed | V4 Flow |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Variables (200 tasks) | ~3 000 bin + 600 cont | exponential in |P| | ~70 000 bin | ~3 000 bin + 600 cont |
| Constraints | ~10·|A| | |cover| + pricing | O(|D|·T) | ~10·|A| |
| LP relaxation tightness | tight (M = resource cap) | very tight | very loose | tight |
| Solver needed | MILP (CPLEX/Gurobi/HiGHS) | LP + pricing + branch-and-price | MILP | MILP |
| Implementation effort | low | high | medium | low |
| Scalability to 200 tasks | excellent | excellent | poor | excellent |
| Handles all constraints (1)–(8) | yes | yes | yes | yes |

**Recommendation: Variant 1.** It is a single, compact MILP that any modern solver will solve to proven optimality in seconds for 200 tasks, the big-M values are the natural resource caps (so the LP relaxation is essentially tight), and the DAG structure removes the need for subtour elimination. Variants 2 and 4 are equivalent in modelling power but require more machinery; Variant 3 does not scale.

---

## 7. Recommended formulation — complete final specification

### 7.1 Sets
```
I = {1, …, 200}
A = {(i,j) ∈ I×I : feasible(i,j)}            (rule in §7.2)
```

### 7.2 Feasible-arc generation rule
For each pair (i, j) with i ≠ j, include (i, j) ∈ A **iff** all of:
1. `s_do(i) = s_pu(j)` (handover station match, both in {A, M, Z}).
2. `t_pu(j) ≥ t_do(i)` (time-forward).
3. Either
   - `same(i,j) = 1` (same train ID and `t_pu(j) = t_do(i)`), **or**
   - `t_pu(j) − t_do(i) ≥ τ_min = 30`.

Set `reset(i,j) = 1` if `t_pu(j) − t_do(i) ≥ R_min = 30`, else `0`. Note: for same-train continuations `gap = 0`, so `reset = 0` and continuous driving accumulates — which is correct, the driver never left the cab.

**Expected size of A**: with ~200 tasks uniformly spread over ~360 minutes and average successor window of ~30–60 minutes, |A| is in the range 1 500–4 000.

### 7.3 Parameters (numeric values)

```
τ_min = 30          R_min = 30          T_c = 120
D_max = 150         L_max = 480
M₁ = 120            M₂ = 150            M₃ = 480
mileage(A,M) = mileage(M,A) = 17.1
mileage(M,Z) = mileage(Z,M) = 26.4
```

### 7.4 Variables

```
x[i,j]  ∈ {0,1}     ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
s[i]    ∈ {0,1}     ∀ i ∈ I
e[i]    ∈ {0,1}     ∀ i ∈ I
f[i]    ∈ [0, 120]  ∀ i ∈ I
m[i]    ∈ [0, 150]  ∀ i ∈ I
b[i]    ∈ ℝ         ∀ i ∈ I          (free, but bounded by (C13))
```

### 7.5 Objective
```
minimize  Σ_{i∈I} s[i]
```

### 7.6 Constraints (numbered, complete)

```
(C1)  Σ_{j:(i,j)∈A} x[i,j] + e[i] = 1                  ∀ i ∈ I
(C2)  Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i] + s[i] = 1                  ∀ i ∈ I
(C3)  (implicit) x[i,j] exists only for (i,j) ∈ A

(C5a) f[i] ≤ dur(i) + 120·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]          ∀ i ∈ I
(C5b) f[i] ≥ dur(i) − 120·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]          ∀ i ∈ I
(C6a) f[i] ≤ f[j] + dur(i) + 120·(1 − x[i,j])           ∀ (i,j)∈A, reset(i,j)=0
(C6b) f[i] ≥ f[j] + dur(i) − 120·(1 − x[i,j])           ∀ (i,j)∈A, reset(i,j)=0
(C7a) f[i] ≤ dur(i) + 120·(1 − x[i,j])                  ∀ (i,j)∈A, reset(i,j)=1
(C7b) f[i] ≥ dur(i) − 120·(1 − x[i,j])                  ∀ (i,j)∈A, reset(i,j)=1
(C8)  f[i] ≤ 120                                        ∀ i ∈ I

(C9a) m[i] ≤ dist(i) + 150·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]         ∀ i ∈ I
(C9b) m[i] ≥ dist(i) − 150·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]         ∀ i ∈ I
(C10a) m[i] ≤ m[j] + dist(i) + 150·(1 − x[i,j])         ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
(C10b) m[i] ≥ m[j] + dist(i) − 150·(1 − x[i,j])         ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
(C11)  m[i] ≤ 150                                       ∀ i ∈ I

(C12a) b[i] ≤ t_pu(i) + 480·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]        ∀ i ∈ I
(C12b) b[i] ≥ t_pu(i) − 480·Σ_{j:(j,i)∈A} x[j,i]        ∀ i ∈ I
(C12c) b[i] ≤ b[j] + 480·(1 − x[i,j])                   ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
(C12d) b[i] ≥ b[j] − 480·(1 − x[i,j])                   ∀ (i,j) ∈ A
(C13)  t_do(i) − b[i] ≤ 480                             ∀ i ∈ I

(C14, optional fairness)  W ≥ m[i]                       ∀ i ∈ I
                          minimize W secondarily
```

### 7.7 Algorithm to extract the optimal task chains

Given the optimal solution (x*, s*, e*, f*, m*, b*):

```
chains ← empty list
starts ← { i ∈ I : s*[i] = 1 }
for each i ∈ starts do
    chain ← [i]
    cur ← i
    while e*[cur] = 0 do
        nxt ← the unique j with x*[cur, j] = 1
        chain.append(nxt)
        cur ← nxt
    end while
    chains.append(chain)
end for

# Sanity checks
assert every task appears in exactly one chain
assert len(chains) = Σ s*[i] = objective value
for each chain c:
    assert continuous driving rule respected (use f*)
    assert Σ_{i∈c} dist(i) ≤ 150
    assert t_do(last) − t_pu(first) ≤ 480
    assert handover station rule respected
```

### 7.8 Connection table output
For each chain c = (i₁, i₂, …, i_k) emit a row:

| chain_id | task_id | train | t_pu | s_pu | t_do | s_do | gap_to_next | reset? | cum_drive | cum_km | duty_span |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 331 | M16 | 10:03 | M | 10:57 | Z | 0:06:21 | no | 54.5 | 26.4 | 0:54 |
| 1 | 332 | N27 | 11:04 | Z | 11:40 | A | … | … | … | … | … |

This table is the direct deliverable for the dispatcher.

---

### Summary
Variant 1 is the formulation to implement. It is a single MILP with ~3 000 binary variables and ~600 continuous variables, ~10·|A| constraints, tight big-M values equal to the resource caps, and a DAG that makes subtour elimination unnecessary. Any modern MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, HiGHS, SCIP) will return a proven-optimal crew plan in well under a minute for the 200-task instance, and the chain-extraction algorithm in §7.7 turns the solution directly into the dispatcher’s connection table.

# MILP Model: Employee Hiring Optimization

## 1. Sets and Indices

Let $I = \{A, B, C, D, E\}$ be the set of candidates.

## 2. Parameters

| Candidate | Salary ($) | Education | Experience (years) |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|--------------------|
| A | 8,100 | Bachelor's | 3 |
| B | 20,000 | Master's | 10 |
| C | 21,000 | PhD | 4 |
| D | 3,000 | No degree | 3 |
| E | 8,000 | No degree | 7 |

Additional parameters:
- $B_{max} = 35{,}000$ — maximum budget
- $N_{max} = 3$ — maximum number of hires
- $N_{min} = 2$ — minimum number of hires
- $E_{min} = 12$ — minimum total years of experience

## 3. Decision Variables

$$
x_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if candidate } i \in I \text{ is hired} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

# MILP Code for Hiring Selection Problem

I'll provide implementations in both **Python (PuLP)** and **GAMS**.

## Python Implementation (using PuLP)

```python
from pulp import *

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Problem data
# ----------------------------------------------------------
candidates = ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E']

salary     = {'A':  8100, 'B': 20000, 'C': 21000, 'D':  3000, 'E':  8000}
experience = {'A':     3, 'B':    10, 'C':     4, 'D':     3, 'E':     7}
# Indicator for advanced degree (Master's or PhD)
adv_deg    = {'A':     0, 'B':     1, 'C':     1, 'D':     0, 'E':     0}

BUDGET_LIMIT = 35000
MIN_HIRES    = 2
MAX_HIRES    = 3
MIN_EXPERIENCE = 12

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Build the MILP
# ----------------------------------------------------------
prob = LpProblem("Hiring_Selection", LpMinimize)

# Decision variables: x_i in {0,1}
x = LpVariable.dicts("hire", candidates, cat='Binary')

# Objective: minimize total salary cost
prob += (
    lpSum(salary[i] * x[i] for i in candidates),
    "Total_Salary"
)

# Constraint 1: Budget
prob += (
    lpSum(salary[i] * x[i] for i in candidates) <= BUDGET_LIMIT,
    "Budget"
)

# Constraint 2: At most 3 hires
prob += (
    lpSum(x[i] for i in candidates) <= MAX_HIRES,
    "Max_Hires"
)

# Constraint 3: At least 2 hires
prob += (
    lpSum(x[i] for i in candidates) >= MIN_HIRES,
    "Min_Hires"
)

# Constraint 4: At least one advanced degree (B or C)
prob += (
    lpSum(adv_deg[i] * x[i] for i in candidates) >= 1,
    "Advanced_Degree"
)

# Constraint 5: Total work experience at least 12 years
prob += (
    lpSum(experience[i] * x[i] for i in candidates) >= MIN_EXPERIENCE,
    "Experience"
)

# Constraint 6: At most one of A and E (similar skills)
prob += (
    x['A'] + x['E'] <= 1,
    "A_or_E"
)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Solve
# ----------------------------------------------------------
prob.solve(PULP_CBC_CMD(msg=0))

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Report results
# ----------------------------------------------------------
print(f"Status           : {LpStatus[prob.status]}")
print(f"Optimal cost (Z) : {value(prob.objective):,.0f}\n")
print("Hiring decisions:")
for i in candidates:
    print(f"  Candidate {i}: hired = {int(value(x[i]))}")
```

Optimal cost (Z) : 23,000

  Candidate C: hired = 0

from pulp import *

candidates = ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E']

BUDGET_LIMIT = 35000

MAX_HIRES    = 3
MIN_EXPERIENCE = 12

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Build the MILP
# ----------------------------------------------------------
prob = LpProblem("Hiring_Selection", LpMinimize)

# Decision variables: x_i in {0,1}
x = LpVariable.dicts("hire", candidates, cat='Binary')

# Objective: minimize total salary cost
prob += (
    lpSum(salary[i] * x[i] for i in candidates),
    "Total_Salary"
)

# Constraint 1: Budget
prob += (
    lpSum(salary[i] * x[i] for i in candidates) <= BUDGET_LIMIT,
    "Budget"
)

# Constraint 2: At most 3 hires
prob += (
    lpSum(x[i] for i in candidates) <= MAX_HIRES,
    "Max_Hires"
)

# Constraint 3: At least 2 hires
prob += (
    lpSum(x[i] for i in candidates) >= MIN_HIRES,
    "Min_Hires"
)

# Constraint 4: At least one advanced degree (B or C)
prob += (
    lpSum(adv_deg[i] * x[i] for i in candidates) >= 1,
    "Advanced_Degree"
)

# Constraint 5: Total work experience at least 12 years
prob += (
    lpSum(experience[i] * x[i] for i in candidates) >= MIN_EXPERIENCE,
    "Experience"
)

# Constraint 6: At most one of A and E (similar skills)
prob += (
    x['A'] + x['E'] <= 1,
    "A_or_E"
)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Solve
# ----------------------------------------------------------
prob.solve(PULP_CBC_CMD(msg=0))

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Report results
# ----------------------------------------------------------

print(f"Optimal cost (Z) : {value(prob.objective):,.0f}\n")
print("Hiring decisions:")
for i in candidates:

messages.content:
# Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) Model: Hiring Decision Problem

## 1. Sets and Indices
- $I = \{A, B, C, D, E\}$ — set of candidates

## 2. Parameters

| Candidate | Salary ($) | Experience (yrs) | Education |
|:---------:|:----------:|:----------------:|:---------:|
| A | 8,100 | 3 | — |
| B | 20,000 | 10 | Master's |
| C | 21,000 | 4 | PhD |
| D | 3,000 | 3 | — |
| E | 8,000 | 7 | — |

Let $s_i$ = salary of candidate $i$, and $e_i$ = years of experience of candidate $i$.

## 3. Decision Variables
$$
x_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if candidate } i \text{ is hired} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad \forall i \in I
$$

## 4. Objective Function
Minimize the total salary paid to the selected candidates:
$$
\min Z = 8100\,x_A + 20000\,x_B + 21000\,x_C + 3000\,x_D + 8000\,x_E
$$

## 5. Constraints

**(C1) Hire at most 3 employees:**
$$
x_A + x_B + x_C + x_D + x_E \leq 3
$$

**(C2) Total salary within budget of $35,000:**
$$
8100\,x_A + 20000\,x_B + 21000\,x_C + 3000\,x_D + 8000\,x_E \leq 35000
$$

**(C3) At least one Master's or PhD candidate (B or C):**
$$
x_B + x_C \geq 1
$$

**(C4) Total work experience of at least 12 years:**
$$
3\,x_A + 10\,x_B + 4\,x_C + 3\,x_D + 7\,x_E \geq 12
$$

**(C5) At most one of A or E (similar skills):**
$$
x_A + x_E \leq 1
$$

**(C6) Hire at least 2 employees:**
$$
x_A + x_B + x_C + x_D + x_E \geq 2
$$

**(C7) Binary (integrality) constraints:**
$$
x_i \in \{0, 1\}, \quad \forall i \in \{A, B, C, D, E\}
$$

## 6. Complete Compact Form

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad & \sum_{i \in I} s_i \, x_i \\[4pt]
\text{s.t.} \quad & 2 \leq \sum_{i \in I} x_i \leq 3 \\
& \sum_{i \in I} s_i \, x_i \leq 35000 \\
& x_B + x_C \geq 1 \\
& \sum_{i \in I} e_i \, x_i \geq 12 \\
& x_A + x_E \leq 1 \\
& x_i \in \{0, 1\}, \quad \forall i \in I
\end{aligned}
$$

## 7. Explanation of Model Elements

- **Decision variables** $x_i$ are **binary**, since each candidate is either hired (1) or not (0).
- **Objective function** is linear in the variables and minimizes total salary expenditure.
- **Constraint C1** caps the team size at 3.
- **Constraint C2** enforces the budget cap by limiting the weighted sum of salaries.
- **Constraint C3** uses an indicator-style inequality to ensure at least one highly educated candidate is selected.
- **Constraint C4** aggregates experience years and requires a minimum total of 12.
- **Constraint C5** is a mutual-exclusivity constraint preventing the simultaneous hiring of A and E.
- **Constraint C6** sets a minimum team size of 2.
- **Constraint C7** enforces integrality, making this a true MILP rather than a pure LP.

## 8. Expected Optimal Solution

Solving this MILP yields the optimal solution:
$$
x_B^* = 1, \quad x_D^* = 1, \quad x_A^* = x_C^* = x_E^* = 0
$$

**Optimal objective value:** $Z^* = 20000 + 3000 = \$23{,}000$

This selection satisfies all constraints: 2 employees hired (within [2,3]), budget used is $23{,}000 \leq \$35{,}000$, B satisfies the Master's requirement, total experience is $10 + 3 = 13 \geq 12$ years, and the A/E conflict is avoided.

|:---------:|:----------:|:---------:|:----------------:|

| D         | 3,000      | None      | 3                |
| E         | 8,000      | None      | 7                |

## 4. Objective Function

Minimize the total salary paid:

$$\min \; Z = 8100\,x_A + 20000\,x_B + 21000\,x_C + 3000\,x_D + 8000\,x_E$$

## 5. Constraints

**(a) Maximum of 3 new employees:**
$$x_A + x_B + x_C + x_D + x_E \leq 3$$

\begin{aligned}

## 1. Sets and Indices

messages.content: Inspired by the provided input: Generate a complete, linear model with variables, objective function and constraints. The MILP should be described completely with equations and assumptions. The input is inspiration, so keep close to it, if you can and if information is missing, make reasonable assumptions and mark them as such. Do not ask questions. Use the following approach for your task: Use the or_coder to generate a code-based model based on the provided input. Interpret the code and just return the equations for objective functions, variables and constraints as text. Do not return any code.

response.reasoning:
Let me think about this problem. We need a MILP: production planning with 40 workers, each producing 20 units/month. Demand table for 6 months. Overtime: each worker can produce max 6 extra units per month, cost 5 euros/unit. Inventory holding: 10 euros per unit per month. Hiring/layoff: max ±5 per month change, hiring cost 500 euros per person, layoff cost 700 euros per person.

Initially warehouse empty, and must be empty at end of semester. Maximize revenue.

We need revenue per unit — hmm, the problem says "maximize revenue". We need a selling price. It's missing; we can make a reasonable assumption and mark it as such. E.g., selling price p per unit. Perhaps assume p = 30 euros/unit? Or we can define it as a parameter. Let's assume p ≥ some value. Let me set p = 30 €/unit as an assumption (or maybe define revenue as p per unit sold). Actually maybe a common textbook version: selling price 30 per unit. Let's just make p a parameter and note a default of 30.

Let me use the or_coder tool to generate the model code, then interpret and write equations.

Let me think about the model structure first.

Sets:
- T = {1,...,6} months.
- Employees i = 1..40 (or just use aggregated headcount W_t).

Variables:
- W_t = number of workers employed in month t (integer, 35 ≤ W_t ≤ 45 since max ±5 change from 40 each month; actually hires limited by ±5 per month).
- Actually with hiring/layoff constraints: |W_t - W_{t-1}| ≤ 5, W_0 = 40, and per month hires H_t ≥ 0, layoffs L_t ≥ 0 with W_t = W_{t-1} + H_t - L_t.
- O_t = overtime units produced in month t (continuous or integer), 0 ≤ O_t ≤ 6 * W_t.
- P_t = production units in month t (from regular time) = 20 * W_t. Could be a variable P_t ≥ 0 with P_t ≤ 20 W_t... but production is exactly what workers produce; maybe regular production can be less than capacity? Since we're maximizing revenue and demand must be met presumably (no backlogging), production can exceed demand to build inventory (which is costly). Actually regular production is at the workers' rate; we could allow idle capacity: 0 ≤ P_t ≤ 20 W_t. Hmm, but if we have to hire workers to meet demand... Actually workers produce 20 units/month each; with 40 workers → 800 units/month regular capacity, plus overtime 240 units → max 1040.

Let's think: demand max is 900 (month 5). Regular 40 workers = 800. So month 5 needs at least 100 overtime units if workforce stays at 40. Max overtime is 240 with 40 workers. Fine.

Model with variables:
- y_{i,t} = binary: worker i employed in month t (or just aggregate). Using aggregate integer W_t is cleaner.

Let's use aggregated: W_t ∈ Z, H_t ≥ 0 integer, L_t ≥ 0 integer.

Hmm, but "max ±5 per month" - so |W_t - W_{t-1}| ≤ 5.

Inventory: I_t ≥ 0, I_0 = 0, I_6 = 0.
Sales: S_t ≤ d_t (demand), and S_t = P_t + O_t + I_{t-1} - I_t.

Objective: maximize p * Σ S_t - 5 Σ O_t - 10 Σ_{t=1}^{5} I_t (holding cost on inventory carried from month t to t+1) - 500 Σ H_t - 700 Σ L_t.

Note: since demand must be met (usually "demand must be satisfied"), we can set S_t = d_t as equality if no backlogging allowed and demand must be met. But then revenue is constant, and the objective reduces to cost minimization. Hmm. The problem says "maximize revenue" — with fixed revenue p*d, maximizing revenue is equivalent to minimizing costs. Maybe better to allow sales ≤ demand and maximize revenue, which naturally forces satisfying demand if the price exceeds marginal cost (holding + overtime costs). Actually with price p = 30 > holding 10, the model would prefer to produce in month 1 and store rather than overtime? Wait: producing early and storing costs 10/unit/month; overtime costs 5/unit. So it's cheaper to overtime in month 5 than to produce early and hold for 2 months (cost 20). But production early requires capacity: regular production capacity is fixed at 20 W_t, and workers are paid regardless (salaries not counted? Workers' salaries aren't in the cost list, interesting). So regular production is essentially free (salaries not modeled) up to capacity, but limited to capacity.

Hmm — if regular production is free and unlimited up to capacity, then the optimal would hire workers to produce more, and store. But hire costs 500 per person, and each person gives 20 units/month → 25 €/unit. Hmm.

So the "free" regular production makes it interesting: hire 5 workers in month 1 (cost 500), produce 100 extra units... Let's not overthink; the model should just be presented.

Let me decide: revenue per unit sold p (assumption: p = 30 €/unit). Actually, to make "maximize revenue" meaningful and avoid the model not meeting demand, let's include sales variables S_t ≤ d_t with the objective maximizing p Σ S_t minus costs. Since all costs are per unit small relative to p=30, all demand would be satisfied in most cases... Let's check: could it be profitable to not meet demand? Meeting demand in month t via overtime costs 5/unit; storing from previous month costs 10/unit/month. Price 30/unit. So always beneficial to meet demand (cost at most 5 or 10 to supply a unit, revenue 30). So demand is satisfied in the optimum. Fine.

Actually wait: could it be cheaper to not meet demand? **Mathematical Formulation:**

Sets:
- T = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} (planning horizon, months)

Parameters:
- W_0 = 40 (initial workforce)
- I_0 = 0 (initial inventory)
- I_final = 0 (required final inventory)

- o_max = 6 (maximum overtime per worker per month)
- c_o = 5 (overtime cost per unit, €/unit)
- c_h = 10 (holding cost per unit per month, €/unit/month)
- c_H = 500 (hiring cost per person, €/person)
- c_L = 700 (layoff cost per person, €/person)
- r = 20 (selling price per unit, €/unit)
- Δ = 5 (maximum workforce change per month)
- d_t = [700, 600, 500, 800, 900, 800] for t = 1,...,6 (demand)

Decision Variables:
- W_t ∈ ℤ_+: number of workers in month t
- H_t ∈ ℤ_+: number of workers hired at start of month t
- L_t ∈ ℤ_+: number of workers laid off at start of month t
- O_t ∈ ℝ_+: overtime units produced in month t
- I_t ∈ ℝ_+: inventory at end of month t
- S_t ∈ ℝ_+: units sold in month t

Objective Function:
Maximize Z = Σ_{t=1}^{6} [r·S_t - c_o·O_t - c_h·I_t - c_H·H_t - c_L·L_t]

Constraints:
1. Workforce balance: W_t = W_{t-1} + H_t - L_t, ∀t ∈ T
2. Hiring limit: H_t ≤ Δ, ∀t ∈ T
3. Layoff limit: L_t ≤ Δ, ∀t ∈ T
4. Overtime limit: O_t ≤ o_max · W_t, ∀t ∈ T
5. Inventory balance: I_t = I_{t-1} + p·W_t + O_t - S_t, ∀t ∈ T
6. Demand satisfaction: S_t = d_t, ∀t ∈ T
7. Initial inventory: I_0 = 0
8. Final inventory: I_6 = 0
9. Non-negativity: W_t, H_t, L_t, O_t, I_t, S_t ≥ 0
10. Integrality: W_t, H_t, L_t ∈ ℤ

Now let me write the COPTPY code.

```python
import coptpy as cp
import numpy as np

def solve_production_planning(integer_vars=True):
    """
    Solve the production planning problem.
    
    Parameters:
    -----------
    integer_vars : bool
        If True, solve MILP (W, H, L are integers).
        If False, solve LP relaxation (all variables continuous).
    
    Returns:
    --------
    obj_val : float
        Optimal objective value (profit).
    solution : dict
        Dictionary with variable values per month.
    """
    # Create COPT environment and model
    env = cp.Envr()
    model = env.createModel("ProductionPlanning")
    
    # ----- Parameters -----
    T = 6                              # Number of months
    W0 = 40                            # Initial workforce
    I0 = 0                             # Initial inventory
    I_final = 0                        # Final inventory (required)
    p = 20                             # Regular production per worker per month
    o_max = 6                          # Max overtime per worker per month
    c_o = 5                            # Overtime cost (€/unit)
    c_h = 10                           # Holding cost (€/unit/month)
    c_H = 500                          # Hiring cost (€/person)
    c_L = 700                          # Layoff cost (€/person)
    r = 20                             # Selling price (€/unit)
    delta = 5                          # Max workforce change per month
    demand = [700, 600, 500, 800, 900, 800]  # Monthly demand
    
    # ----- Variable types -----
    vtype_int = cp.COPT.INTEGER if integer_vars else cp.COPT.CONTINUOUS
    
    # ----- Decision Variables -----
    W = model.addVars(T, lb=0, vtype=vtype_int, nameprefix="W")
    H = model.addVars(T, lb=0, vtype=vtype_int, nameprefix="H")
    L = model.addVars(T, lb=0, vtype=vtype_int, nameprefix="L")
    O = model.addVars(T, lb=0, vtype=cp.COPT.CONTINUOUS, nameprefix="O")
    I = model.addVars(T, lb=0, vtype=cp.COPT.CONTINUOUS, nameprefix="I")
    S = model.addVars(T, lb=0, vtype=cp.COPT.CONTINUOUS, nameprefix="S")
    
    # ----- Objective: Maximize profit -----
    profit = cp.LinExpr()
    for t in range(T):
        profit += r * S[t]                    # Revenue
        profit -= c_o * O[t]                  # Overtime cost
        profit -= c_h * I[t]                  # Holding cost
        profit -= c_H * H[t]                  # Hiring cost
        profit -= c_L * L[t]                  # Layoff cost
    model.setObjective(profit, sense=cp.COPT.MAXIMIZE)
    
    # ----- Constraints -----
    for t in range(T):
        # 1. Workforce balance
        if t == 0:
            model.addConstr(W[t] == W0 + H[t] - L[t], name=f"workforce_{t}")
        else:
            model.addConstr(W[t] == W[t-1] + H[t] - L[t], name=f"workforce_{t}")
        
        # 2. Hiring limit
        model.addConstr(H[t] <= delta, name=f"hire_limit_{t}")
        
        # 3. Layoff limit
        model.addConstr(L[t] <= delta, name=f"layoff_limit_{t}")
        
        # 4. Overtime limit
        model.addConstr(O[t] <= o_max * W[t], name=f"overtime_limit_{t}")
        
        # 5. Inventory balance
        if t == 0:
            model.addConstr(I[t] == I0 + p * W[t] + O[t] - S[t], name=f"inventory_{t}")
        else:
            model.addConstr(I[t] == I[t-1] + p * W[t] + O[t] - S[t], name=f"inventory_{t}")
        
        # 6. Demand satisfaction
        model.addConstr(S[t] == demand[t], name=f"demand_{t}")
    
    # 7. Final inventory
    model.addConstr(I[T-1] == I_final, name="final_inventory")
    
    # ----- Solve -----
    model.solve()
    
    # ----- Extract solution -----
    obj_val = model.objval
    solution = {
        'W': [W[t].x for t in range(T)],
        'H': [H[t].x for t in range(T)],
        'L': [L[t].x for t in range(T)],
        'O': [O[t].x for t in range(T)],
        'I': [I[t].x for t in range(T)],
        'S': [S[t].x for t in range(T)],
    }
    
    return obj_val, solution

# Solve MILP
milp_obj, milp_sol = solve_production_planning(integer_vars=True)
print("=" * 60)
print("MILP SOLUTION")
print("=" * 60)
print(f"Optimal Profit: {milp_obj:.2f} €")
print(f"{'Month':<8}{'W':<8}{'H':<8}{'L':<8}{'O':<10}{'I':<10}{'S':<10}")
for t in range(6):
    print(f"{t+1:<8}{milp_sol['W'][t]:<8.0f}{milp_sol['H'][t]:<8.0f}{milp_sol['L'][t]:<8.0f}{milp_sol['O'][t]:<10.2f}{milp_sol['I'][t]:<10.2f}{milp_sol['S'][t]:<10.0f}")

# Solve LP relaxation
lp_obj, lp_sol = solve_production_planning(integer_vars=False)
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("LP RELAXATION SOLUTION")

\[
T=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}

\[
W_0=40,\qquad I_0=0

Demand parameters:

\[
(d_1,d_2,d_3,d_4,d_5,d_6)
=(700,600,500,800,900,800)
\]

All model constraints below apply for every \(t\in T\).

---

## 2. Decision variables

| Variable | Meaning | Domain |
|---|---|---|
| \(W_t\) | Workers employed during month \(t\) | \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) |
| \(H_t\) | Workers hired at the beginning of month \(t\) | \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) |
| \(F_t\) | Workers laid off at the beginning of month \(t\) | \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) |
| \(O_t\) | Overtime production in month \(t\), in units | \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) |
| \(I_t\) | Ending inventory in month \(t\), in units | \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) |
| \(S_t\) | Units sold in month \(t\) | \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) |

This is a pure integer linear program, and therefore a special case of a MILP.

---

## 3. Objective function

Minimize total operating cost:

\[
\boxed{
\min Z=
\sum_{t=1}^{6}
\left(
5O_t+10I_t+500H_t+700F_t
\right)
}
\]

The terms represent:

- \(5O_t\): overtime production cost;
- \(10I_t\): inventory holding cost on ending inventory;
- \(500H_t\): hiring cost;
- \(700F_t\): layoff cost.

Regular-time production has no explicit production cost in the model. If the selling price is a constant \(p\), total revenue is

\[
p\sum_{t=1}^{6}d_t=4300p,
\]

which is fixed because all demand must be met. Thus minimizing \(Z\) is equivalent to maximizing profit.

---

## 4. Constraints

### 4.1 Workforce balance

\[
\boxed{
W_t-W_{t-1}-H_t+F_t=0
\qquad \forall t\in T
}
\]

with

\[
W_0=40.
\]

This states that month-\(t\) employment equals prior employment plus hires minus layoffs.

### 4.2 Hiring and layoff limits

\[
\boxed{
0\le H_t\le 5
\qquad \forall t\in T
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
0\le F_t\le 5
\qquad \forall t\in T
}
\]

These are separate gross hiring and layoff limits, as specified in the description.

### 4.3 Overtime capacity

\[
\boxed{
O_t\le 6W_t
\qquad \forall t\in T
}
\]

Each worker can produce at most six overtime units per month.

### 4.4 Inventory balance

\[
\boxed{
I_t-I_{t-1}-20W_t-O_t+S_t=0
\qquad \forall t\in T
}
\]

with

\[
I_0=0.
\]

Regular production in month \(t\) is \(20W_t\), overtime production is \(O_t\), and sales are \(S_t\).

### 4.5 Demand satisfaction

\[
\boxed{
S_t=d_t
\qquad \forall t\in T
}
\]

or explicitly,

\[
\begin{aligned}
S_1&=700,\\
S_2&=600,\\
S_3&=500,\\
S_4&=800,\\
S_5&=900,\\
S_6&=800.
\end{aligned}
\]

Because all demand must be met, there are no lost-sales or backlogging variables.

### 4.6 Required ending inventory

\[
\boxed{
I_6=0
}
\]

The company may build inventory during the semester, but no inventory may remain at the end of month 6.

### 4.7 Variable domains

\[
\boxed{
W_t,H_t,F_t,O_t,I_t,S_t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}
\qquad \forall t\in T
}
\]

---

## 5. Complete MILP

The model can be written compactly as:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad
& \sum_{t=1}^{6}
\left(5O_t+10I_t+500H_t+700F_t\right) \\[1mm]
\text{s.t.}\quad

&& \forall t\in T,\\
& 0\le H_t\le5
&& \forall t\in T,\\
& 0\le F_t\le5
&& \forall t\in T,\\
& O_t\le6W_t
&& \forall t\in T,\\
& I_t-I_{t-1}-20W_t-O_t+S_t=0
&& \forall t\in T,\\
& S_t=d_t
&& \forall t\in T,\\
& I_6=0,\\
& W_0=40,\qquad I_0=0,\\
& W_t,H_t,F_t,O_t,I_t,S_t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}
&& \forall t\in T.
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(S_t=d_t\) fixes sales, an equivalent reduced formulation eliminates \(S_t\) and uses

\[
I_t=I_{t-1}+20W_t+O_t-d_t
\qquad \forall t\in T.
\]

---

## 6. LP relaxation and integrality gap

To obtain the LP relaxation, replace the integer domains with continuous domains:

\[
W_t,H_t,F_t,O_t,I_t,S_t\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}
\qquad \forall t\in T,
\]

while retaining all objective coefficients and constraints.

Let:

- \(Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}\) be the optimal MILP objective value;
- \(Z_{\mathrm{LP}}\) be the optimal LP-relaxation objective value.

Since every integer-feasible solution is also LP-feasible,

\[
\boxed{Z_{\mathrm{LP}}\le Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}.}
\]

The absolute integrality gap is

\[
\boxed{
G_{\mathrm{abs}}=Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}-Z_{\mathrm{LP}}
}
\]

and, when \(Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}>0\), the relative integrality gap can be measured as

\[
\boxed{
G_{\mathrm{rel}}
=
\frac{Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}-Z_{\mathrm{LP}}}
{Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}}.
}
\]

A larger gap indicates that imposing integer-valued workforce and production decisions has a greater cost relative to the continuous relaxation.

messages.content: Based on your input, generate a complete, linear MILP with variables, objective function and constraints. Explain the elements of the model.
<benchmark text>

response.content:
## 1. Sets and data

\[
T=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}
\]

Initial conditions:

\[
W_0=40,\qquad I_0=0
\]

Demand parameters:

\[
(d_1,d_2,d_3,d_4,d_5,d_6)
=(700,600,500,800,900,800)
\]

All model constraints below apply for every \(t\in T\).

---

## 2. Decision variables

| Variable | Meaning | Domain |
|---|---|---|
| \(W_t\) | Workers employed during month \(t\) | \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) |
| \(H_t\) | Workers hired at the beginning of month \(t\) | \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) |
| \(F_t\) | Workers laid off at the beginning of month \(t\) | \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) |
| \(O_t\) | Overtime production in month \(t\), in units | \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) |
| \(I_t\) | Ending inventory in month \(t\), in units | \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) |
| \(S_t\) | Units sold in month \(t\) | \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) |

This is a pure integer linear program, and therefore a special case of a MILP.

---

## 3. Objective function

Minimize total operating cost:

\[
\boxed{
\min Z=
\sum_{t=1}^{6}
\left(
5O_t+10I_t+500H_t+700F_t
\right)
}
\]

The terms represent:

- \(5O_t\): overtime production cost;
- \(10I_t\): inventory holding cost on ending inventory;
- \(500H_t\): hiring cost;
- \(700F_t\): layoff cost.

Regular-time production has no explicit production cost in the model. If the selling price is a constant \(p\), total revenue is

\[
p\sum_{t=1}^{6}d_t=4300p,
\]

which is fixed because all demand must be met. Thus minimizing \(Z\) is equivalent to maximizing profit.

---

## 4. Constraints

### 4.1 Workforce balance

\[
\boxed{
W_t-W_{t-1}-H_t+F_t=0
\qquad \forall t\in T
}
\]

with

\[
W_0=40.
\]

This states that month-\(t\) employment equals prior employment plus hires minus layoffs.

### 4.2 Hiring and layoff limits

\[
\boxed{
0\le H_t\le 5
\qquad \forall t\in T
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
0\le F_t\le 5
\qquad \forall t\in T
}
\]

These are separate gross hiring and layoff limits, as specified in the description.

### 4.3 Overtime capacity

\[
\boxed{
O_t\le 6W_t
\qquad \forall t\in T
}
\]

Each worker can produce at most six overtime units per month.

### 4.4 Inventory balance

\[
\boxed{
I_t-I_{t-1}-20W_t-O_t+S_t=0
\qquad \forall t\in T
}
\]

with

\[
I_0=0.
\]

Regular production in month \(t\) is \(20W_t\), overtime production is \(O_t\), and sales are \(S_t\).

### 4.5 Demand satisfaction

\[
\boxed{
S_t=d_t
\qquad \forall t\in T
}
\]

or explicitly,

\[
\begin{aligned}
S_1&=700,\\
S_2&=600,\\
S_3&=500,\\
S_4&=800,\\
S_5&=900,\\
S_6&=800.
\end{aligned}
\]

Because all demand must be met, there are no lost-sales or backlogging variables.

### 4.6 Required ending inventory

\[
\boxed{
I_6=0
}
\]

The company may build inventory during the semester, but no inventory may remain at the end of month 6.

### 4.7 Variable domains

\[
\boxed{
W_t,H_t,F_t,O_t,I_t,S_t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}
\qquad \forall t\in T
}
\]

---

## 5. Complete MILP

The model can be written compactly as:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad
& \sum_{t=1}^{6}
\left(5O_t+10I_t+500H_t+700F_t\right) \\[1mm]
\text{s.t.}\quad
& W_t-W_{t-1}-H_t+F_t=0
&& \forall t\in T,\\
& 0\le H_t\le5
&& \forall t\in T,\\
& 0\le F_t\le5
&& \forall t\in T,\\
& O_t\le6W_t
&& \forall t\in T,\\
& I_t-I_{t-1}-20W_t-O_t+S_t=0
&& \forall t\in T,\\
& S_t=d_t
&& \forall t\in T,\\
& I_6=0,\\
& W_0=40,\qquad I_0=0,\\
& W_t,H_t,F_t,O_t,I_t,S_t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}
&& \forall t\in T.
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(S_t=d_t\) fixes sales, an equivalent reduced formulation eliminates \(S_t\) and uses

\[
I_t=I_{t-1}+20W_t+O_t-d_t
\qquad \forall t\in T.
\]

---

## 6. LP relaxation and integrality gap

To obtain the LP relaxation, replace the integer domains with continuous domains:

\[
W_t,H_t,F_t,O_t,I_t,S_t\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}
\qquad \forall t\in T,
\]

while retaining all objective coefficients and constraints.

Let:

- \(Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}\) be the optimal MILP objective value;
- \(Z_{\mathrm{LP}}\) be the optimal LP-relaxation objective value.

Since every integer-feasible solution is also LP-feasible,

\[
\boxed{Z_{\mathrm{LP}}\le Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}.}
\]

The absolute integrality gap is

\[
\boxed{
G_{\mathrm{abs}}=Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}-Z_{\mathrm{LP}}
}
\]

and, when \(Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}>0\), the relative integrality gap can be measured as

\[
\boxed{
G_{\mathrm{rel}}
=
\frac{Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}-Z_{\mathrm{LP}}}
{Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}}.
}
\]

A larger gap indicates that imposing integer-valued workforce and production decisions has a greater cost relative to the continuous relaxation.

messages.content: Based on your input, generate a complete, linear MILP with variables, objective function and constraints. Explain the elements of the model.
<benchmark text>

response.content:
## 1. Sets and parameters

\[
T=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
W_0&=40, & I_0&=0,\\
p&=20, & p_{\text{extra}}&=6,\\
c_{\text{overtime}}&=5, & c_{\text{hold}}&=10,\\
c_{\text{hire}}&=500, & c_{\text{fire}}&=700,\\
\max_{\text{change}}&=5,
\end{aligned}
\]

with demand

\[
(d_1,d_2,d_3,d_4,d_5,d_6)=(700,600,500,800,900,800).
\]

## 2. Decision variables

For each month \(t\in T\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
W_t &\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0} &&\text{workers employed during month }t,\\
H_t &\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0} &&\text{workers hired at the beginning of month }t,\\
F_t &\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0} &&\text{workers laid off at the beginning of month }t,\\
O_t &\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0} &&\text{overtime units produced in month }t,\\
I_t &\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0} &&\text{inventory at the end of month }t,\\
S_t &\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0} &&\text{units sold in month }t.
\end{aligned}
\]

The boundary values \(W_0=40\) and \(I_0=0\) are fixed parameters, not decision variables.

---

## 3. Complete MILP formulation

### Objective function

Minimize total overtime, inventory-holding, hiring, and layoff costs:

\[
\boxed{
\min Z=
\sum_{t=1}^{6}
\left(
5O_t+10I_t+500H_t+700F_t
\right)
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\min Z=
5\sum_{t=1}^{6}O_t
+10\sum_{t=1}^{6}I_t
+500\sum_{t=1}^{6}H_t
+700\sum_{t=1}^{6}F_t.
\]

### Constraints

#### Workforce balance

\[
W_t-W_{t-1}-H_t+F_t=0,
\qquad t\in T,
\]

with

\[
W_0=40.
\]

#### Hiring and layoff limits

\[
0\le H_t\le 5,
\qquad t\in T,
\]

\[
0\le F_t\le 5,
\qquad t\in T.
\]

#### Overtime capacity

\[
O_t-6W_t\le 0,
\qquad t\in T.
\]

Equivalently, \(O_t\le 6W_t\).

#### Inventory balance

\[
I_t-I_{t-1}-20W_t-O_t+S_t=0,
\qquad t\in T,
\]

with

\[
I_0=0.
\]

#### Demand satisfaction

\[
S_t=d_t,
\qquad t\in T.
\]

Written explicitly:

\[
\begin{aligned}
S_1&=700,\\
S_2&=600,\\
S_3&=500,\\
S_4&=800,\\
S_5&=900,\\
S_6&=800.
\end{aligned}
\]

#### Required ending inventory

\[
I_6=0.
\]

#### Variable domains

\[
W_t,H_t,F_t,O_t,I_t,S_t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0},
\qquad t\in T.
\]

---

## 4. Compact mathematical formulation

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad
&\sum_{t\in T}
\left(
5O_t+10I_t+500H_t+700F_t
\right)\\[1mm]
\text{s.t.}\quad
&W_t-W_{t-1}-H_t+F_t=0,
&&t\in T,\\
&0\le H_t\le 5,
&&t\in T,\\
&0\le F_t\le 5,
&&t\in T,\\
&O_t-6W_t\le 0,
&&t\in T,\\
&I_t-I_{t-1}-20W_t-O_t+S_t=0,
&&t\in T,\\
&S_t=d_t,
&&t\in T,\\
&I_6=0,\\
&W_0=40,\qquad I_0=0,\\
&W_t,H_t,F_t,O_t,I_t,S_t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},
&&t\in T.
\end{aligned}
\]

## 5. Model interpretation

- **Workforce balance:** The workforce in month \(t\) equals the previous month's workforce plus hires minus layoffs.
- **Hiring/layoff limits:** At most five workers may be hired and at most five may be laid off in any month.
- **Overtime capacity:** Each worker can produce at most six additional overtime units during the month.
- **Inventory balance:** Regular production is \(20W_t\), overtime production is \(O_t\), and sales are \(S_t\). The difference between production and sales becomes ending inventory.
- **Demand satisfaction:** Sales are exactly equal to demand, so lost sales and backlogging are not permitted.
- **Ending inventory:** All inventory produced or purchased for use during the semester must be sold by the end of month 6.
- **Objective:** Overtime, ending inventory, hiring, and layoffs are all penalized. Since sales are fixed at \(d_t\), revenue is constant and minimizing these costs is equivalent to maximizing profit.

No separate constraint prohibiting simultaneous hiring and layoffs is needed: because both hiring and layoff costs are positive, an optimal solution will never hire and lay off workers in the same month simultaneously.

## 6. LP relaxation and integrality gap

For the LP relaxation, replace the integer domains with

\[
W_t,H_t,F_t,O_t,I_t,S_t\in\mathbb R_{\ge0},
\qquad t\in T,
\]

while retaining the same objective and constraints. If the resulting objective is \(Z_{\mathrm{LP}}\) and the MILP objective is \(Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}\), then

\[
Z_{\mathrm{LP}}\le Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}.
\]

The absolute integrality gap can be measured as

\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{abs}}=Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}-Z_{\mathrm{LP}},
\]

and, when \(Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}\neq 0\), the relative gap is

\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{rel}}
=
\frac{Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}-Z_{\mathrm{LP}}}
{|Z_{\mathrm{MILP}}|}\times 100\%.
\]

This gap represents the additional cost caused by requiring workers, overtime production, inventory, and sales to be integer-valued.

messages.content: Inspired by the provided input: Generate a complete, linear model with variables, objective function and constraints. The MILP should be described completely with equations and assumptions. The input is inspiration, so keep close to it, if you can and if information is missing, make reasonable assumptions and mark them as such. Do not ask questions. Use the or_factory to generate a model based on the provided input, then choose the best. Just return the best model.
<benchmark text>

function.arguments:
{"count": 3, "description": "Workforce planning MILP for a single-product company over a 6-month semester.

Sets:
- T = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} (months of the planning horizon)

Parameters:
- W0 = 40 (initial number of workers)
- p = 20 (regular production rate per worker per month, units)
- p_extra = 6 (max overtime units per worker per month)
- c_overtime = 5 (cost per overtime unit, euros)
- c_hold = 10 (inventory holding cost per unit per month, euros)
- c_hire = 500 (hiring cost per worker, euros)
- c_fire = 700 (layoff cost per worker, euros)
- max_change = 5 (max number of workers that can be hired or laid off per month)
- d = [700, 600, 500, 800, 900, 800] (demand per month, units)
- I0 = 0 (initial inventory)
- I_end = 0 (required final inventory at end of month 6)

Decision variables (integer):
- W_t >= 0: number of workers employed in month t
- H_t >= 0: number of workers hired at the beginning of month t
- F_t >= 0: number of workers laid off at the beginning of month t
- O_t >= 0: overtime units produced in month t
- I_t >= 0: inventory at the end of month t
- S_t >= 0: units sold in month t

Constraints:
1) Workforce balance: W_t = W_{t-1} + H_t - F_t, for t in T, with W_0 = 40
2) Hiring/layoff limits: H_t <= 5, F_t <= 5, for t in T
3) Overtime capacity: O_t <= 6 * W_t, for t in T
4) Inventory balance: I_t = I_{t-1} + 20 * W_t + O_t - S_t, for t in T, with I_0 = 0
5) Demand satisfaction: S_t = d_t, for t in T (all demand must be met)
6) Final inventory: I_6 = 0

Objective: Minimize total cost (equivalent to maximizing profit when all demand is met at a fixed selling price):
min sum_{t in T} (5 * O_t + 10 * I_t + 500 * H_t + 700 * F_t)

Assumptions:
- Selling price is constant, so maximizing profit = minimizing total operating cost
- All demand must be met (no lost sales, no backlogging)
- Production in regular time is fixed at 20 units per worker per month regardless of W_t
- Hiring and layoff happen at the beginning of the month and affect production immediately
- Inventory is measured at end of month after production and sales
- Workers are integer-valued; overtime units and inventory are also integer

Second part: when all variables (W_t, H_t, F_t, O_t, I_t, S_t) are relaxed to be continuous (>= 0), the LP relaxation will yield an objective value <= the MILP optimal value. The gap quantifies the cost of integrality."}

## 1. Sets and Data

$$T = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$$

**Initial conditions:** $W_0 = 40$, $I_0 = 0$

**Demand:** $(d_1, d_2, d_3, d_4, d_5, d_6) = (700, 600, 500, 800, 900, 800)$

**Cost parameters:**
- Overtime: $c_o = 5$ €/unit
- Holding: $c_h = 10$ €/unit/month
- Hiring: $c_H = 500$ €/worker
- Layoff: $c_F = 700$ €/worker

**Capacity parameters:**
- Regular production: $p = 20$ units/worker/month
- Overtime cap: $p_e = 6$ units/worker/month
- Hiring/layoff limit: $\Delta = 5$ workers/month

## 2. Decision Variables

| Variable | Meaning | Domain |
|---|---|---|
| $W_t$ | Workers employed in month $t$ | $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ |
| $H_t$ | Workers hired at start of month $t$ | $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ |
| $F_t$ | Workers laid off at start of month $t$ | $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ |
| $O_t$ | Overtime units produced in month $t$ | $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ |
| $I_t$ | Ending inventory in month $t$ | $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ |
| $S_t$ | Units sold in month $t$ | $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ |

## 3. Objective Function

Since revenue $p \cdot \sum_t d_t = 4300p$ is fixed (all demand must be met), maximizing profit is equivalent to **minimizing total operating cost**:

$$\boxed{\min Z = \sum_{t=1}^{6} \left( 5\,O_t + 10\,I_t + 500\,H_t + 700\,F_t \right)}$$

## 4. Constraints

**Workforce balance:**
$$W_t - W_{t-1} - H_t + F_t = 0 \qquad \forall t \in T$$

**Hiring/layoff limits:**
$$0 \leq H_t \leq 5, \quad 0 \leq F_t \leq 5 \qquad \forall t \in T$$

**Overtime capacity:**
$$O_t \leq 6\,W_t \qquad \forall t \in T$$

**Inventory balance:**
$$I_t - I_{t-1} - 20\,W_t - O_t + S_t = 0 \qquad \forall t \in T$$

**Demand satisfaction (all demand must be met):**
$$S_t = d_t \qquad \forall t \in T$$

**Final warehouse condition:**
$$I_6 = 0$$

**Integrality:**
$$W_t, H_t, F_t, O_t, I_t, S_t \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} \qquad \forall t \in T$$

## 5. Compact MILP

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad & \sum_{t=1}^{6} (5O_t + 10I_t + 500H_t + 700F_t) \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & W_t - W_{t-1} - H_t + F_t = 0 && \forall t \\
& 0 \leq H_t \leq 5 && \forall t \\
& 0 \leq F_t \leq 5 && \forall t \\
& O_t \leq 6W_t && \forall t \\
& I_t - I_{t-1} - 20W_t - O_t + d_t = 0 && \forall t \\
& I_6 = 0 \\
& W_0 = 40,\ I_0 = 0 \\
& W_t, H_t, F_t, O_t, I_t \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} && \forall t
\end{aligned}
$$

## 6. LP Relaxation and Integrality Gap

When all variables are relaxed to continuous ($W_t, H_t, F_t, O_t, I_t \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$), every integer-feasible solution remains feasible, so:

$$\boxed{Z_{\text{LP}} \leq Z_{\text{MILP}}}$$

- **Absolute integrality gap:** $\Delta_{\text{abs}} = Z_{\text{MILP}} - Z_{\text{LP}}$
- **Relative integrality gap:** $\Delta_{\text{rel}} = \dfrac{Z_{\text{MILP}} - Z_{\text{LP}}}{|Z_{\text{MILP}}|} \times 100\%$

The LP relaxation typically allows fractional hires/layoffs and fractional overtime, which can reduce costs by smoothing the workforce trajectory. The gap measures the cost of forcing integer workforce decisions.

## 7. COPTPY Implementation Sketch

```python
from coptpy import *

env = Envr()
model = env.createModel(name="workforce")

T = range(1, 7)
d = {1:700, 2:600, 3:500, 4:800, 5:900, 6:800}

W = model.addVars(T, vtype=COPT.INTEGER, lb=0, nameprefix="W")
H = model.addVars(T, vtype=COPT.INTEGER, lb=0, ub=5, nameprefix="H")
F = model.addVars(T, vtype=COPT.INTEGER, lb=0, ub=5, nameprefix="F")
O = model.addVars(T, vtype=COPT.INTEGER, lb=0, nameprefix="O")
I = model.addVars(T, vtype=COPT.INTEGER, lb=0, nameprefix="I")

# Workforce balance
model.addConstrs((W[t] - (40 if t==1 else W[t-1]) - H[t] + F[t] == 0
                  for t in T), nameprefix="wf")

# Overtime capacity
model.addConstrs((O[t] <= 6*W[t] for t in T), nameprefix="ot")

# Inventory balance
prev_I = 0
for t in T:
    model.addConstr(I[t] == prev_I + 20*W[t] + O[t] - d[t], nameprefix=f"inv{t}")
    prev_I = I[t]

# Final inventory
model.addConstr(I[6] == 0, name="end_inv")

# Objective
model.setObjective(sum(5*O[t] + 10*I[t] + 500*H[t] + 700*F[t] for t in T),
                   sense=COPT.MINIMIZE)

model.solve()
print("MILP cost:", model.objval)
for t in T:
    print(f"t={t}: W={int(W[t].x)}, H={int(H[t].x)}, F={int(F[t].x)}, "
          f"O={int(O[t].x)}, I={int(I[t].x)}")

# LP relaxation: change vtype=COPT.CONTINUOUS for all variables, re-solve
```

## 8. Assumptions Made

1. **Constant selling price** — revenue is fixed, so maximizing profit = minimizing cost.
2. **No backlogging or lost sales** — all demand must be met each month.
3. **Hiring and layoffs occur at the start of the month** and immediately affect production.
4. **No simultaneous hire-and-fire in the same month** (implicitly optimal since both costs are positive).
5. **No regular-time production cost** — only overtime, holding, hiring, and layoff are penalized.
6. **Inventory measured at end of month** after production and sales.

```python
import pulp as pl

# -----------------------------
# Data (costs and budget in dollars)
# -----------------------------
restaurants = {
    "A": {"cost": 1_600_000, "income": 15_000},
    "B": {"cost": 2_500_000, "income": 40_000},
    "C": {"cost": 1_800_000, "income": 30_000},
    "D": {"cost": 3_000_000, "income": 50_000},
}

budget = 6_000_000

# -----------------------------
# MILP model
# -----------------------------
model = pl.LpProblem("Zhang_Restaurant_Capital_Budgeting", pl.LpMaximize)

# Binary purchase variables
x = {
    i: pl.LpVariable(f"x_{i}", cat=pl.LpBinary)
    for i in restaurants
}

# Objective: maximize total annual income
model += pl.lpSum(
    restaurants[i]["income"] * x[i] for i in restaurants
), "Total_Annual_Income"

# Capital budget constraint
model += pl.lpSum(
    restaurants[i]["cost"] * x[i] for i in restaurants
) <= budget, "Capital_Budget"

# Explicit at-most-once constraints
# (redundant given the binary domains, but included as requested)
for i in restaurants:
    model += x[i] <= 1, f"Purchase_At_Most_Once_{i}"

# Logical incompatibility: D cannot be purchased with A
model += x["A"] + x["D"] <= 1, "Incompatibility_A_D"

# -----------------------------
# Solve
# -----------------------------
solver = pl.PULP_CBC_CMD(msg=False)
status_code = model.solve(solver)
status = pl.LpStatus[status_code]

if status != "Optimal":
    raise RuntimeError(f"Optimization failed with status: {status}")

selected = [i for i in restaurants if pl.value(x[i]) > 0.5]
total_income = sum(restaurants[i]["income"] for i in selected)
total_cost = sum(restaurants[i]["cost"] for i in selected)
unused_budget = budget - total_cost

print(f"Solver status: {status}")
for i in restaurants:
    print(f"x_{i} = {int(round(pl.value(x[i])))}")
print(f"Purchased restaurants: {', '.join(selected)}")
print(f"Total annual income: ${total_income:,.0f}")
print(f"Total cost: ${total_cost:,.0f}")
print(f"Unused budget: ${unused_budget:,.0f}")
```

### Optimal solution

```text
Solver status: Optimal
x_A = 0
x_B = 1
x_C = 0
x_D = 1
Purchased restaurants: B, D
Total annual income: $90,000
Total cost: $5,500,000
Unused budget: $500,000
```

Thus, the family should purchase **Restaurants B and D**, generating **$90,000 in annual income** while remaining **$500,000 below the investment budget**.
