response.content:
## 1. Sets and data

Let the item set be

\[
I=\{\text{okra, carrots, celery, cabbage, salmon, beef, pork}\},
\]

with vegetable set

\[
V=\{\text{okra, carrots, celery, cabbage}\}
\]

and protein set

\[
P=\{\text{salmon, beef, pork}\}.
\]

For each item \(i\), let:

- \(f_i\): grams of fiber per 100 g;
- \(c_i\): price in dollars per 100 g.

| Item \(i\) | \(f_i\) | \(c_i\) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Okra | 3.2 | 2.60 |
| Carrots | 2.7 | 1.20 |
| Celery | 1.6 | 1.60 |
| Cabbage | 2.0 | 2.30 |
| Salmon | 0.0 | 4.00 |
| Beef | 0.0 | 3.60 |
| Pork | 0.0 | 1.80 |

## 2. Decision variables

For every item \(i\in I\):

\[
q_i\ge 0
\]

is the continuous quantity purchased, measured in units of 100 grams. Thus, \(q_i=1\) means 100 grams.

\[
y_i\in\{0,1\}
\]

indicates whether item \(i\) is purchased:

\[
y_i=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if item }i\text{ is bought},\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

## 3. MILP formulation

### Objective: maximize fiber

\[
\max \quad
3.2q_{\text{okra}}
+2.7q_{\text{carrots}}
+1.6q_{\text{celery}}
+2.0q_{\text{cabbage}}.
\]

The protein variables do not appear in the objective because they contain no fiber.

### Budget constraint

\[
\begin{aligned}
2.6q_{\text{okra}}
+1.2q_{\text{carrots}}
+1.6q_{\text{celery}}
+2.3q_{\text{cabbage}}
+4.0q_{\text{salmon}}\\
+3.6q_{\text{beef}}
+1.8q_{\text{pork}}
\le 15.
\end{aligned}
\]

### Total quantity constraint

\[
q_{\text{okra}}
+q_{\text{carrots}}
+q_{\text{celery}}
+q_{\text{cabbage}}
+q_{\text{salmon}}
+q_{\text{beef}}
+q_{\text{pork}}
=6,
\]

because six units of 100 grams equal a 600-gram dinner.

### Item-selection linking constraints

For every item \(i\in I\),

\[
q_i\le 6y_i,
\]

\[
q_i\ge y_i.
\]

Explicitly, the upper constraints are

\[
\begin{aligned}
q_{\text{okra}}&\le 6y_{\text{okra}},&
q_{\text{carrots}}&\le 6y_{\text{carrots}},\\
q_{\text{celery}}&\le 6y_{\text{celery}},&
q_{\text{cabbage}}&\le 6y_{\text{cabbage}},\\
q_{\text{salmon}}&\le 6y_{\text{salmon}},&
q_{\text{beef}}&\le 6y_{\text{beef}},\\
q_{\text{pork}}&\le 6y_{\text{pork}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The lower constraints are

\[
\begin{aligned}
q_{\text{okra}}&\ge y_{\text{okra}},&
q_{\text{carrots}}&\ge y_{\text{carrots}},\\
q_{\text{celery}}&\ge y_{\text{celery}},&
q_{\text{cabbage}}&\ge y_{\text{cabbage}},\\
q_{\text{salmon}}&\ge y_{\text{salmon}},&
q_{\text{beef}}&\ge y_{\text{beef}},\\
q_{\text{pork}}&\ge y_{\text{pork}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

These constraints ensure:

- If \(y_i=0\), then \(q_i=0\).
- If \(y_i=1\), then at least one 100-gram unit is purchased.
- If \(q_i>0\), then \(y_i=1\).

### Vegetable-count constraint

At least two distinct vegetables must be selected:

\[
y_{\text{okra}}
+y_{\text{carrots}}
+y_{\text{celery}}
+y_{\text{cabbage}}
\ge 2.
\]

### Protein-count constraint

Exactly one protein must be selected:

\[
y_{\text{salmon}}
+y_{\text{beef}}
+y_{\text{pork}}
=1.
\]

### Variable domains

\[
q_i\ge 0 \qquad \forall i\in I,
\]

\[
y_i\in\{0,1\} \qquad \forall i\in I.
\]

## 4. Interpretation

- The objective maximizes total dietary fiber.
- The budget constraint prevents spending more than \$15.
- The total-quantity constraint fixes the dinner weight at 600 grams.
- The linking constraints make the binary variables correctly represent whether an item is purchased.
- The vegetable-count constraint requires at least two different vegetables.
- The protein-count constraint permits exactly one type of protein.
- Only the \(y_i\) variables are binary, so this is a mixed-integer linear program.

For verification, an optimal solution is

\[
q_{\text{okra}}=4,\qquad
q_{\text{carrots}}=1,\qquad
q_{\text{pork}}=1,
\]

with all other quantities equal to zero. This purchases 400 g of okra, 100 g of carrots, and 100 g of pork, for:

\[
\text{Cost}=4(2.60)+1(1.20)+1(1.80)=\$13.40,
\]

\[
\text{Fiber}=4(3.2)+1(2.7)=15.5\text{ grams}.
\]

response.content:
## MILP formulation

Let the seven items be:

- Vegetables: okra (\(O\)), carrots (\(R\)), celery (\(L\)), cabbage (\(K\))
- Proteins: salmon (\(S\)), beef (\(B\)), pork (\(P\))

### Decision variables

For each item \(i\), define:

\[
q_i \ge 0
\]

where \(q_i\) is the quantity purchased in units of 100 grams. Thus, \(q_i=1\) means 100 grams and \(q_i=6\) means 600 grams.

Also define:

\[
y_i \in \{0,1\}
\]

where \(y_i=1\) if item \(i\) is purchased and \(y_i=0\) otherwise.

The data are:

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
\text{Item} & \text{Fiber per 100 g} & \text{Price per 100 g}\\ \hline
\text{Okra} & 3.2 & 2.6\\
\text{Carrots} & 2.7 & 1.2\\
\text{Celery} & 1.6 & 1.6\\
\text{Cabbage} & 2.0 & 2.3\\
\text{Salmon} & 0 & 4.0\\
\text{Beef} & 0 & 3.6\\
\text{Pork} & 0 & 1.8
\end{array}
\]

### Objective function

Maximize the total grams of fiber:

\[
\max \quad
Z =
3.2q_O+2.7q_R+1.6q_L+2.0q_K
\]

The protein variables do not appear in the objective because they contain no fiber.

### Constraints

#### 1. Total dinner size

Since 600 grams equals six 100-gram units:

\[
q_O+q_R+q_L+q_K+q_S+q_B+q_P=6
\]

#### 2. Budget constraint

\[
2.6q_O+1.2q_R+1.6q_L+2.3q_K
+4.0q_S+3.6q_B+1.8q_P
\le 15
\]

#### 3. At least two distinct vegetables

\[
y_O+y_R+y_L+y_K \ge 2
\]

#### 4. Exactly one protein

\[
y_S+y_B+y_P=1
\]

#### 5. Linking constraints

For every item \(i\in\{O,R,L,K,S,B,P\}\):

\[
q_i \le 6y_i
\]

\[
q_i \ge y_i
\]

Equivalently, written out:

\[
\begin{aligned}
q_O&\le6y_O, & q_O&\ge y_O,\\
q_R&\le6y_R, & q_R&\ge y_R,\\
q_L&\le6y_L, & q_L&\ge y_L,\\
q_K&\le6y_K, & q_K&\ge y_K,\\
q_S&\le6y_S, & q_S&\ge y_S,\\
q_B&\le6y_B, & q_B&\ge y_B,\\
q_P&\le6y_P, & q_P&\ge y_P.
\end{aligned}
\]

#### 6. Variable domains

\[
q_i\ge0 \qquad \forall i
\]

\[
y_i\in\{0,1\} \qquad \forall i
\]

### Complete model

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\max &
3.2q_O+2.7q_R+1.6q_L+2.0q_K \\[1mm]
\text{s.t.}
&
q_O+q_R+q_L+q_K+q_S+q_B+q_P=6,\\
&
2.6q_O+1.2q_R+1.6q_L+2.3q_K
+4.0q_S+3.6q_B+1.8q_P\le15,\\
&
y_O+y_R+y_L+y_K\ge2,\\
&
y_S+y_B+y_P=1,\\
&
q_i\le6y_i,\qquad \forall i,\\
&q_i\ge y_i,\qquad \forall i,\\
&q_i\ge0,\qquad \forall i,\\
&y_i\in\{0,1\},\qquad \forall i.
\end{array}
\]

The linking constraints ensure that an unselected item has zero quantity, while a selected item has at least 100 grams. Since all continuous quantities are measured in 100-gram units, the budget and total-weight equations use the given prices and fiber values directly.

Under these assumptions, one optimal solution is:

\[
q_O=4,\qquad q_R=1,\qquad q_P=1,
\]

with all other quantities equal to zero. This corresponds to 400 g of okra, 100 g of carrots, and 100 g of pork, costing \(\$13.40\) and providing \(15.5\) grams of fiber.

## Sets and parameters

Let

\[
V=\{\text{okra},\text{carrots},\text{celery},\text{cabbage}\},
\]

\[
P=\{\text{salmon},\text{beef},\text{pork}\}.
\]

The fiber content per 100 grams is

\[
f_{\text{okra}}=3.2,\quad
f_{\text{carrots}}=2.7,\quad
f_{\text{celery}}=1.6,\quad
f_{\text{cabbage}}=2.0.
\]

Since \(x_i\) and \(w_j\) are measured in grams, the fiber contributions per gram are

\[
\frac{f_i}{100}=(0.032,\;0.027,\;0.016,\;0.020).
\]

Using prices in dollars per gram, define

\[
(p_{\text{okra}},p_{\text{carrots}},p_{\text{celery}},p_{\text{cabbage}})
=(0.026,0.012,0.016,0.023),
\]

\[
(q_{\text{salmon}},q_{\text{beef}},q_{\text{pork}})
=(0.040,0.036,0.018).
\]

## Decision variables

\[
x_i\ge 0
\]

is the number of grams of vegetable \(i\in V\) purchased.

\[
w_j\ge 0
\]

is the number of grams of protein source \(j\in P\) purchased.

\[
y_i\in\{0,1\}
\]

equals 1 if vegetable \(i\in V\) is purchased, and 0 otherwise.

\[
z_j\in\{0,1\}
\]

equals 1 if protein source \(j\in P\) is purchased, and 0 otherwise.

## MILP formulation

### Objective

Maximize total fiber intake:

\[
\max \quad
F=
0.032x_{\text{okra}}
+0.027x_{\text{carrots}}
+0.016x_{\text{celery}}
+0.020x_{\text{cabbage}}.
\]

No fiber values were provided for the protein sources, so their fiber contribution is omitted as specified.

### Constraints

**1. Exactly 600 grams of total food**

\[
x_{\text{okra}}+x_{\text{carrots}}+x_{\text{celery}}+x_{\text{cabbage}}
+w_{\text{salmon}}+w_{\text{beef}}+w_{\text{pork}}
=600.
\]

**2. Budget of at most \$15**

\[
\begin{aligned}
&0.026x_{\text{okra}}
+0.012x_{\text{carrots}}
+0.016x_{\text{celery}}
+0.023x_{\text{cabbage}}\\
&\qquad
+0.040w_{\text{salmon}}
+0.036w_{\text{beef}}
+0.018w_{\text{pork}}
\le 15.
\end{aligned}
\]

**3. At least two different vegetables**

\[
y_{\text{okra}}+y_{\text{carrots}}
+y_{\text{celery}}+y_{\text{cabbage}}
\ge 2.
\]

**4. Exactly one protein source**

\[
z_{\text{salmon}}+z_{\text{beef}}+z_{\text{pork}}=1.
\]

**5. Vegetable selection and minimum-portion linking**

For every \(i\in V\),

\[
100y_i\le x_i\le 600y_i.
\]

Explicitly,

\[
\begin{aligned}
100y_{\text{okra}}&\le x_{\text{okra}}\le600y_{\text{okra}},\\
100y_{\text{carrots}}&\le x_{\text{carrots}}\le600y_{\text{carrots}},\\
100y_{\text{celery}}&\le x_{\text{celery}}\le600y_{\text{celery}},\\
100y_{\text{cabbage}}&\le x_{\text{cabbage}}\le600y_{\text{cabbage}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

**6. Protein selection and minimum-portion linking**

For every \(j\in P\),

\[
100z_j\le w_j\le600z_j.
\]

Explicitly,

\[
\begin{aligned}
100z_{\text{salmon}}&\le w_{\text{salmon}}\le600z_{\text{salmon}},\\
100z_{\text{beef}}&\le w_{\text{beef}}\le600z_{\text{beef}},\\
100z_{\text{pork}}&\le w_{\text{pork}}\le600z_{\text{pork}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

**7. Variable domains**

\[
x_i,w_j\ge0,\qquad y_i,z_j\in\{0,1\}.
\]

## Interpretation of the linking constraints

- If \(y_i=0\), then \(x_i\le0\), so no grams of vegetable \(i\) are purchased.
- If \(y_i=1\), then \(x_i\ge100\), so every selected vegetable is purchased in a meaningful portion.
- The analogous statements hold for each protein source using \(z_j\) and \(w_j\).
- Thus, exactly one protein is purchased, in a quantity of at least 100 grams.

As a check, one optimal solution is

\[
x_{\text{okra}}=400,\qquad
x_{\text{carrots}}=100,\qquad
w_{\text{pork}}=100,
\]

with all other purchase quantities equal to zero. This plan costs

\[
0.026(400)+0.012(100)+0.018(100)=\$13.40
\]

and provides

\[
0.032(400)+0.027(100)=15.5\text{ grams of fiber}.
\]

Model 2:
# Meal Planning MILP for Mary

## 1. Sets / Indices

- $V = \{\text{okra, carrots, celery, cabbage}\}$ — set of vegetables, indexed by $i$
- $P = \{\text{salmon, beef, pork}\}$ — set of protein sources, indexed by $j$

## 2. Data (Parameters)

**Fiber content** $f_i$ (grams of fiber per gram of food):

| Vegetable $i$ | $f_i$ (g fiber / g) |
|---|---|
| okra    | 0.032 |
| carrots | 0.027 |
| celery  | 0.016 |
| cabbage | 0.020 |

**Price** $c_i$ for vegetables, $q_j$ for proteins ($ per gram):

| Item | Price ($/g) |
|---|---|
| salmon  | 0.040 |
| beef    | 0.036 |
| pork    | 0.018 |
| okra    | 0.026 |
| carrots | 0.012 |
| celery  | 0.016 |
| cabbage | 0.023 |

Other parameters:
- Total intake target: $G = 600$ g
- Budget: $B = 15$ $
- Minimum portion if selected: $M = 100$ g
- Minimum number of vegetables: $K = 2$

## 3. Decision Variables

- $x_i \ge 0$ — grams of vegetable $i$ purchased (continuous)
- $w_j \ge 0$ — grams of protein $j$ purchased (continuous)
- $y_i \in \{0,1\}$ — 1 if vegetable $i$ is selected, 0 otherwise
- $z_j \in \{0,1\}$ — 1 if protein $j$ is selected, 0 otherwise

## 4. Objective Function

Maximize total fiber intake:

$$
\max \; Z \;=\; \sum_{i \in V} f_i \, x_i \;+\; \sum_{j \in P} 0 \cdot w_j \;=\; \sum_{i \in V} f_i \, x_i
$$

(Proteins contribute no fiber in the data, so only vegetables appear.)

## 5. Constraints

**(a) Exact total intake of 600 g:**

$$
\sum_{i \in V} x_i \;+\; \sum_{j \in P} w_j \;=\; 600
$$

**(b) Budget limit:**

$$
\sum_{i \in V} c_i \, x_i \;+\; \sum_{j \in P} q_j \, w_j \;\le\; 15
$$

**(c) At least two vegetables must be selected:**

$$
\sum_{i \in V} y_i \;\ge\; 2
$$

**(d) Exactly one protein must be selected:**

$$
\sum_{j \in P} z_j \;=\; 1
$$

**(e) Linking — upper bound (cannot buy more than the whole meal of an unselected item):**

$$
x_i \;\le\; 600 \, y_i \quad \forall i \in V
$$
$$
w_j \;\le\; 600 \, z_j \quad \forall j \in P
$$

**(f) Linking — minimum meaningful portion of 100 g if selected:**

$$
x_i \;\ge\; 100 \, y_i \quad \forall i \in V
$$
$$
w_j \;\ge\; 100 \, z_j \quad \forall j \in P
$$

**(g) Non-negativity and binary domains:**

$$
x_i \ge 0,\; w_j \ge 0,\; y_i \in \{0,1\},\; z_j \in \{0,1\}
$$

## 6. Compact Form

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max_{x,w,y,z} \quad & \sum_{i \in V} f_i x_i \\[2pt]
\text{s.t.} \quad & \sum_{i \in V} x_i + \sum_{j \in P} w_j = 600 \\
& \sum_{i \in V} c_i x_i + \sum_{j \in P} q_j w_j \le 15 \\
& \sum_{i \in V} y_i \ge 2 \\
& \sum_{j \in P} z_j = 1 \\
& 100\, y_i \le x_i \le 600\, y_i \quad \forall i \in V \\
& 100\, z_j \le w_j \le 600\, z_j \quad \forall j \in P \\
& x_i, w_j \ge 0,\quad y_i, z_j \in \{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
$$

## 7. Explanation of the Model

- **Decision variables** are split into *continuous* quantities ($x_i, w_j$) and *binary* selection indicators ($y_i, z_j$). The binaries are needed because Mary must commit to whole items (you cannot buy "half a vegetable"), while the grams of each chosen item are continuous.
- **Constraints (e)–(f)** are the classic "big-M / linking" constraints that connect the binaries to the continuous quantities. Together they enforce the *either-or* logic: if $y_i = 0$ then $x_i = 0$ (no purchase); if $y_i = 1$ then $100 \le x_i \le 600$. The same applies to proteins via $z_j$.
- **Constraint (a)** pins the total meal size to exactly 600 g.
- **Constraint (b)** enforces the spending cap, using per-gram prices.
- **Constraints (c) and (d)** encode the dietary rules about variety: at least two different vegetables, exactly one protein.
- **Objective** is purely fiber-based; proteins contribute 0 in the data, so the optimizer will (i) pick the cheapest protein (pork at \$0.018/g) to leave budget for vegetables, and (ii) concentrate vegetable grams into the highest-fiber, lowest-cost-per-fiber option (okra) while keeping a second vegetable at its 100 g minimum to satisfy (c).

## 8. Optimal Solution (for verification)

Solving the model yields:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| $x_{\text{okra}}$ | 500 g |
| $x_{\text{carrots}}$ | 100 g |
| $x_{\text{celery}}, x_{\text{cabbage}}$ | 0 g |
| $w_{\text{pork}}$ | 100 g |
| $w_{\text{salmon}}, w_{\text{beef}}$ | 0 g |
| $y_{\text{okra}}, y_{\text{carrots}}$ | 1 |
| $y_{\text{celery}}, y_{\text{cabbage}}$ | 0 |
| $z_{\text{pork}}$ | 1 |
| $z_{\text{salmon}}, z_{\text{beef}}$ | 0 |

- Total fiber: $Z^* = 0.032(500) + 0.027(100) = 16.0 + 2.7 = \mathbf{18.7}$ g
- Total cost: $0.026(500) + 0.012(100) + 0.018(100) = 13.00 + 1.20 + 1.80 = \$14.20$ (≤ \$15 ✓)
- Total grams: 700 g ❌ — wait, $500 + 100 + 100 = 700$, which violates (a).

Let me re-check the budget calculation: $0.026 \times 500 = 13.00$, $0.012 \times 100 = 1.20$, $0.018 \times 100 = 1.80$. Total = $16.00$, not $14.20$. So this solution is **infeasible** (over budget). The correct optimal is:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| $x_{\text{okra}}$ | 400 g |
| $x_{\text{carrots}}$ | 100 g |
| $w_{\text{pork}}$ | 100 g |

- Total grams: $400 + 100 + 100 = 600$ ✓
- Total cost: $0.026(400) + 0.012(100) + 0.018(100) = 10.40 + 1.20 + 1.80 = \$13.40$ ✓
- Total fiber: $0.032(400) + 0.027(100) = 12.8 + 2.7 = \mathbf{15.5}$ g

So the true optimum under all constraints is **15.5 g of fiber**, achieved with 400 g okra, 100 g carrots, and 100 g pork.

## Best Model (selected from 8 candidates — all converged to the same formulation and solution)

### 1. Sets

- Vegetables: \(V=\{\text{okra, carrots, celery, cabbage}\}\)
- Proteins: \(P=\{\text{salmon, beef, pork}\}\)
- All items: \(I=V\cup P\)

### 2. Parameters

Fiber \(f_i\) (g per 100 g) and price \(c_i\) (\$ per 100 g):

| Item \(i\) | \(f_i\) | \(c_i\) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Okra | 3.2 | 2.60 |
| Carrots | 2.7 | 1.20 |
| Celery | 1.6 | 1.60 |
| Cabbage | 2.0 | 2.30 |
| Salmon | 0 | 4.00 |
| Beef | 0 | 3.60 |
| Pork | 0 | 1.80 |

Meal size \(G=600\) g \(=6\) units of 100 g; budget \(B=\$15\); minimum portion \(m=1\) unit (100 g); minimum vegetable count \(K=2\).

### 3. Variables

- \(q_i\ge 0\): quantity of item \(i\) purchased, **in units of 100 g** (\(q_i=1\) ⇒ 100 g)
- \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\): 1 if item \(i\) is purchased, 0 otherwise

### 4. Objective — maximize fiber intake

\[
\max \; Z=3.2\,q_{\text{okra}}+2.7\,q_{\text{carrots}}+1.6\,q_{\text{celery}}+2.0\,q_{\text{cabbage}}
\]

(Proteins carry no fiber per the data, so their quantities do not appear in the objective.)

### 5. Constraints

**(a) Total intake = 600 g:**
\[
q_{\text{okra}}+q_{\text{carrots}}+q_{\text{celery}}+q_{\text{cabbage}}+q_{\text{salmon}}+q_{\text{beef}}+q_{\text{pork}}=6
\]

**(b) Budget ≤ \$15:**
\[
2.6q_{\text{okra}}+1.2q_{\text{carrots}}+1.6q_{\text{celery}}+2.3q_{\text{cabbage}}+4.0q_{\text{salmon}}+3.6q_{\text{beef}}+1.8q_{\text{pork}}\le 15
\]

**(c) At least two distinct vegetables:**
\[
y_{\text{okra}}+y_{\text{carrots}}+y_{\text{celery}}+y_{\text{cabbage}}\ge 2
\]

**(d) Exactly one protein source:**
\[
y_{\text{salmon}}+y_{\text{beef}}+y_{\text{pork}}=1
\]

**(e) Linking (selection ↔ quantity), for all \(i\in I\):**
\[
q_i\le 6\,y_i \qquad\forall i\in I \quad\text{(if }y_i=0\Rightarrow q_i=0\text{)}
\]
\[
q_i\ge 1\,y_i \qquad\forall i\in I \quad\text{(if }y_i=1\Rightarrow q_i\ge1\text{, i.e. }\ge100\text{ g)}
\]
\(M=6\) is valid because no single item can exceed the 600 g meal.

**(f) Domains:** \(q_i\ge0,\; y_i\in\{0,1\}\).

### 6. Assumptions (marked, as data were incomplete)
1. **Minimum meaningful portion:** a selected item must be bought in ≥ 100 g portions (otherwise "selecting" a vegetable would be meaningless). *This is the key assumption driving the answer.*
2. **Protein fiber = 0** (not specified in the data), so protein contributes nothing to the objective and only displaces vegetables.
3. **Budget is an upper bound** (≤ \$15); total intake is **exactly** 600 g.
4. Purchased grams = consumed grams; quantities are continuous and divisible within the 100 g unit.

### 7. Optimal solution

| Variable | Value | Grams |
|---|---|---|
| \(q_{\text{okra}}\) | 4 | 400 g |
| \(q_{\text{carrots}}\) | 1 | 100 g |
| \(q_{\text{pork}}\) | 1 | 100 g |
| \(q_{\text{celery}}, q_{\text{cabbage}}, q_{\text{salmon}}, q_{\text{beef}}\) | 0 | — |

**Verification:** total \(=400+100+100=600\) g ✓; cost \(=4(2.60)+1(1.20)+1(1.80)=\$13.40\le \$15\) ✓; two vegetables selected ✓; exactly one protein (pork, the cheapest at \$1.80/100 g) ✓.

**Maximum fiber: \(Z^*=4(3.2)+1(2.7)=15.5\) grams.**

*Why this is optimal:* with one 100 g protein portion fixed (pork is cheapest, \$1.8), 5 vegetable units remain. Okra has the highest fiber per unit (3.2), but the "at least two vegetables" rule forces ≥1 unit of a second vegetable; carrots are the best such second vegetable (2.7 vs. cabbage 2.0, celery 1.6). Hence okra 4 units + carrots 1 unit; any shift (e.g. 3 okra + 2 carrots = 15.0 g) is worse, and the budget is non-binding at \$13.40.
response.reasoning:
All models are essentially identical. Let me verify the optimal solution myself.

Variables in 100g units: q_O, q_R, q_L, q_K, q_S, q_B, q_P. Sum = 6. Cost <= 15. At least two vegetables each with q >= 1. Exactly one protein with q >= 1.

Protein minimum 1 unit (100g). Cheapest protein: pork $1.8/100g.

Let's think: choose pork q_P = 1 (cost 1.8). Remaining 5 units of vegetables, budget remaining 13.2. At least two vegetables with ≥1 unit each.

Fiber per 100g: okra 3.2, carrots 2.7, celery 1.6, cabbage 2.0. Prices: okra 2.6, carrots 1.2, celery 1.6, cabbage 2.3.

Options: okra at 2.6 gives 3.2 fiber per $2.6 → 1.2308 fiber per dollar. Carrots: 2.7 per $1.2 → 2.25 fiber per dollar! Celery: 1.6/1.6 = 1.0. Cabbage: 2.0/2.3 = 0.87.

So carrots are much more fiber-efficient per dollar. But carrots limited by total 600g.

Total budget 15, protein at least 1 unit pork = $1.8. Remaining $13.2 for 5 units of vegetables (500 g).

Minimize cost of 5 units while maximizing fiber. Let's try: carrots as much as possible. We need at least 2 vegetables, so at least 1 unit of okra (or another).

Case: 4 units carrots + 1 unit okra = 5 units. Cost = 4(1.2)+1(2.6)=4.8+2.6=7.4. Plus pork 1.8 = 9.2 ≤ 15. Fiber = 4(2.7)+3.2 = 10.8+3.2 = 14.0. Hmm, less than 15.5.

Case: okra 4 + carrots 1: fiber = 4(3.2)+2.7 = 12.8+2.7=15.5, cost = 10.4+1.2=11.6 + 1.8 = 13.4 ≤ 15. Fiber 15.5.

Case: okra 3, carrots 2: fiber = 9.6+5.4 = 15.0. Cost = 7.8+2.4=10.2+1.8=12. Fiber 15.0.

## Best Model (selected from 8 candidates — all converged to the same formulation and solution)

### 1. Sets

- Vegetables: \(V=\{\text{okra, carrots, celery, cabbage}\}\)
- Proteins: \(P=\{\text{salmon, beef, pork}\}\)
- All items: \(I=V\cup P\)

### 2. Parameters

Fiber \(f_i\) (g per 100 g) and price \(c_i\) (\$ per 100 g):

| Item \(i\) | \(f_i\) | \(c_i\) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Okra | 3.2 | 2.60 |
| Carrots | 2.7 | 1.20 |
| Celery | 1.6 | 1.60 |
| Cabbage | 2.0 | 2.30 |
| Salmon | 0 | 4.00 |
| Beef | 0 | 3.60 |
| Pork | 0 | 1.80 |

Meal size \(G=600\) g \(=6\) units of 100 g; budget \(B=\$15\); minimum portion \(m=1\) unit (100 g); minimum vegetable count \(K=2\).

### 3. Variables

- \(q_i\ge 0\): quantity of item \(i\) purchased, **in units of 100 g** (\(q_i=1\) ⇒ 100 g)
- \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\): 1 if item \(i\) is purchased, 0 otherwise

### 4. Objective — maximize fiber intake

\[
\max \; Z=3.2\,q_{\text{okra}}+2.7\,q_{\text{carrots}}+1.6\,q_{\text{celery}}+2.0\,q_{\text{cabbage}}
\]

(Proteins carry no fiber per the data, so their quantities do not appear in the objective.)

### 5. Constraints

**(a) Total intake = 600 g:**
\[
q_{\text{okra}}+q_{\text{carrots}}+q_{\text{celery}}+q_{\text{cabbage}}+q_{\text{salmon}}+q_{\text{beef}}+q_{\text{pork}}=6
\]

**(b) Budget ≤ \$15:**
\[
2.6q_{\text{okra}}+1.2q_{\text{carrots}}+1.6q_{\text{celery}}+2.3q_{\text{cabbage}}+4.0q_{\text{salmon}}+3.6q_{\text{beef}}+1.8q_{\text{pork}}\le 15
\]

**(c) At least two distinct vegetables:**
\[
y_{\text{okra}}+y_{\text{carrots}}+y_{\text{celery}}+y_{\text{cabbage}}\ge 2
\]

**(d) Exactly one protein source:**
\[
y_{\text{salmon}}+y_{\text{beef}}+y_{\text{pork}}=1
\]

**(e) Linking (selection ↔ quantity), for all \(i\in I\):**
\[
q_i\le 6\,y_i \qquad\forall i\in I \quad\text{(if }y_i=0\Rightarrow q_i=0\text{)}
\]
\[
q_i\ge 1\,y_i \qquad\forall i\in I \quad\text{(if }y_i=1\Rightarrow q_i\ge1\text{, i.e. }\ge100\text{ g)}
\]
\(M=6\) is valid because no single item can exceed the 600 g meal.

**(f) Domains:** \(q_i\ge0,\; y_i\in\{0,1\}\).

### 6. Assumptions (marked, as data were incomplete)
1. **Minimum meaningful portion:** a selected item must be bought in ≥ 100 g portions (otherwise "selecting" a vegetable would be meaningless). *This is the key assumption driving the answer.*
2. **Protein fiber = 0** (not specified in the data), so protein contributes nothing to the objective and only displaces vegetables.
3. **Budget is an upper bound** (≤ \$15); total intake is **exactly** 600 g.
4. Purchased grams = consumed grams; quantities are continuous and divisible within the 100 g unit.

### 7. Optimal solution

| Variable | Value | Grams |
|---|---|---|
| \(q_{\text{okra}}\) | 4 | 400 g |
| \(q_{\text{carrots}}\) | 1 | 100 g |
| \(q_{\text{pork}}\) | 1 | 100 g |
| \(q_{\text{celery}}, q_{\text{cabbage}}, q_{\text{salmon}}, q_{\text{beef}}\) | 0 | — |

**Verification:** total \(=400+100+100=600\) g ✓; cost \(=4(2.60)+1(1.20)+1(1.80)=\$13.40\le \$15\) ✓; two vegetables selected ✓; exactly one protein (pork, the cheapest at \$1.80/100 g) ✓.

**Maximum fiber: \(Z^*=4(3.2)+1(2.7)=15.5\) grams.**

*Why this is optimal:* with one 100 g protein portion fixed (pork is cheapest, \$1.8), 5 vegetable units remain. Okra has the highest fiber per unit (3.2), but the "at least two vegetables" rule forces ≥1 unit of a second vegetable; carrots are the best such second vegetable (2.7 vs. cabbage 2.0, celery 1.6). Hence okra 4 units + carrots 1 unit; any shift (e.g. 3 okra + 2 carrots = 15.0 g) is worse, and the budget is non-binding at \$13.40.

function.arguments:
{"description": "Build a MILP (python, using PuLP) for the following investment problem.

CONTEXT
An investor has 100,000 yuan available at time 0 (beginning of year 1) and wants to maximize the amount of money he owns at the end of year 3 (time 3). He may split his money between two investments, and money that comes back can be reinvested in subsequent years. Money that is not invested may be held idle (zero return).

INVESTMENT OPTIONS
- Type 1 (short term): 1 yuan invested at the beginning of year t (t = 0, 1, 2) gives a profit of 0.7 yuan per yuan invested, i.e. 1.7 yuan cash back at the end of year t+1. It can be taken again in any later year (repeatable).
- Type 2 (long term): 1 yuan invested at the beginning of year t gives a profit of 2 yuan per yuan invested, i.e. 3 yuan cash back at the end of year t+2. The investment period must be a multiple of 2 years; since only 3 years of horizon exist, only a 2-year term is feasible, so Type 2 can only be started at t = 0 (matures at t = 2) or at t = 1 (matures at t = 3). No Type 2 investment may be started at t = 2 because it would mature after the horizon.

DECISION VARIABLES (all >= 0; declare them integer if amounts must be whole yuan, which keeps the model a MILP)
- x[t] for t in {0,1,2}: amount of money invested in Type 1 at the beginning of year t (i.e., maturing at end of year t+1)
- y[t] for t in {0,1}: amount of money invested in Type 2 (2-year term) at the beginning of year t (i.e., maturing at end of year t+2)
- c[t] for t in {0,1,2}: amount of idle cash held at the end of year t (0 <= t <= 2)
- Z: total money owned at the end of year 3

OBJECTIVE
Maximize Z, with Z = 1.7*x[2] + 3*y[1] + c[2]   (cash realized at the end of year 3 from the Type 1 investment started in year 2, the Type 2 investment started in year 1, and the cash held at the end of year 2)

CASH FLOW / BUDGET CONSTRAINTS
- End of year 0: x[0] + y[0] + c[0] = 100000
- End of year 1: 1.7*x[0] + c[0] = x[1] + y[1] + c[1]
- End of year 2: 1.7*x[1] + 3*y[0] + c[1] = x[2] + c[2]
- Definition of Z: Z = 1.7*x[2] + 3*y[1] + c[2]
- Variable bounds: x, y, c >= 0 (integer if desired)

Please also solve it and report the optimal values of x, y, c and Z, and explain the optimal strategy."}

CONTEXT
An investor has 100,000 yuan available at time 0 (beginning of year 1) and wants to maximize the amount of money he owns at the end of year 3 (time 3). He may split his money between two investments, and money that comes back can be reinvested in subsequent years. Money that is not invested may be held idle (zero return).

INVESTMENT OPTIONS
- Type 1 (short term): 1 yuan invested at the beginning of year t (t = 0, 1, 2) gives a profit of 0.7 yuan per yuan invested, i.e. 1.7 yuan cash back at the end of year t+1. It can be taken again in any later year (repeatable).
- Type 2 (long term): 1 yuan invested at the beginning of year t gives a profit of 2 yuan per yuan invested, i.e. 3 yuan cash back at the end of year t+2. The investment period must be a multiple of 2 years; since only 3 years of horizon exist, only a 2-year term is feasible, so Type 2 can only be started at t = 0 (matures at t = 2) or at t = 1 (matures at t = 3). No Type 2 investment may be started at t = 2 because it would mature after the horizon.

DECISION VARIABLES (all >= 0; declare them integer if amounts must be whole yuan, which keeps the model a MILP)
- x[t] for t in {0,1,2}: amount of money invested in Type 1 at the beginning of year t (i.e., maturing at end of year t+1)
- y[t] for t in {0,1}: amount of money invested in Type 2 (2-year term) at the beginning of year t (i.e., maturing at end of year t+2)
- c[t] for t in {0,1,2}: amount of idle cash held at the end of year t (0 <= t <= 2)
- Z: total money owned at the end of year 3

OBJECTIVE
Maximize Z, with Z = 1.7*x[2] + 3*y[1] + c[2]   (cash realized at the end of year 3 from the Type 1 investment started in year 2, the Type 2 investment started in year 1, and the cash held at the end of year 2)

CASH FLOW / BUDGET CONSTRAINTS
- End of year 0: x[0] + y[0] + c[0] = 100000
- End of year 1: 1.7*x[0] + c[0] = x[1] + y[1] + c[1]
- End of year 2: 1.7*x[1] + 3*y[0] + c[1] = x[2] + c[2]
- Definition of Z: Z = 1.7*x[2] + 3*y[1] + c[2]
- Variable bounds: x, y, c >= 0 (integer if desired)

Please also solve it and report the optimal values of x, y, c and Z, and explain the optimal strategy."}

{"description": "Build a MILP (python, using PuLP) for the following investment problem.

CONTEXT
An investor has 100,000 yuan available at time 0 (beginning of year 1) and wants to maximize the amount of money he owns at the end of year 3 (time 3). He may split his money between two investments, and money that comes back can be reinvested in subsequent years. Money that is not invested may be held idle (zero return).

INVESTMENT OPTIONS
- Type 1 (short term): 1 yuan invested at the beginning of year t (t = 0, 1, 2) gives a profit of 0.7 yuan per yuan invested, i.e. 1.7 yuan cash back at the end of year t+1. It can be taken again in any later year (repeatable).
- Type 2 (long term): 1 yuan invested at the beginning of year t gives a profit of 2 yuan per yuan invested, i.e. 3 yuan cash back at the end of year t+2. The investment period must be a multiple of 2 years; since only 3 years of horizon exist, only a 2-year term is feasible, so Type 2 can only be started at t = 0 (matures at t = 2) or at t = 1 (matures at t = 3). No Type 2 investment may be started at t = 2 because it would mature after the horizon.

DECISION VARIABLES (all >= 0; declare them integer if amounts must be whole yuan, which keeps the model a MILP)
- x[t] for t in {0,1,2}: amount of money invested in Type 1 at the beginning of year t (i.e., maturing at end of year t+1)
- y[t] for t in {0,1}: amount of money invested in Type 2 (2-year term) at the beginning of year t (i.e., maturing at end of year t+2)
- c[t] for t in {0,1,2}: amount of idle cash held at the end of year t (0 <= t <= 2)
- Z: total money owned at the end of year 3

OBJECTIVE
Maximize Z, with Z = 1.7*x[2] + 3*y[1] + c[2]   (cash realized at the end of year 3 from the Type 1 investment started in year 2, the Type 2 investment started in year 1, and the cash held at the end of year 2)

CASH FLOW / BUDGET CONSTRAINTS
- End of year 0: x[0] + y[0] + c[0] = 100000
- End of year 1: 1.7*x[0] + c[0] = x[1] + y[1] + c[1]
- End of year 2: 1.7*x[1] + 3*y[0] + c[1] = x[2] + c[2]
- Definition of Z: Z = 1.7*x[2] + 3*y[1] + c[2]
- Variable bounds: x, y, c >= 0 (integer if desired)

Please also solve it and report the optimal values of x, y, c and Z, and explain the optimal strategy."}

response.content:
## 1. Interpretation and Assumptions

**Time axis.** The investor starts at the beginning of Year 1 with $W_0 = 100{,}000$ yuan. The horizon ends at the end of Year 3. Index $t=0,1,2$ denotes "the beginning of Year $t+1$"; the terminal moment is the end of Year 3.

**The two options (return conventions).**

* **Type 1 (1‑year option):** 1 yuan invested at the beginning of Year $t+1$ returns **1.7 yuan** at the end of Year $t+1$ (i.e. profit 0.7 yuan per yuan). It may be repeated in every year.
* **Type 2 (2‑year option):** 1 yuan invested at the beginning of Year $t+1$ returns **3.0 yuan** at the end of Year $t+2$ (profit 2 yuan per yuan). Because "the investment time must be a multiple of two years", the money can only be withdrawn after a whole 2‑year block, and a block may only be *started* if it fits completely inside the 3‑year horizon.

**Assumptions (marked, since the statement leaves them open).**

* **A1 (reinvestment).** Money received at the end of a year may be re‑invested in a later year, or simply held idle (idle cash earns 0). This is the natural reading of "maximize the money earned by the third year".
* **A2 (horizon for Type 2).** A 2‑year block may start at the beginning of Year 1 (ends end of Year 2) or at the beginning of Year 2 (ends end of Year 3); a block starting at the beginning of Year 3 would end at the end of Year 4, outside the horizon, so it is **not** allowed (this is where the "multiple of two years" rule bites).
* **A3 (integrality).** If the amounts must be whole yuan, the variables are restricted to non‑negative integers and the model becomes a MILP; the optimal value below is unchanged.

---

## 2. Sets, parameters, variables

**Sets:** $T=\{0,1,2\}$ (beginning of Years 1,2,3); $T_2=\{0,1\}$ (legal starting times of the 2‑year block).

**Parameters:**
$$R_1=1.7 \ \text{(cash per yuan after 1 year)},\qquad R_2=3.0 \ \text{(cash per yuan after 2 years)},\qquad W_0=100{,}000 .$$

**Decision variables** (all $\ge 0$; integer if A3 is imposed):

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $x_t,\ t\in T$ | yuan invested in the **1‑year option** at the beginning of Year $t+1$ (matures end of Year $t+1$) |
| $y_t,\ t\in T_2$ | yuan invested in the **2‑year option** at the beginning of Year $t+1$ (matures end of Year $t+2$) |
| $c_t,\ t\in T$ | idle cash held at the end of Year $t+1$ (no interest) |
| $Z$ | total wealth owned at the **end of Year 3** |

There is no variable $y_2$: the 2‑year block cannot start in Year 3 (A2).

---

## 3. Objective function

$$\max\; Z$$

with $Z$ defined by the terminal cash‑flow equation below. (Equivalently, maximising the *earned profit* $Z-W_0$ gives the identical optimum; see §5 for the equivalent reduced objective.)

---

## 4. Constraints

**(B0) Allocation of the initial capital (end of Year 0 / beginning of Year 1):**
$$x_0+y_0+c_0 = W_0 = 100{,}000$$

**(B1) Cash balance at the end of Year 1** (in: $1.7x_0$ matures + $c_0$ carried over; out: new investments + cash kept):
$$1.7\,x_0+c_0 = x_1+y_1+c_1$$

**(B2) Cash balance at the end of Year 2** (in: $1.7x_1$ from the 1‑year option and $3y_0$ from the 2‑year block both mature; out: 1‑year investment started in Year 3 + cash kept):
$$1.7\,x_1+3\,y_0+c_1 = x_2+c_2$$

**(D) Terminal wealth at the end of Year 3** (in: $1.7x_2$ from the 1‑year option of Year 3 and $3y_1$ from the 2‑year block started in Year 2; plus $c_2$):
$$Z = 1.7\,x_2+3\,y_1+c_2$$

**(N) Bounds / integrality:**
$$x_t\ge 0\ (t\in T),\qquad y_t\ge 0\ (t\in T_2),\qquad c_t\ge 0\ (t\in T),\qquad Z\ge 0$$
$$x_t,\;y_t,\;c_t \in \mathbb{Z}_+ \quad\text{(if A3 is imposed)}$$

*(No additional constraint is needed for the 2‑year rule: it is enforced by the index set $T_2=\{0,1\}$ and by the maturity dates used in (B1)–(B2), (D).)*

---

## 5. Solution

**Optimal value:**
$$\boxed{Z^{*}=510{,}000\ \text{yuan}\quad(\text{profit } 410{,}000\ \text{yuan})}$$

**Optimal strategy.** Let $a$ be any number with $0\le a\le 100{,}000$. An entire family of optimal solutions is:

$$x_0=a,\quad y_0=100{,}000-a,\quad c_0=0$$
$$x_1=0,\quad y_1=1.7\,a,\quad c_1=0$$
$$x_2=3\,(100{,}000-a),\quad c_2=0,\qquad Z=510{,}000 .$$

Two clean representative solutions (endpoints of this family):

* **(A) Long first, short last:** Invest all $100{,}000$ in the **2‑year option** over Years 1–2 → $300{,}000$ at the end of Year 2 → invest all $300{,}000$ in the **1‑year option** in Year 3 → $1.7\times300{,}000 = 510{,}000$ at the end of Year 3.
* **(B) Short first, long last:** Invest all $100{,}000$ in the **1‑year option** in Year 1 → $170{,}000$ at the end of Year 1 → invest all $170{,}000$ in the **2‑year option** over Years 2–3 → $3\times170{,}000 = 510{,}000$ at the end of Year 3.

**Why this is optimal.** Eliminating $c_0,c_1,c_2$ from the constraints gives the equivalent objective

$$Z = 100{,}000+\underbrace{0.7(x_0+x_1+x_2)}_{\text{profit of 1‑year options}}+\underbrace{2(y_0+y_1)}_{\text{profit of 2‑year blocks}} .$$

The per‑yuan profit rates are $0.7$ per year for Type 1 and $2$ per 2‑year block $=1$ per year for Type 2, so Type 2 is the better use of money over a 2‑year horizon — but a 2‑year block must be placed either in Years 1–2 (then the proceeds earn $0.7$ once more in Year 3) or in Years 2–3 (then it is fed by the $0.7$-profit Year‑1 money). Either way the chain yields $0.7+2=2.7$ profit per yuan over the three years, i.e. $5.1\times100{,}000$, and the constraints forbid doing better:

* all‑Type‑1 gives $100{,}000\cdot1.7^3 = 491{,}300 < 510{,}000$;
* a 2‑year block started in Year 3 is infeasible (A2);
* holding idle cash ($c_t>0$) only destroys profit.

Hence $Z^{*}=510{,}000$ and the degenerate family above is optimal.

**Remark on the alternative reading.** If reinvestment of matured money were forbidden (A1 dropped), the model would collapse to $\max\{1.7\sum x_t+3\sum y_t:\ \sum x_t+\sum y_t\le 100{,}000\}$, whose optimum is to put everything into the 2‑year block, giving $300{,}000$ at the end of Year 3. The LP above is the correct formulation under the standard assumption A1.

final_answer:
## 1. Interpretation and Assumptions

**Time axis.** The investor starts at the beginning of Year 1 with $W_0 = 100{,}000$ yuan. The horizon ends at the end of Year 3. Index $t=0,1,2$ denotes "the beginning of Year $t+1$"; the terminal moment is the end of Year 3.

**The two options (return conventions).**

* **Type 1 (1‑year option):** 1 yuan invested at the beginning of Year $t+1$ returns **1.7 yuan** at the end of Year $t+1$ (i.e. profit 0.7 yuan per yuan). It may be repeated in every year.
* **Type 2 (2‑year option):** 1 yuan invested at the beginning of Year $t+1$ returns **3.0 yuan** at the end of Year $t+2$ (profit 2 yuan per yuan). Because "the investment time must be a multiple of two years", the money can only be withdrawn after a whole 2‑year block, and a block may only be *started* if it fits completely inside the 3‑year horizon.

**Assumptions (marked, since the statement leaves them open).**

* **A1 (reinvestment).** Money received at the end of a year may be re‑invested in a later year, or simply held idle (idle cash earns 0). This is the natural reading of "maximize the money earned by the third year".
* **A2 (horizon for Type 2).** A 2‑year block may start at the beginning of Year 1 (ends end of Year 2) or at the beginning of Year 2 (ends end of Year 3); a block starting at the beginning of Year 3 would end at the end of Year 4, outside the horizon, so it is **not** allowed (this is where the "multiple of two years" rule bites).
* **A3 (integrality).** If the amounts must be whole yuan, the variables are restricted to non‑negative integers and the model becomes a MILP; the optimal value below is unchanged.

---

## 2. Sets, parameters, variables

**Sets:** $T=\{0,1,2\}$ (beginning of Years 1,2,3); $T_2=\{0,1\}$ (legal starting times of the 2‑year block).

**Parameters:**
$$R_1=1.7 \ \text{(cash per yuan after 1 year)},\qquad R_2=3.0 \ \text{(cash per yuan after 2 years)},\qquad W_0=100{,}000 .$$

**Decision variables** (all $\ge 0$; integer if A3 is imposed):

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $x_t,\ t\in T$ | yuan invested in the **1‑year option** at the beginning of Year $t+1$ (matures end of Year $t+1$) |
| $y_t,\ t\in T_2$ | yuan invested in the **2‑year option** at the beginning of Year $t+1$ (matures end of Year $t+2$) |
| $c_t,\ t\in T$ | idle cash held at the end of Year $t+1$ (no interest) |
| $Z$ | total wealth owned at the **end of Year 3** |

There is no variable $y_2$: the 2‑year block cannot start in Year 3 (A2).

---

## 3. Objective function

$$\max\; Z$$

with $Z$ defined by the terminal cash‑flow equation below. (Equivalently, maximising the *earned profit* $Z-W_0$ gives the identical optimum; see §5 for the equivalent reduced objective.)

---

## 4. Constraints

**(B0) Allocation of the initial capital (end of Year 0 / beginning of Year 1):**
$$x_0+y_0+c_0 = W_0 = 100{,}000$$

**(B1) Cash balance at the end of Year 1** (in: $1.7x_0$ matures + $c_0$ carried over; out: new investments + cash kept):
$$1.7\,x_0+c_0 = x_1+y_1+c_1$$

**(B2) Cash balance at the end of Year 2** (in: $1.7x_1$ from the 1‑year option and $3y_0$ from the 2‑year block both mature; out: 1‑year investment started in Year 3 + cash kept):
$$1.7\,x_1+3\,y_0+c_1 = x_2+c_2$$

**(D) Terminal wealth at the end of Year 3** (in: $1.7x_2$ from the 1‑year option of Year 3 and $3y_1$ from the 2‑year block started in Year 2; plus $c_2$):
$$Z = 1.7\,x_2+3\,y_1+c_2$$

**(N) Bounds / integrality:**
$$x_t\ge 0\ (t\in T),\qquad y_t\ge 0\ (t\in T_2),\qquad c_t\ge 0\ (t\in T),\qquad Z\ge 0$$
$$x_t,\;y_t,\;c_t \in \mathbb{Z}_+ \quad\text{(if A3 is imposed)}$$

*(No additional constraint is needed for the 2‑year rule: it is enforced by the index set $T_2=\{0,1\}$ and by the maturity dates used in (B1)–(B2), (D).)*

---

## 5. Solution

**Optimal value:**
$$\boxed{Z^{*}=510{,}000\ \text{yuan}\quad(\text{profit } 410{,}000\ \text{yuan})}$$

**Optimal strategy.** Let $a$ be any number with $0\le a\le 100{,}000$. An entire family of optimal solutions is:

$$x_0=a,\quad y_0=100{,}000-a,\quad c_0=0$$
$$x_1=0,\quad y_1=1.7\,a,\quad c_1=0$$
$$x_2=3\,(100{,}000-a),\quad c_2=0,\qquad Z=510{,}000 .$$

Two clean representative solutions (endpoints of this family):

* **(A) Long first, short last:** Invest all $100{,}000$ in the **2‑year option** over Years 1–2 → $300{,}000$ at the end of Year 2 → invest all $300{,}000$ in the **1‑year option** in Year 3 → $1.7\times300{,}000 = 510{,}000$ at the end of Year 3.
* **(B) Short first, long last:** Invest all $100{,}000$ in the **1‑year option** in Year 1 → $170{,}000$ at the end of Year 1 → invest all $170{,}000$ in the **2‑year option** over Years 2–3 → $3\times170{,}000 = 510{,}000$ at the end of Year 3.

**Why this is optimal.** Eliminating $c_0,c_1,c_2$ from the constraints gives the equivalent objective

$$Z = 100{,}000+\underbrace{0.7(x_0+x_1+x_2)}_{\text{profit of 1‑year options}}+\underbrace{2(y_0+y_1)}_{\text{profit of 2‑year blocks}} .$$

The per‑yuan profit rates are $0.7$ per year for Type 1 and $2$ per 2‑year block $=1$ per year for Type 2, so Type 2 is the better use of money over a 2‑year horizon — but a 2‑year block must be placed either in Years 1–2 (then the proceeds earn $0.7$ once more in Year 3) or in Years 2–3 (then it is fed by the $0.7$-profit Year‑1 money). Either way the chain yields $0.7+2=2.7$ profit per yuan over the three years, i.e. $5.1\times100{,}000$, and the constraints forbid doing better:

* all‑Type‑1 gives $100{,}000\cdot1.7^3 = 491{,}300 < 510{,}000$;
* a 2‑year block started in Year 3 is infeasible (A2);
* holding idle cash ($c_t>0$) only destroys profit.

Hence $Z^{*}=510{,}000$ and the degenerate family above is optimal.

**Remark on the alternative reading.** If reinvestment of matured money were forbidden (A1 dropped), the model would collapse to $\max\{1.7\sum x_t+3\sum y_t:\ \sum x_t+\sum y_t\le 100{,}000\}$, whose optimum is to put everything into the 2‑year block, giving $300{,}000$ at the end of Year 3. The LP above is the correct formulation under the standard assumption A1.

messages.content:
# Complete MILP Formulation and Solution

## 1. Corrected Model

### Sets and indices
- $T_1=\{1,2,3\}$ — beginnings of years in which the 1-year option may be started.
- $T_2=\{1,2\}$ — beginnings of years in which the 2-year option may be started (starting at year 3 would mature after the horizon).
- $T=\{1,2,3,4\}$ — cash states; $t=4$ is the end of year 3.

### Parameters
- $W_0 = 100{,}000$ (initial wealth, available at $t=1$).
- 1-year option: principal $B$ at $t$ becomes $1.7B$ at $t+1$ (profit $0.7B$).
- 2-year option: principal $B$ at $t$ becomes $3B$ at $t+2$ (profit $2B$).
- $M$ — big-M; a tight choice is $M=100{,}000$ for $t=1$ and $M=170{,}000$ for $t=2$ (the largest cash that can ever sit at $t=2$).

### Decision variables
| Variable | Meaning | Domain |
|---|---|---|
| $x_1[t]$ | yuan placed in the 1-year option at the beginning of year $t$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T_1$ |
| $x_2[t]$ | yuan placed in the 2-year option at the beginning of year $t$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T_2$ |
| $s[t]$   | idle cash at the beginning of year $t$ ($s[1]=W_0$, $s[4]$ = final idle cash) | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T$ |
| $y[t]$   | 1 if the 2-year option is started at the beginning of year $t$ | $\{0,1\}$, $t\in T_2$ |

### Objective
$$
\max\; W \;=\; s[4]\;+\;1.7\,x_1[3]\;+\;3\,x_2[2]
$$

### Constraints (cash-flow balance at the beginning of each year)

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\text{C1})\quad & x_1[1] + x_2[1] + s[2] = 100{,}000 &&\text{(begin year 1)}\\
(\text{C2})\quad & x_1[2] + x_2[2] + s[3] = s[2] + 1.7\,x_1[1] &&\text{(begin year 2)}\\
(\text{C3})\quad & x_1[3] + s[4] = s[3] + 1.7\,x_1[2] + 3\,x_2[1] &&\text{(begin year 3)}\\
(\text{C4})\quad & x_2[t] \le M\,y[t],\quad t\in T_2 &&\text{(link to binary)}\\
(\text{C5})\quad & s[1] = 100{,}000 &&\text{(fixed initial cash)}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Correction of the suggested structure
The draft used $0.7\,x_1[\cdot]$ and $2\,x_2[\cdot]$ (profits only) on the right-hand sides of (C2)–(C3) and in the objective. That double-counts the principal as "lost". The correct maturity cash-flows are $1.7\,x_1[\cdot]$ and $3\,x_2[\cdot]$ (principal + profit), and the objective must use the same multipliers.

### Stated assumptions
1. Profits are deterministic and guaranteed; no risk, no liquidity premium.
2. No early withdrawal; cash from an option is received only at maturity.
3. Funds are perfectly divisible (yuan units relaxed to continuous).
4. Idle cash earns 0 (no interest, no inflation adjustment).
5. No transaction costs, no minimum investment, no fixed cost for opening an option.
6. The 2-year option cannot be started at $t=3$ because it would mature at $t=5$, beyond the horizon.
7. The 1-year option started at $t=3$ matures exactly at $t=4$ (end of year 3) and is therefore feasible.

Because there is no fixed cost, the binaries $y[t]$ are **redundant**: at any optimum with $x_2[t]>0$ we simply have $y[t]=1$, and (C4) is non-binding. The MILP therefore collapses to a pure LP.

---

## 2. Optimal Solution

### Optimal value
$$
W^\star \;=\; 510{,}000 \text{ yuan.}
$$

### Optimal strategies (the LP has a continuum of optima)
Because $1.7\times 3 = 3\times 1.7 = 5.1$, any sequence that fills the 3-year horizon with one 1-year and one 2-year leg yields the same final wealth. Two corner-point optima are:

**Strategy A — "2-year first, then 1-year":**

| $t$ | $x_1[t]$ | $x_2[t]$ | $s[t]$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 100,000 | 100,000 |
| 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 3 | 300,000 | — | 0 |
| 4 | — | — | 0 |

Cash trace: $100{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 3} 300{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 1.7} 510{,}000$.

**Strategy B — "1-year first, then 2-year":**

| $t$ | $x_1[t]$ | $x_2[t]$ | $s[t]$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 100,000 | 0 | 100,000 |
| 2 | 0 | 170,000 | 0 |
| 3 | 0 | — | 0 |
| 4 | — | — | 0 |

Cash trace: $100{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 1.7} 170{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 3} 510{,}000$.

**Strategy C (any convex combination):** pick any $\alpha\in[0,1]$ and set
$x_1[1]=100{,}000\,\alpha,\; x_2[1]=100{,}000\,(1-\alpha),\; x_2[2]=170{,}000\,\alpha,\; x_1[3]=300{,}000\,(1-\alpha)$, all other variables 0. Final wealth is always $5.1\cdot 100{,}000=510{,}000$.

---

## 3. LP / Dual Argument for Optimality

Let $\pi_1,\pi_2,\pi_3$ be the dual multipliers of (C1)–(C3). The dual is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& 100{,}000\,\pi_1\\
\text{s.t. }& \pi_1 - 1.7\pi_2 \ge 0 &&(x_1[1])\\
& \pi_1 - 3\pi_3 \ge 0 &&(x_2[1])\\
& \pi_1 - \pi_2 \ge 0 &&(s[2])\\
& \pi_2 - 1.7\pi_3 \ge 0 &&(x_1[2])\\
& \pi_2 \ge 3 &&(x_2[2])\\
& \pi_2 - \pi_3 \ge 0 &&(s[3])\\
& \pi_3 \ge 1.7 &&(x_1[3])\\
& \pi_3 \ge 1 &&(s[4]).
\end{aligned}
$$

Tightening the binding constraints $\pi_2\ge 3$ and $\pi_3\ge 1.7$ forces
$\pi_1 \ge 1.7\pi_2 = 5.1$ and $\pi_1 \ge 3\pi_3 = 5.1$. The minimum is

$$
\boxed{\;\pi_1^\star = 5.1,\quad \pi_2^\star = 3,\quad \pi_3^\star = 1.7\;}
$$

giving dual objective $100{,}000\times 5.1 = 510{,}000$. By strong LP duality, $W^\star = 510{,}000$.

**Economic reading of the duals (shadow prices of cash at the beginning of each year):**
- $\pi_3^\star = 1.7$: one extra yuan at $t=3$ is worth $1.7$ yuan at $t=4$ (use the 1-year option).
- $\pi_2^\star = 3$: one extra yuan at $t=2$ is worth $3$ yuan at $t=4$ (use the 2-year option).
- $\pi_1^\star = 5.1$: one extra yuan at $t=1$ is worth $5.1$ yuan at $t=4$ (combine the two options over the 3-year horizon).

**Complementary slackness** confirms the structure of the optimal set: $\pi_1-\pi_2=2.1>0 \Rightarrow s[2]=0$; $\pi_2-\pi_3=1.3>0 \Rightarrow s[3]=0$; $\pi_3-1=0.7>0 \Rightarrow s[4]=0$; $\pi_2-1.7\pi_3=0.11>0 \Rightarrow x_1[2]=0$. The remaining primal variables $x_1[1],x_2[1],x_2[2],x_1[3]$ are free to vary along the face $x_1[1]+x_2[1]=100{,}000,\; x_2[2]=1.7\,x_1[1],\; x_1[3]=3\,x_2[1]$, which is exactly the family of optima described above.

---

## 4. Bottom Line

- The corrected MILP has 8 continuous variables, 2 binaries (redundant), 3 equality constraints, and 2 big-M linking constraints.
- **Optimal final wealth: $W^\star = 510{,}000$ yuan** (a $5.1\times$ return on the initial $100{,}000$).
- Any plan that uses the 3-year horizon with exactly one 1-year leg and one 2-year leg is optimal; the simplest is to invest everything in the 2-year option at $t=1$ and roll the proceeds into the 1-year option at $t=3$.
The model is structurally sound and I've verified the dual, complementary slackness, and the primal optimum family. Let me send refinement feedback.

Option 2 ("long"): guarantees a profit of 2 yuan per 1 yuan invested, paid after two years; the investment time must be a multiple of two years, so within this 3-year horizon it can only be started at the beginning of Year 1 (matures end of Year 2) or at the beginning of Year 2 (matures end of Year 3). 1 yuan invested grows to 3 yuan at maturity.

Any money not invested is held idle (no interest) until the end of Year 3. All funds available at the beginning of a year may be split freely between the two options and idle cash.

Task: Formulate this as a linear (MILP) program with explicit decision variables, objective function and constraints, and state the optimal allocation and the optimal final wealth. Please write it out with equations, index sets, and explain the assumptions."}

messages.content:
# Complete MILP Formulation and Solution

## 1. Corrected Model

### Sets and indices
- $T_1=\{1,2,3\}$ — beginnings of years in which the 1-year option may be started.
- $T_2=\{1,2\}$ — beginnings of years in which the 2-year option may be started (starting at year 3 would mature after the horizon).
- $T=\{1,2,3,4\}$ — cash states; $t=4$ is the end of year 3.

### Parameters
- $W_0 = 100{,}000$ (initial wealth, available at $t=1$).
- 1-year option: principal $B$ at $t$ becomes $1.7B$ at $t+1$ (profit $0.7B$).
- 2-year option: principal $B$ at $t$ becomes $3B$ at $t+2$ (profit $2B$).
- $M$ — big-M; a tight choice is $M=100{,}000$ for $t=1$ and $M=170{,}000$ for $t=2$ (the largest cash that can ever sit at $t=2$).

### Decision variables
| Variable | Meaning | Domain |
|---|---|---|
| $x_1[t]$ | yuan placed in the 1-year option at the beginning of year $t$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T_1$ |
| $x_2[t]$ | yuan placed in the 2-year option at the beginning of year $t$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T_2$ |
| $s[t]$   | idle cash at the beginning of year $t$ ($s[1]=W_0$, $s[4]$ = final idle cash) | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T$ |
| $y[t]$   | 1 if the 2-year option is started at the beginning of year $t$ | $\{0,1\}$, $t\in T_2$ |

### Objective
$$
\max\; W \;=\; s[4]\;+\;1.7\,x_1[3]\;+\;3\,x_2[2]
$$

### Constraints (cash-flow balance at the beginning of each year)

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\text{C1})\quad & x_1[1] + x_2[1] + s[2] = 100{,}000 &&\text{(begin year 1)}\\
(\text{C2})\quad & x_1[2] + x_2[2] + s[3] = s[2] + 1.7\,x_1[1] &&\text{(begin year 2)}\\
(\text{C3})\quad & x_1[3] + s[4] = s[3] + 1.7\,x_1[2] + 3\,x_2[1] &&\text{(begin year 3)}\\
(\text{C4})\quad & x_2[t] \le M\,y[t],\quad t\in T_2 &&\text{(link to binary)}\\
(\text{C5})\quad & s[1] = 100{,}000 &&\text{(fixed initial cash)}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Correction of the suggested structure
The draft used $0.7\,x_1[\cdot]$ and $2\,x_2[\cdot]$ (profits only) on the right-hand sides of (C2)–(C3) and in the objective. That double-counts the principal as "lost". The correct maturity cash-flows are $1.7\,x_1[\cdot]$ and $3\,x_2[\cdot]$ (principal + profit), and the objective must use the same multipliers.

### Stated assumptions
1. Profits are deterministic and guaranteed; no risk, no liquidity premium.
2. No early withdrawal; cash from an option is received only at maturity.
3. Funds are perfectly divisible (yuan units relaxed to continuous).
4. Idle cash earns 0 (no interest, no inflation adjustment).
5. No transaction costs, no minimum investment, no fixed cost for opening an option.
6. The 2-year option cannot be started at $t=3$ because it would mature at $t=5$, beyond the horizon.
7. The 1-year option started at $t=3$ matures exactly at $t=4$ (end of year 3) and is therefore feasible.

Because there is no fixed cost, the binaries $y[t]$ are **redundant**: at any optimum with $x_2[t]>0$ we simply have $y[t]=1$, and (C4) is non-binding. The MILP therefore collapses to a pure LP.

---

## 2. Optimal Solution

### Optimal value
$$
W^\star \;=\; 510{,}000 \text{ yuan.}
$$

### Optimal strategies (the LP has a continuum of optima)
Because $1.7\times 3 = 3\times 1.7 = 5.1$, any sequence that fills the 3-year horizon with one 1-year and one 2-year leg yields the same final wealth. Two corner-point optima are:

**Strategy A — "2-year first, then 1-year":**

| $t$ | $x_1[t]$ | $x_2[t]$ | $s[t]$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 100,000 | 100,000 |
| 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 3 | 300,000 | — | 0 |
| 4 | — | — | 0 |

Cash trace: $100{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 3} 300{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 1.7} 510{,}000$.

**Strategy B — "1-year first, then 2-year":**

| $t$ | $x_1[t]$ | $x_2[t]$ | $s[t]$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 100,000 | 0 | 100,000 |
| 2 | 0 | 170,000 | 0 |
| 3 | 0 | — | 0 |
| 4 | — | — | 0 |

Cash trace: $100{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 1.7} 170{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 3} 510{,}000$.

**Strategy C (any convex combination):** pick any $\alpha\in[0,1]$ and set
$x_1[1]=100{,}000\,\alpha,\; x_2[1]=100{,}000\,(1-\alpha),\; x_2[2]=170{,}000\,\alpha,\; x_1[3]=300{,}000\,(1-\alpha)$, all other variables 0. Final wealth is always $5.1\cdot 100{,}000=510{,}000$.

---

## 3. LP / Dual Argument for Optimality

Let $\pi_1,\pi_2,\pi_3$ be the dual multipliers of (C1)–(C3). The dual is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& 100{,}000\,\pi_1\\
\text{s.t. }& \pi_1 - 1.7\pi_2 \ge 0 &&(x_1[1])\\
& \pi_1 - 3\pi_3 \ge 0 &&(x_2[1])\\
& \pi_1 - \pi_2 \ge 0 &&(s[2])\\
& \pi_2 - 1.7\pi_3 \ge 0 &&(x_1[2])\\
& \pi_2 \ge 3 &&(x_2[2])\\
& \pi_2 - \pi_3 \ge 0 &&(s[3])\\
& \pi_3 \ge 1.7 &&(x_1[3])\\
& \pi_3 \ge 1 &&(s[4]).
\end{aligned}
$$

Tightening the binding constraints $\pi_2\ge 3$ and $\pi_3\ge 1.7$ forces
$\pi_1 \ge 1.7\pi_2 = 5.1$ and $\pi_1 \ge 3\pi_3 = 5.1$. The minimum is

$$
\boxed{\;\pi_1^\star = 5.1,\quad \pi_2^\star = 3,\quad \pi_3^\star = 1.7\;}
$$

giving dual objective $100{,}000\times 5.1 = 510{,}000$. By strong LP duality, $W^\star = 510{,}000$.

**Economic reading of the duals (shadow prices of cash at the beginning of each year):**
- $\pi_3^\star = 1.7$: one extra yuan at $t=3$ is worth $1.7$ yuan at $t=4$ (use the 1-year option).
- $\pi_2^\star = 3$: one extra yuan at $t=2$ is worth $3$ yuan at $t=4$ (use the 2-year option).
- $\pi_1^\star = 5.1$: one extra yuan at $t=1$ is worth $5.1$ yuan at $t=4$ (combine the two options over the 3-year horizon).

**Complementary slackness** confirms the structure of the optimal set: $\pi_1-\pi_2=2.1>0 \Rightarrow s[2]=0$; $\pi_2-\pi_3=1.3>0 \Rightarrow s[3]=0$; $\pi_3-1=0.7>0 \Rightarrow s[4]=0$; $\pi_2-1.7\pi_3=0.11>0 \Rightarrow x_1[2]=0$. The remaining primal variables $x_1[1],x_2[1],x_2[2],x_1[3]$ are free to vary along the face $x_1[1]+x_2[1]=100{,}000,\; x_2[2]=1.7\,x_1[1],\; x_1[3]=3\,x_2[1]$, which is exactly the family of optima described above.

---

## 4. Bottom Line

- The corrected MILP has 8 continuous variables, 2 binaries (redundant), 3 equality constraints, and 2 big-M linking constraints.
- **Optimal final wealth: $W^\star = 510{,}000$ yuan** (a $5.1\times$ return on the initial $100{,}000$).
- Any plan that uses the 3-year horizon with exactly one 1-year leg and one 2-year leg is optimal; the simplest is to invest everything in the 2-year option at $t=1$ and roll the proceeds into the 1-year option at $t=3$.
The model is structurally sound and I've verified the dual, complementary slackness, and the primal optimum family. Let me send refinement feedback.

response.content:
# Complete MILP Formulation and Solution

## 1. Corrected Model

### Sets and indices
- $T_1=\{1,2,3\}$ — beginnings of years in which the 1-year option may be started.
- $T_2=\{1,2\}$ — beginnings of years in which the 2-year option may be started (starting at year 3 would mature after the horizon).
- $T=\{1,2,3,4\}$ — cash states; $t=4$ is the end of year 3.

### Parameters
- $W_0 = 100{,}000$ (initial wealth, available at $t=1$).
- 1-year option: principal $B$ at $t$ becomes $1.7B$ at $t+1$ (profit $0.7B$).
- 2-year option: principal $B$ at $t$ becomes $3B$ at $t+2$ (profit $2B$).
- $M$ — big-M; a tight choice is $M=100{,}000$ for $t=1$ and $M=170{,}000$ for $t=2$ (the largest cash that can ever sit at $t=2$).

### Decision variables
| Variable | Meaning | Domain |
|---|---|---|
| $x_1[t]$ | yuan placed in the 1-year option at the beginning of year $t$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T_1$ |
| $x_2[t]$ | yuan placed in the 2-year option at the beginning of year $t$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T_2$ |
| $s[t]$   | idle cash at the beginning of year $t$ ($s[1]=W_0$, $s[4]$ = final idle cash) | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T$ |
| $y[t]$   | 1 if the 2-year option is started at the beginning of year $t$ | $\{0,1\}$, $t\in T_2$ |

### Objective
$$
\max\; W \;=\; s[4]\;+\;1.7\,x_1[3]\;+\;3\,x_2[2]
$$

### Constraints (cash-flow balance at the beginning of each year)

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\text{C1})\quad & x_1[1] + x_2[1] + s[2] = 100{,}000 &&\text{(begin year 1)}\\
(\text{C2})\quad & x_1[2] + x_2[2] + s[3] = s[2] + 1.7\,x_1[1] &&\text{(begin year 2)}\\
(\text{C3})\quad & x_1[3] + s[4] = s[3] + 1.7\,x_1[2] + 3\,x_2[1] &&\text{(begin year 3)}\\
(\text{C4})\quad & x_2[t] \le M\,y[t],\quad t\in T_2 &&\text{(link to binary)}\\
(\text{C5})\quad & s[1] = 100{,}000 &&\text{(fixed initial cash)}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Correction of the suggested structure
The draft used $0.7\,x_1[\cdot]$ and $2\,x_2[\cdot]$ (profits only) on the right-hand sides of (C2)–(C3) and in the objective. That double-counts the principal as "lost". The correct maturity cash-flows are $1.7\,x_1[\cdot]$ and $3\,x_2[\cdot]$ (principal + profit), and the objective must use the same multipliers.

### Stated assumptions
1. Profits are deterministic and guaranteed; no risk, no liquidity premium.
2. No early withdrawal; cash from an option is received only at maturity.
3. Funds are perfectly divisible (yuan units relaxed to continuous).
4. Idle cash earns 0 (no interest, no inflation adjustment).
5. No transaction costs, no minimum investment, no fixed cost for opening an option.
6. The 2-year option cannot be started at $t=3$ because it would mature at $t=5$, beyond the horizon.
7. The 1-year option started at $t=3$ matures exactly at $t=4$ (end of year 3) and is therefore feasible.

Because there is no fixed cost, the binaries $y[t]$ are **redundant**: at any optimum with $x_2[t]>0$ we simply have $y[t]=1$, and (C4) is non-binding. The MILP therefore collapses to a pure LP.

---

## 2. Optimal Solution

### Optimal value
$$
W^\star \;=\; 510{,}000 \text{ yuan.}
$$

### Optimal strategies (the LP has a continuum of optima)
Because $1.7\times 3 = 3\times 1.7 = 5.1$, any sequence that fills the 3-year horizon with one 1-year and one 2-year leg yields the same final wealth. Two corner-point optima are:

**Strategy A — "2-year first, then 1-year":**

| $t$ | $x_1[t]$ | $x_2[t]$ | $s[t]$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 100,000 | 100,000 |
| 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 3 | 300,000 | — | 0 |
| 4 | — | — | 0 |

Cash trace: $100{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 3} 300{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 1.7} 510{,}000$.

**Strategy B — "1-year first, then 2-year":**

| $t$ | $x_1[t]$ | $x_2[t]$ | $s[t]$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 100,000 | 0 | 100,000 |
| 2 | 0 | 170,000 | 0 |
| 3 | 0 | — | 0 |
| 4 | — | — | 0 |

Cash trace: $100{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 1.7} 170{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 3} 510{,}000$.

**Strategy C (any convex combination):** pick any $\alpha\in[0,1]$ and set
$x_1[1]=100{,}000\,\alpha,\; x_2[1]=100{,}000\,(1-\alpha),\; x_2[2]=170{,}000\,\alpha,\; x_1[3]=300{,}000\,(1-\alpha)$, all other variables 0. Final wealth is always $5.1\cdot 100{,}000=510{,}000$.

---

## 3. LP / Dual Argument for Optimality

Let $\pi_1,\pi_2,\pi_3$ be the dual multipliers of (C1)–(C3). The dual is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& 100{,}000\,\pi_1\\
\text{s.t. }& \pi_1 - 1.7\pi_2 \ge 0 &&(x_1[1])\\
& \pi_1 - 3\pi_3 \ge 0 &&(x_2[1])\\
& \pi_1 - \pi_2 \ge 0 &&(s[2])\\
& \pi_2 - 1.7\pi_3 \ge 0 &&(x_1[2])\\
& \pi_2 \ge 3 &&(x_2[2])\\
& \pi_2 - \pi_3 \ge 0 &&(s[3])\\
& \pi_3 \ge 1.7 &&(x_1[3])\\
& \pi_3 \ge 1 &&(s[4]).
\end{aligned}
$$

Tightening the binding constraints $\pi_2\ge 3$ and $\pi_3\ge 1.7$ forces
$\pi_1 \ge 1.7\pi_2 = 5.1$ and $\pi_1 \ge 3\pi_3 = 5.1$. The minimum is

$$
\boxed{\;\pi_1^\star = 5.1,\quad \pi_2^\star = 3,\quad \pi_3^\star = 1.7\;}
$$

giving dual objective $100{,}000\times 5.1 = 510{,}000$. By strong LP duality, $W^\star = 510{,}000$.

**Economic reading of the duals (shadow prices of cash at the beginning of each year):**
- $\pi_3^\star = 1.7$: one extra yuan at $t=3$ is worth $1.7$ yuan at $t=4$ (use the 1-year option).
- $\pi_2^\star = 3$: one extra yuan at $t=2$ is worth $3$ yuan at $t=4$ (use the 2-year option).
- $\pi_1^\star = 5.1$: one extra yuan at $t=1$ is worth $5.1$ yuan at $t=4$ (combine the two options over the 3-year horizon).

**Complementary slackness** confirms the structure of the optimal set: $\pi_1-\pi_2=2.1>0 \Rightarrow s[2]=0$; $\pi_2-\pi_3=1.3>0 \Rightarrow s[3]=0$; $\pi_3-1=0.7>0 \Rightarrow s[4]=0$; $\pi_2-1.7\pi_3=0.11>0 \Rightarrow x_1[2]=0$. The remaining primal variables $x_1[1],x_2[1],x_2[2],x_1[3]$ are free to vary along the face $x_1[1]+x_2[1]=100{,}000,\; x_2[2]=1.7\,x_1[1],\; x_1[3]=3\,x_2[1]$, which is exactly the family of optima described above.

---

## 4. Bottom Line

- The corrected MILP has 8 continuous variables, 2 binaries (redundant), 3 equality constraints, and 2 big-M linking constraints.
- **Optimal final wealth: $W^\star = 510{,}000$ yuan** (a $5.1\times$ return on the initial $100{,}000$).
- Any plan that uses the 3-year horizon with exactly one 1-year leg and one 2-year leg is optimal; the simplest is to invest everything in the 2-year option at $t=1$ and roll the proceeds into the 1-year option at $t=3$.

messages.content:
# Complete MILP Formulation and Solution

## 1. Corrected Model

### Sets and indices
- $T_1=\{1,2,3\}$ — beginnings of years in which the 1-year option may be started.
- $T_2=\{1,2\}$ — beginnings of years in which the 2-year option may be started (starting at year 3 would mature after the horizon).
- $T=\{1,2,3,4\}$ — cash states; $t=4$ is the end of year 3.

### Parameters
- $W_0 = 100{,}000$ (initial wealth, available at $t=1$).
- 1-year option: principal $B$ at $t$ becomes $1.7B$ at $t+1$ (profit $0.7B$).
- 2-year option: principal $B$ at $t$ becomes $3B$ at $t+2$ (profit $2B$).
- $M$ — big-M; a tight choice is $M=100{,}000$ for $t=1$ and $M=170{,}000$ for $t=2$ (the largest cash that can ever sit at $t=2$).

### Decision variables
| Variable | Meaning | Domain |
|---|---|---|
| $x_1[t]$ | yuan placed in the 1-year option at the beginning of year $t$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T_1$ |
| $x_2[t]$ | yuan placed in the 2-year option at the beginning of year $t$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T_2$ |
| $s[t]$   | idle cash at the beginning of year $t$ ($s[1]=W_0$, $s[4]$ = final idle cash) | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T$ |
| $y[t]$   | 1 if the 2-year option is started at the beginning of year $t$ | $\{0,1\}$, $t\in T_2$ |

### Objective
$$
\max\; W \;=\; s[4]\;+\;1.7\,x_1[3]\;+\;3\,x_2[2]
$$

### Constraints (cash-flow balance at the beginning of each year)

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\text{C1})\quad & x_1[1] + x_2[1] + s[2] = 100{,}000 &&\text{(begin year 1)}\\
(\text{C2})\quad & x_1[2] + x_2[2] + s[3] = s[2] + 1.7\,x_1[1] &&\text{(begin year 2)}\\
(\text{C3})\quad & x_1[3] + s[4] = s[3] + 1.7\,x_1[2] + 3\,x_2[1] &&\text{(begin year 3)}\\
(\text{C4})\quad & x_2[t] \le M\,y[t],\quad t\in T_2 &&\text{(link to binary)}\\
(\text{C5})\quad & s[1] = 100{,}000 &&\text{(fixed initial cash)}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Correction of the suggested structure
The draft used $0.7\,x_1[\cdot]$ and $2\,x_2[\cdot]$ (profits only) on the right-hand sides of (C2)–(C3) and in the objective. That double-counts the principal as "lost". The correct maturity cash-flows are $1.7\,x_1[\cdot]$ and $3\,x_2[\cdot]$ (principal + profit), and the objective must use the same multipliers.

### Stated assumptions
1. Profits are deterministic and guaranteed; no risk, no liquidity premium.
2. No early withdrawal; cash from an option is received only at maturity.
3. Funds are perfectly divisible (yuan units relaxed to continuous).
4. Idle cash earns 0 (no interest, no inflation adjustment).
5. No transaction costs, no minimum investment, no fixed cost for opening an option.
6. The 2-year option cannot be started at $t=3$ because it would mature at $t=5$, beyond the horizon.
7. The 1-year option started at $t=3$ matures exactly at $t=4$ (end of year 3) and is therefore feasible.

Because there is no fixed cost, the binaries $y[t]$ are **redundant**: at any optimum with $x_2[t]>0$ we simply have $y[t]=1$, and (C4) is non-binding. The MILP therefore collapses to a pure LP.

---

## 2. Optimal Solution

### Optimal value
$$
W^\star \;=\; 510{,}000 \text{ yuan.}
$$

### Optimal strategies (the LP has a continuum of optima)
Because $1.7\times 3 = 3\times 1.7 = 5.1$, any sequence that fills the 3-year horizon with one 1-year and one 2-year leg yields the same final wealth. Two corner-point optima are:

**Strategy A — "2-year first, then 1-year":**

| $t$ | $x_1[t]$ | $x_2[t]$ | $s[t]$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 100,000 | 100,000 |
| 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 3 | 300,000 | — | 0 |
| 4 | — | — | 0 |

Cash trace: $100{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 3} 300{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 1.7} 510{,}000$.

**Strategy B — "1-year first, then 2-year":**

| $t$ | $x_1[t]$ | $x_2[t]$ | $s[t]$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 100,000 | 0 | 100,000 |
| 2 | 0 | 170,000 | 0 |
| 3 | 0 | — | 0 |
| 4 | — | — | 0 |

Cash trace: $100{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 1.7} 170{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 3} 510{,}000$.

**Strategy C (any convex combination):** pick any $\alpha\in[0,1]$ and set
$x_1[1]=100{,}000\,\alpha,\; x_2[1]=100{,}000\,(1-\alpha),\; x_2[2]=170{,}000\,\alpha,\; x_1[3]=300{,}000\,(1-\alpha)$, all other variables 0. Final wealth is always $5.1\cdot 100{,}000=510{,}000$.

---

## 3. LP / Dual Argument for Optimality

Let $\pi_1,\pi_2,\pi_3$ be the dual multipliers of (C1)–(C3). The dual is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& 100{,}000\,\pi_1\\
\text{s.t. }& \pi_1 - 1.7\pi_2 \ge 0 &&(x_1[1])\\
& \pi_1 - 3\pi_3 \ge 0 &&(x_2[1])\\
& \pi_1 - \pi_2 \ge 0 &&(s[2])\\
& \pi_2 - 1.7\pi_3 \ge 0 &&(x_1[2])\\
& \pi_2 \ge 3 &&(x_2[2])\\
& \pi_2 - \pi_3 \ge 0 &&(s[3])\\
& \pi_3 \ge 1.7 &&(x_1[3])\\
& \pi_3 \ge 1 &&(s[4]).
\end{aligned}
$$

Tightening the binding constraints $\pi_2\ge 3$ and $\pi_3\ge 1.7$ forces
$\pi_1 \ge 1.7\pi_2 = 5.1$ and $\pi_1 \ge 3\pi_3 = 5.1$. The minimum is

$$
\boxed{\;\pi_1^\star = 5.1,\quad \pi_2^\star = 3,\quad \pi_3^\star = 1.7\;}
$$

giving dual objective $100{,}000\times 5.1 = 510{,}000$. By strong LP duality, $W^\star = 510{,}000$.

**Economic reading of the duals (shadow prices of cash at the beginning of each year):**
- $\pi_3^\star = 1.7$: one extra yuan at $t=3$ is worth $1.7$ yuan at $t=4$ (use the 1-year option).
- $\pi_2^\star = 3$: one extra yuan at $t=2$ is worth $3$ yuan at $t=4$ (use the 2-year option).
- $\pi_1^\star = 5.1$: one extra yuan at $t=1$ is worth $5.1$ yuan at $t=4$ (combine the two options over the 3-year horizon).

**Complementary slackness** confirms the structure of the optimal set: $\pi_1-\pi_2=2.1>0 \Rightarrow s[2]=0$; $\pi_2-\pi_3=1.3>0 \Rightarrow s[3]=0$; $\pi_3-1=0.7>0 \Rightarrow s[4]=0$; $\pi_2-1.7\pi_3=0.11>0 \Rightarrow x_1[2]=0$. The remaining primal variables $x_1[1],x_2[1],x_2[2],x_1[3]$ are free to vary along the face $x_1[1]+x_2[1]=100{,}000,\; x_2[2]=1.7\,x_1[1],\; x_1[3]=3\,x_2[1]$, which is exactly the family of optima described above.

---

## 4. Bottom Line

- The corrected MILP has 8 continuous variables, 2 binaries (redundant), 3 equality constraints, and 2 big-M linking constraints.
- **Optimal final wealth: $W^\star = 510{,}000$ yuan** (a $5.1\times$ return on the initial $100{,}000$).
- Any plan that uses the 3-year horizon with exactly one 1-year leg and one 2-year leg is optimal; the simplest is to invest everything in the 2-year option at $t=1$ and roll the proceeds into the 1-year option at $t=3$.
The model is structurally sound and I've verified the dual, complementary slackness, and the primal optimum family. Let me send refinement feedback.

messages.content:
# Complete MILP Formulation and Solution

## 1. Corrected Model

### Sets and indices
- $T_1=\{1,2,3\}$ — beginnings of years in which the 1-year option may be started.
- $T_2=\{1,2\}$ — beginnings of years in which the 2-year option may be started (starting at year 3 would mature after the horizon).
- $T=\{1,2,3,4\}$ — cash states; $t=4$ is the end of year 3.

### Parameters
- $W_0 = 100{,}000$ (initial wealth, available at $t=1$).
- 1-year option: principal $B$ at $t$ becomes $1.7B$ at $t+1$ (profit $0.7B$).
- 2-year option: principal $B$ at $t$ becomes $3B$ at $t+2$ (profit $2B$).
- $M$ — big-M; a tight choice is $M=100{,}000$ for $t=1$ and $M=170{,}000$ for $t=2$ (the largest cash that can ever sit at $t=2$).

### Decision variables
| Variable | Meaning | Domain |
|---|---|---|
| $x_1[t]$ | yuan placed in the 1-year option at the beginning of year $t$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T_1$ |
| $x_2[t]$ | yuan placed in the 2-year option at the beginning of year $t$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T_2$ |
| $s[t]$   | idle cash at the beginning of year $t$ ($s[1]=W_0$, $s[4]$ = final idle cash) | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T$ |
| $y[t]$   | 1 if the 2-year option is started at the beginning of year $t$ | $\{0,1\}$, $t\in T_2$ |

### Objective
$$
\max\; W \;=\; s[4]\;+\;1.7\,x_1[3]\;+\;3\,x_2[2]
$$

### Constraints (cash-flow balance at the beginning of each year)

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\text{C1})\quad & x_1[1] + x_2[1] + s[2] = 100{,}000 &&\text{(begin year 1)}\\
(\text{C2})\quad & x_1[2] + x_2[2] + s[3] = s[2] + 1.7\,x_1[1] &&\text{(begin year 2)}\\
(\text{C3})\quad & x_1[3] + s[4] = s[3] + 1.7\,x_1[2] + 3\,x_2[1] &&\text{(begin year 3)}\\
(\text{C4})\quad & x_2[t] \le M\,y[t],\quad t\in T_2 &&\text{(link to binary)}\\
(\text{C5})\quad & s[1] = 100{,}000 &&\text{(fixed initial cash)}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Correction of the suggested structure
The draft used $0.7\,x_1[\cdot]$ and $2\,x_2[\cdot]$ (profits only) on the right-hand sides of (C2)–(C3) and in the objective. That double-counts the principal as "lost". The correct maturity cash-flows are $1.7\,x_1[\cdot]$ and $3\,x_2[\cdot]$ (principal + profit), and the objective must use the same multipliers.

### Stated assumptions
1. Profits are deterministic and guaranteed; no risk, no liquidity premium.
2. No early withdrawal; cash from an option is received only at maturity.
3. Funds are perfectly divisible (yuan units relaxed to continuous).
4. Idle cash earns 0 (no interest, no inflation adjustment).
5. No transaction costs, no minimum investment, no fixed cost for opening an option.
6. The 2-year option cannot be started at $t=3$ because it would mature at $t=5$, beyond the horizon.
7. The 1-year option started at $t=3$ matures exactly at $t=4$ (end of year 3) and is therefore feasible.

Because there is no fixed cost, the binaries $y[t]$ are **redundant**: at any optimum with $x_2[t]>0$ we simply have $y[t]=1$, and (C4) is non-binding. The MILP therefore collapses to a pure LP.

---

## 2. Optimal Solution

### Optimal value
$$
W^\star \;=\; 510{,}000 \text{ yuan.}
$$

### Optimal strategies (the LP has a continuum of optima)
Because $1.7\times 3 = 3\times 1.7 = 5.1$, any sequence that fills the 3-year horizon with one 1-year and one 2-year leg yields the same final wealth. Two corner-point optima are:

**Strategy A — "2-year first, then 1-year":**

| $t$ | $x_1[t]$ | $x_2[t]$ | $s[t]$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 100,000 | 100,000 |
| 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 3 | 300,000 | — | 0 |
| 4 | — | — | 0 |

Cash trace: $100{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 3} 300{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 1.7} 510{,}000$.

**Strategy B — "1-year first, then 2-year":**

| $t$ | $x_1[t]$ | $x_2[t]$ | $s[t]$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 100,000 | 0 | 100,000 |
| 2 | 0 | 170,000 | 0 |
| 3 | 0 | — | 0 |
| 4 | — | — | 0 |

Cash trace: $100{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 1.7} 170{,}000 \xrightarrow{\times 3} 510{,}000$.

**Strategy C (any convex combination):** pick any $\alpha\in[0,1]$ and set
$x_1[1]=100{,}000\,\alpha,\; x_2[1]=100{,}000\,(1-\alpha),\; x_2[2]=170{,}000\,\alpha,\; x_1[3]=300{,}000\,(1-\alpha)$, all other variables 0. Final wealth is always $5.1\cdot 100{,}000=510{,}000$.

---

## 3. LP / Dual Argument for Optimality

Let $\pi_1,\pi_2,\pi_3$ be the dual multipliers of (C1)–(C3). The dual is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& 100{,}000\,\pi_1\\
\text{s.t. }& \pi_1 - 1.7\pi_2 \ge 0 &&(x_1[1])\\
& \pi_1 - 3\pi_3 \ge 0 &&(x_2[1])\\
& \pi_1 - \pi_2 \ge 0 &&(s[2])\\
& \pi_2 - 1.7\pi_3 \ge 0 &&(x_1[2])\\
& \pi_2 \ge 3 &&(x_2[2])\\
& \pi_2 - \pi_3 \ge 0 &&(s[3])\\
& \pi_3 \ge 1.7 &&(x_1[3])\\
& \pi_3 \ge 1 &&(s[4]).
\end{aligned}
$$

Tightening the binding constraints $\pi_2\ge 3$ and $\pi_3\ge 1.7$ forces
$\pi_1 \ge 1.7\pi_2 = 5.1$ and $\pi_1 \ge 3\pi_3 = 5.1$. The minimum is

$$
\boxed{\;\pi_1^\star = 5.1,\quad \pi_2^\star = 3,\quad \pi_3^\star = 1.7\;}
$$

giving dual objective $100{,}000\times 5.1 = 510{,}000$. By strong LP duality, $W^\star = 510{,}000$.

**Economic reading of the duals (shadow prices of cash at the beginning of each year):**
- $\pi_3^\star = 1.7$: one extra yuan at $t=3$ is worth $1.7$ yuan at $t=4$ (use the 1-year option).
- $\pi_2^\star = 3$: one extra yuan at $t=2$ is worth $3$ yuan at $t=4$ (use the 2-year option).
- $\pi_1^\star = 5.1$: one extra yuan at $t=1$ is worth $5.1$ yuan at $t=4$ (combine the two options over the 3-year horizon).

**Complementary slackness** confirms the structure of the optimal set: $\pi_1-\pi_2=2.1>0 \Rightarrow s[2]=0$; $\pi_2-\pi_3=1.3>0 \Rightarrow s[3]=0$; $\pi_3-1=0.7>0 \Rightarrow s[4]=0$; $\pi_2-1.7\pi_3=0.11>0 \Rightarrow x_1[2]=0$. The remaining primal variables $x_1[1],x_2[1],x_2[2],x_1[3]$ are free to vary along the face $x_1[1]+x_2[1]=100{,}000,\; x_2[2]=1.7\,x_1[1],\; x_1[3]=3\,x_2[1]$, which is exactly the family of optima described above.

---

## 4. Bottom Line

- The corrected MILP has 8 continuous variables, 2 binaries (redundant), 3 equality constraints, and 2 big-M linking constraints.
- **Optimal final wealth: $W^\star = 510{,}000$ yuan** (a $5.1\times$ return on the initial $100{,}000$).
- Any plan that uses the 3-year horizon with exactly one 1-year leg and one 2-year leg is optimal; the simplest is to invest everything in the 2-year option at $t=1$ and roll the proceeds into the 1-year option at $t=3$.
The model is structurally sound and I've verified the dual, complementary slackness, and the primal optimum family. Let me send refinement feedback.

{"description": "Investment planning problem. An investor has 100,000 yuan to invest at the beginning of Year 1 and wants to maximize the total amount of money (principal + profit) held at the end of Year 3. There are two investment options:

Option 1 ("short"): guarantees a profit of 0.7 yuan per 1 yuan invested, paid after one year. So 1 yuan invested at the beginning of a year grows to 1.7 yuan at the end of that year, and the money can be reinvested in later years.

Option 2 ("long"): guarantees a profit of 2 yuan per 1 yuan invested, paid after two years; the investment time must be a multiple of two years, so within this 3-year horizon it can only be started at the beginning of Year 1 (matures end of Year 2) or at the beginning of Year 2 (matures end of Year 3). 1 yuan invested grows to 3 yuan at maturity.

Any money not invested is held idle (no interest) until the end of Year 3. All funds available at the beginning of a year may be split freely between the two options and idle cash.

Task: Formulate this as a linear (MILP) program with explicit decision variables, objective function and constraints, and state the optimal allocation and the optimal final wealth. Please write it out with equations, index sets, and explain the assumptions."}

{"description": "Please build a complete MILP for this investment problem and then solve/report the optimal solution.

PROBLEM DATA
- Initial wealth: W0 = 100,000 yuan, available at the beginning of Year 1 (time t = 0).
- Horizon: end of Year 3 (time t = 3). Money not invested is held idle with zero interest.
- Option 1 (call it the 1-year option): investing B yuan at time t yields profit 0.7*B after exactly one year (so B becomes 1.7*B at time t+1). It can be started at the beginning of any year t = 0, 1, 2.
- Option 2 (call it the 2-year option): investing B yuan at time t yields profit 2*B after exactly two years (so B becomes 3*B at time t+1+1). Its holding period must be a multiple of two years, so inside this 3-year horizon it can only be started at time t = 0 (matures at t = 2) or t = 1 (matures at t = 3). Starting it at t = 2 is infeasible because it would mature after the horizon.
- All funds available at a point in time may be split arbitrarily between the two options and idle cash. Proceeds of an investment become available exactly at its maturity date.
- Goal: maximize the total wealth (principal + profit) in hand at the end of Year 3.

SUGGESTED MODEL STRUCTURE (please refine, correct and complete it)

# Complete MILP Formulation and Solution

## 1. Corrected Model

### Sets and indices
- $T_1=\{1,2,3\}$ — beginnings of years in which the 1-year option may be started.
- $T_2=\{1,2\}$ — beginnings of years in which the 2-year option may be started (starting at year 3 would mature after the horizon).
- $T=\{1,2,3,4\}$ — cash states; $t=4$ is the end of year 3.

### Parameters
- $W_0 = 100{,}000$ (initial wealth, available at $t=1$).
- 1-year option: principal $B$ at $t$ becomes $1.7B$ at $t+1$ (profit $0.7B$).
- 2-year option: principal $B$ at $t$ becomes $3B$ at $t+2$ (profit $2B$).
- $M$ — big-M; a tight choice is $M=100{,}000$ for $t=1$ and $M=170{,}000$ for $t=2$ (the largest cash that can ever sit at $t=2$).

### Decision variables
| Variable | Meaning | Domain |
|---|---|---|
| $x_1[t]$ | yuan placed in the 1-year option at the beginning of year $t$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T_1$ |
| $x_2[t]$ | yuan placed in the 2-year option at the beginning of year $t$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T_2$ |
| $s[t]$   | idle cash at the beginning of year $t$ ($s[1]=W_0$, $s[4]$ = final idle cash) | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $t\in T$ |
| $y[t]$   | 1 if the 2-year option is started at the beginning of year $t$ | $\{0,1\}$, $t\in T_2$ |

### Objective
$$
\max\; W \;=\; s[4]\;+\;1.7\,x_1[3]\;+\;3\,x_2[2]
$$

### Constraints (cash-flow balance at the beginning of each year)

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\text{C1})\quad & x_1[1] + x_2[1] + s[2] = 100{,}000 &&\text{(begin year 1)}\\

(\text{C5})\quad & s[1] = 100{,}000 &&\text{(fixed initial cash)}
\end{aligned}
$$

1. Profits are deterministic and guaranteed; no risk, no liquidity premium.
